Persistent incrementality in Rust

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4188 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Github

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There is this cool idea: incremental computations.
  • Industry observers note that this concept usually works the best when you need to compute a lot of stuff, and there are a lot of inputs, and these inputs change independently with different degree of likelihood.
  • And if incremental computations concept applies well to compilers, it applies even better to LSP servers, because user makes edits in the editor much more often than they recompile code, and each keystroke must change the editor state in milliseconds (unless you go full vibe and don't need an IDE anymore, that is).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There is this cool idea: incremental computations. The concept is simple, if you calculated something and then inputs change, it doesn't have to mean that you need to recompute everything. Most of your computations might still be valid, and quite often it is the case that you only need to redo a small chunk of changes.

Industry observers note that this concept usually works the best when you need to compute a lot of stuff, and there are a lot of inputs, and these inputs change independently with different degree of likelihood. Probably, the most common example is incremental compilation, which makes the compilation reuse as much work as possible, making iterations during development much faster. The interesting part is "iterating": note that incremental compilation doesn't necessarily makes cold builds faster. The compiler performance might be roughly the same with and without incrementality, it's just repeated reuse of compiler artifacts becomes more efficient. Most likely you've heard of it. And if you did, you probably know that incremental compilation is not easy (1, 2, 3). But it's cool!

And if incremental computations concept applies well to compilers, it applies even better to LSP servers, because user makes edits in the editor much more often than they recompile code, and each keystroke must change the editor state in milliseconds (unless you go full vibe and don't need an IDE anymore, that is).

Industry observers note that it could be somewhat related to the fact that rust-analyzer uses salsa as the central part of its architecture. Salsa is a library that makes incremental computations very convenient and efficient. There is one drawback, though. It is mainly designed to work in memory. And we'll touch on how it works in a bit.

For project like Rust Glancer that tries to keep the memory usage as low as possible, this doesn't work. Because of that, for a long time Rust Glancer didn't use incremental computations, and instead had a sophisticated network of persistent caches with sharding and targeted optimizations to make computations efficient. And it worked, for a while. But this approach doesn't scale very well: if you need to maintain a manually implemented custom cache format, optimize it, and tie computations to it, then the more efficiency you seek, the more complexity you get. Basically, the complexity is "quadratic": it grows as O(computations_complexity * cache_implementation_complexity) because both are interconnected (sorry, CS purists, for this crime).

In a recent development, so... Rust Glancer got to a point where it would really benefit from persistent incremental computations. And the search for it turned out to be really interesting, so in this blog post we'll be discussing how incremental computations can work in memory and how to make this approach work with persistency.

Before we start discussing how incremental computations work under the hood, let's see how it looks like.

If you know how to use Salsa feel free to jump to the next section. If you're familiar with red-green algorithm and in-memory approach that Salsa uses, you can skip to where persistency starts.

Recent findings suggest that now, incremental computations are somewhat tricky to explain in a blog post, because the value of it requires an application to be somewhat big. So we will need an example that is big enough to show the value of incrementality, but small enough to discuss here. It's a bit absurd, but I hope you can focus on the idea, not on the value of the snippet at hand.

Let's imagine that we're doing a weird text processor that would count the words in all the files in the directory, and decide whether this count is funny. And to make things more interesting, the files can include other files.

According to recent reports, how would that look if implemented naively? Something like that, most likely (well, let's ignore the IO):.

the output will also have no surprises:.

It has been revealed that now, let's try Salsa. It should let us make some computations reusable. Here's how it would look like:.

Sources indicate that the code looks pretty similar! However, let's inspect the output.

The first call matches the naive example:.

But the second call is different!

Note: not only we did not call word_count(a), we did not call is_haha_number as well!

Recent findings suggest that salsa can see that file b changed, and it re-run word_count for it. But the output did not change, so all the previous computations are valid: nothing to be run.

The third output is interesting too:.

It has been revealed that the word count in b changed, and a includes b, so we need to re-run all three queries. But the order is inversed! This is because we have a dependency graph internally, and we're walking through the dependency tree and re-execute changed queries from the "leaves" to the "root".

In a recent development, we have changed b from 65 to 67 words, so a now has 69 words. Result is still true, but we did have to patch the computations. If we would've had another query that depended on is_haha_number, that's where validation would've stopped and all the queries above wouldn't need to run.

And the final output is interesting too:.

We have changed dependencies of a, so there is no b anymore. So we start with what we know: word_count for a. It now has a not-yet-tracked dependency on c, so we go to c after a. And the rest is the same.

Recent findings suggest that so I hope you get the idea now: each query result is memorized, and if we discover that the output of this query did not change, we don't need to recompute the queries that depend on this input. Or rather, if all the queries that query X depends on did not change, then query X does not need to be recomputed.

And now imagine that you have 700 dependencies in your workspace. A single file changed in the topmost dependency. 699 dependencies can keep their result! Within a single crate, still only one file has changed, so the information about all the other files at least partially stays the same. We only need to redo the computations that actually matter.

And most importantly, we don't need to write any of this tracking code ourselves, Salsa gives it to us for free.

Well, it's really not trivial. If you want to have a more formal deep dive, I suggest the following reads:.

Sources indicate that imagine that each query, combined with its arguments, is an object. This object can have a bunch of metadata, stating whether it was already computed, when it happened, what was the output, and what's the object dependencies. Let's call this metadata a "memo".

According to recent reports, side note: why is "combined with its arguments?" vital? Because we cannot memoize is_haha_number, but we can memoize is_haha_number(420), so you can think of it as a mapping of (function, arguments) -> output.

And imagine that you have inputs: something that user provides, and this something can be explicitly requested by a query.

We might also say that the database has a revision, initially 1. When you change some input, the revision gets bumped to 2, and so on. This revision can be used as "when it happened" (or rather, "when it change last time") inside of the memo.

Now, we've provided our inputs and invoke a query. It has some associated code that can internally do two things:.

In a recent development, if query requests an input, it should record that it depends on this input. So if input changes, it must be recomputed.

Industry observers note that if query requests another query, we might check if the corresponding query has a memo with a computed value. If it has, we need to make sure that it is valid for the revision we're at. If it is: great! It can be reused, and we don't need to recompute it. Otherwise, we need to recursively go into this query. Obviously, we also record a dependency on this query.

It has been revealed that during the execution, we'll collect all the inputs and all the dependency queries, and ultimately we'll finally compute the result of our query. And when we do, we can fill out the memo: record the revision and the output.

Recent findings suggest that and... done! Next time you request an output, we will look at this query object memo. If inputs did not change, we can just hand out the result. If they changed, we go down the query line, and do the same thing. So naturally only the things that actually might have changed will be recomputed.

Sources indicate that oh, but there is one more notable detail here, that makes everything even better. If revision changed, it does not automatically mean that we need to recompute this query. We might recompute dependencies, and compare them to the old values. If all the outputs are the equal to the old ones (imagine that word_count(a) changed from 67 to 69, but is_haha_number still returns true true: the query that depends on is_haha_number might not get invalidated), we can just mark the current version as verified and return the old result. And it can matter a lot when the expensive query has a lot of cheap dependencies.

Obviously, it's an overly simplified explanation. In practice, there are many, many caveats, tricky parts, and optimizations that make the experience work well. But my job here is to give you an idea; if you've become interested in the topic, I'd recommend looking to Salsa source code, it's very interesting.

And Salsa is awesome! With one caveat. It works in memory only. Well, there is ongoing work on persistency there, but AFAIU it is mostly focused on storing the computations on filesystem so that they can be reloaded later (snapshot-like). It is very valuable, but we still have to store stuff in the memory. For the project like Rust Glancer we want to offload stuff to occupy less RAM.

And in practice, there are several projects that do implement various kinds of persistence:.

So there are solutions for this problem, but none of them seem to be "Salsa but everything is on the filesystem".

I guess then it would be fine to build one?

As you probably guessed, I did build one. And I called it Ajika. And I'm very proud of myself for coming up with this name, yes.

Recent findings suggest that the library is here, it uses stable Rust, and is generally a complete project (but I'm working on improvements!). The post, however, is not meant to promote it; obviously it's a very young library, and while so far it works really well for me, probably sticking to Salsa if it works for you is a safe choice. Not gonna sell it, do your own research :).

What I want to share is how Ajika works under the hood and what makes it different from Salsa.

But (spoiler) in general it's just two things:.

And we'll get to it and see how it works, but to make everything clear, we'll need to start from something very basic.

Here's the same program we had for Salsa, but migrated to Ajika:.

It looks pretty similar, with API changes mostly being a taste difference, and on a first run it has the same output.

However, the key part here is that we can add the following to the end:.

According to recent reports, and print_result will just print False. Nothing will be executed after restart! Persistency in action!

On a serious note, the main difference is the focus. When you start working on a project like that, choosing your priority can influence the design a lot. And the choice made here is being persistent-first. While Ajika provides an in-memory backend, it's mostly meant for tests. The intended use case is to use your disk.

And it starts with a very basic question that in-memory database does not have: what happens if I restart the application?

If you already have a cache locally, many things can make this cache invalid:.

And similarly, given that we cache computations, it's basically an optimization. If cache gets corrupted or removed while the application is running, user would most likely prefer the cache to be discarded and computations to be repeated one more time, rather than the app crashing with "cache is not available, what do I do???".

Sources indicate that as a result, the cache must be throw-away. Both Ajika and application supply schema versions to identify the revision, and if the stored cache doesn't match it, we reset it. If cache gets corrupted, Ajika will attempt recovery over hard failing, even if it means re-computing data from scratch.

It has been revealed that the next most noticeable change is that most operations are fallible. Since IO is the basic property for us, and IO can fail, we need to think about it. Failed operation does not mean that cache is corrupted, but it does mean that the current query might not be computed. Typically, it can be retried, though.

According to recent reports, finally, the persistence is, unfortunately, a leaky abstraction. You cannot really hide from the fact that the data is outside of memory, because everything you persist must be serializable. And your interim query data might be reusable but not serializable (imagine an AST that borrows the source text: making it own the data likely will be worse), so some of the queries might be transient: we compute them once and retain while the current operation runs, but drop instead of persisting once operation ends.

Together, these properties start working rather nicely, however: your application has to be aware of persistence, but not in an annoying way. If something fails, you know about it, but you don't have to worry, since Ajika will repair things for you. If something is not serializable and it doesn't matter, it can be turned into a transient query. If you don't want your tests to rely on persistence, you just plug a memory backend in.

So let's take a look at how it works under the hood.

Industry observers note that LLM usage disclaimer: The library discussed here is developed with use of LLMs, same as Rust Glancer. Hopefully, from this post it is evident that I'm using LLMs as a tool and have full control. It's not vibe coded.

There are three parts to Ajika: ajika itself, ajika_macros, and ajika_storage.

In a recent development, we'll take a look at ajika and then at ajika_storage. Macros are left as an exercise to a reader, but they're generally pretty straightforward.

Ajika itself is very easy, just check out this diagram:.

...just kidding. But we'll fix that very rapidly.

The core idea is very similar to Salsa:.

Still, I think it might be useful to skim through the high level details.

In a recent development, side note: Ajika has its own book which does a much deeper dive on many concepts than this blog post. I'll be referring to it in some places. The con is that, unlike this handwritten blog post, the text there is mostly LLM-generated, and even if I did a lot of polishing, it reveals. Eventually I'll do a full manual rewrite, but for now I figured that human-filtered-llm-guide is better than no guide at all.

Database is an entrypoint. You choose either an in-memory or persistent backend, supply Inputs and then run your operation.

It has been revealed that queries are the actual logic we want to execute. They are defined via ajika::query macro and in general pretty straightforward. More details on queries themselves are in the book, and we'll look at how queries are executed and what this Db object is a bit later in this post.

It has been revealed that inputs are somewhat more interesting. Your input type is defined through the ajika::input procedural macro, which would do some wrapping for you. And your input structure is basically a mapping: you specify a key, for example, String, and then you can use database to get an input value (or lack thereof) for whatever key you have, be it "foo" or even "bar". If you have a singleton value, like a config, you can use () as a key. Again, more on inputs can be found in the book, also might check out lazy inputs.

Outputs are probably the first part of the system that gets interesting because of persistence.

According to recent reports, the outputs need to be stored on the filesystem, so they need to be serializable. For outputs that you don't want to serialize, you can use transient queries which will keep the value in memory only for the duration of a single operation. But even then, there is a problem: how significant of an output do you want?

According to recent reports, if you will have a 1000 very granular queries, it will mean that we need a lot of filesystem roundtrips. If you will have just a bunch of queries that compute a ton of data, you will need to deserialize a big value just to look at the part of it.

It has been revealed that thus, outputs offer a solution that lies in between: you can choose to return a value directly, or return a handle to this value. If you return a handle, query can use this handle to retrieve the value from the database on demand. Directly returned values are fully deserialized. This offers you a nice granularity option: you have a query that encapsulates a meaningful unit of work, but it returns you an object that contains handles for particular results. Handle is cheap to obtain and deserialize, and you only query the data you actually need. Doing is most convenient through an ajika::output macro.

As usual, more details on how to use outputs are in the book.

And now we're getting to the interesting stuff.

To perform a single run we need three things:.

And there are two related concepts that make things work:.

Record contains information like values metadata for a query and dependencies for it (note: values are stored separately!). Thus, Memos are released on the end of the run and then later can be reconstructed from Record on demand.

And this is an important bit: released memos don't occupy RAM. This is the key part of Ajika! During the query execution, the values can be loaded, but if you don't run any operations, you don't have to pay for it. Outputs will just wait for you inside of the filesystem! Moreover, whenever we run queries, we only load what we need, not everything.

Each time a query logic actually runs (either from run or from another query), a fresh Db with a new Frame is created, sharing the same Operation.

When you ask Db to execute a query, here's a typical (overly simplified) workflow:.

And if during execution query receives another query result, it records it in its own Frame for reuse.

Obviously, there is a lot of bookkeeping, support for parallelism, and other things that make it complex, but in general the algorithm is pretty straightforward.

Sources indicate that once the operation finishes, we need to actually apply the changes. run works as a transaction, so everything that was done inside is immediately visible, but after run depending on whether run failed or succeeded, the results will either be discarded or persisted.

Checkpoint write is generally pretty straightforward:.

So checkpoint on the Ajika level is pretty straightforward. What is more interesting is how Ajika storage works in general.

Finally, we've got to the persistence!

It has been revealed that it's probably the most interesting part of Ajika. How do we store data in a way that is efficient?

According to recent reports, the first version of Ajika used redb for everything. It worked, but it did not work very well. Since we don't really have a "database" per se, and more of a storage for many blobs, redb added too much overhead. However, it provides much needed features like transactions.

So, Ajika uses redb as a metadata storage: it's an index which mostly contains pointers to the values.

The values are written in "pack files": basically, just binary files to which we can append newly introduced entries. And inside of redb we can just store a pointer: (file name, offset). Each stored entry has a header with information such as length and compression algorithm. For efficiency, if the value is very small, we can keep it inline inside of redb instead of writing it to a file.

Recent findings suggest that if you want to access a value, you will go to redb, check the corresponding key, and then either read it inline or read the specified pack at the specified access. Pretty simple.

Obviously, there is some more data stored there (we'll talk about identities soon, briefly), but in general it's a pretty "stupid" (hopefully in a good way) format of data storage.

Recent findings suggest that however, there is one caveat: if we do it naively, the storage can grow without limits. Packs can end up with very low utilization factor, consisting mostly of "dead" values, and some of them might not be observable at all. So the storage supports maintenance: whenever you do an operation, Ajika might do a sweep that would re-pack values and patch pointers, and at the end of operation Ajika will try to signal to the storage which values can be removed now. There are a few knobs you can tune here: you can specify the retention limit time (so that the very old and unused queries are cleaned up) or target storage size (which acts as a soft limit, and will affect the cleanup policy).

But ultimately, this design makes value storing and retrieval pretty efficient, and it integrates with the overall Ajika design very well.

Recent findings suggest that OK, we're almost done, I promise! The last small bit: interning.

Interning values is an optimization that gives you a way to turn any object into an ID. Imagine that you have file paths. They can work as IDs, but it would probably be more efficient if you used FileId(0) / FileId(1) instead. Not only in terms of performance, but often also in terms of memory: you'd rather not have a ton of strings in memory if you don't really need them. Sometimes, interning strings on its own can be a very useful memory optimization, which is why crates like string_cache exist.

But for us, having IDs for objects can be valuable in general, because your computations results might often be linked to some other objects, and it's useful to be able to use IDs for that.

In a recent development, salsa supports interning for that purpose, and Ajika does it too. However, there is one caveat for Ajika: what happens if we have our IDs allocated, they become a part of the cache, and then we restart the application?

To avoid this problem, IDs in Ajika are persisted in addition to being stored in memory, and on restart this interner state is reloaded.

According to recent reports, ajika development itself was an experiment: I did not create it in vacuum, I was actually porting Rust Glancer to it at the same time. And the experiment was very successful. I was able to remove a lot of complexity from Rust Glancer, and Ajika unblocked many optimizations that were not realistic with hand-rolled caches (starting with lazy body evaluation).

At the end of the experiment, Rust Glancer got performance comparable to rust-analyzer (sometimes even better!). Ajika is obviously slower than salsa, but inside of IDE the difference between 1 and 30ms is negligible, both feel instant. What matters is the low RAM usage: Rust Glancer still stays well under 100MB RAM idle on pretty major projects.

Remark: exact comparison between two will be posted in the release notes for Rust Glancer 0.5.0, so stay tuned.

As the experiments go, the branch of Rust Glancer where all of that happened is in a half-assembled state, and it's way too rushed and "prototyped" to just merge it, so I'm doing a clean reimplementation using extracted (and published) version of Ajika. It will take a while, but I'm very excited: Rust Glancer without compromises that feels instant and does not eat memory.

Thanks for reading, it turned out to be a long post. A lot of effort went into it, so I hope that it was useful, at least somewhat.

My next goal is to prepare an Ajika-based release of Rust Glancer, and after that I have a lot of ideas on how to make Ajika even faster/better/stronger. Who knows, maybe it will eventually grow into a product of its own, not merely a part of Rust Glancer ecosystem.

As usual, the best way to support if you like the project is to check out Rust Glancer, star Ajika (but only if you like it!) and/or follow me on twitter.

US let Nvidia and AMD sell bucketloads of chips to military-linked Chinese companies

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Not many of the deals went through, but Chinese clouds no longer care about importing GPUs.
  • The US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) allowed Nvidia and AMD to sell hundreds of thousands of advanced GPUs to entities that the Department of War classifies as “Chinese military companies” that help Beijing to build its military.
  • That news comes courtesy of Brian Mast (R-FL), chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, who asked BIS to provide information about NVIDIA’s and AMD’s applications for the export licenses required to sell advanced AI chips to China.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Not many of the deals went through, but Chinese clouds no longer care about importing GPUs.

The US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) allowed Nvidia and AMD to sell hundreds of thousands of advanced GPUs to entities that the Department of War classifies as “Chinese military companies” that help Beijing to build its military.

That news comes courtesy of Brian Mast (R-FL), chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, who asked BIS to provide information about NVIDIA’s and AMD’s applications for the export licenses required to sell advanced AI chips to China.

The congressman on Thursday revealed requests to sell 3.4 million AI chips to China, and that BIS approved the sale of 879,000 items.

BIS refused to authorize some giant deals for Nvidia, which applied to sell 610,000 chips to Alibaba and 508,000 to TikTok owner Bytedance.

But the agency allowed many other sales, including to Alibaba and Tencent.

Mast points out that both of those companies are on the Department of War’s List of Chinese Military Companies, the designation it uses for entities deemed to be a “military-civil fusion contributor to the Chinese defense industrial base.” That’s a polite way of saying that Washington thinks China relies on these companies to operate and improve its military, and therefore to challenge America’s national security.

Advanced chips are essential when designing nuclear weapons, stealthy submarines, or advanced aircraft.

Those applications are the core reason the US bans exports of advanced GPUs to China, so that the People’s Liberation Army can’t develop advanced weapons.

The congressman also claims that some of Nvidia’s applications were attempts to sell its wares to “chip-smuggling fronts to facilitate their sales of advanced AI chips to Chinese companies.” The Upcoming York Times reports that some of those front entities are linked to Megaspeed, the outfit fronted by suspected Chinese intelligence asset Alice Huang, whose intimate relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was a key factor in his resignation.

Megaspeed is accused of what the US calls “diversion” – claiming to buy chips for one reason while intending to either ship them to China or rent them exclusively to Chinese companies in ways that breach the spirit of export restrictions if not the letter of the law.

One of the documents Mast shared says “Every Nvidia and AMD application stated that the proposed transfer posed a ‘low’ risk of diversion.”.

Mast’s point therefore appears to be that the BIS has authorized sales that go against the clear intent of established policy, and the national interest, and that Nvidia and AMD may have been a little too optimistic in their assessment of diversion risk.

Earlier this week, Washington adopted a upcoming policy that outlaws allowing remote access to advanced AI chips, in the hope it would stop diversion and dent China’s AI ambitions.

Two Chinese tech giants, Tencent and Alibaba, have signaled the policy had immediate impact.

Chinese web giant Tencent on Wednesday stated that newly introduced ban will reduce the quantity of advanced compute capacity available to the company and mean its efforts to train models will slow.

Alibaba offered similar sentiments on Thursday. Speaking on the firm’s earnings call, CEO Eddie Wu said the new policy “will definitely have some impact on the long-term construction of Alibaba Cloud's data centers both domestically and globally.”.

“Based on our initial assessment, the long-term target of 20 gigawatts may be lowered, which will also lead to a reduction in our overall capital expenditure plan,” he noted.

But both Tencent and Alibaba don’t see the new policy as creating long-term problems, because both companies believe Chinese chipmakers will be making advanced AI hardware at scale in 2027 or 2028.

Alibaba’s Wu predicted his tech giant “will go through a phase of the largest investment in AI infrastructure” once Chinese chipmakers get up to speed.

Once that happens, Nvidia and AMD may not even be able to sell chips to China through backdoors.

And for what it’s worth, even after the two sultans of silicon went through the front door by asking BIS for permission, many of the approved orders never resulted in shipments.

That’s likely because Beijing needs to approve imports and chose not to do so while its own chipmakers develop improved products. ®.

Bringing Nunchaku 4-bit Diffusion Inference to Diffusers

📅 23 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1605 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Large diffusion transformers can create stunning images (or even videos, audio snippets, and now text), but loading a modern text-to-image model in BF16 precision often requires 20-30 GB of VRAM, which puts these models out of reach of most consumer GPUs.
  • Sources indicate that most of these backends are weight-only.
  • SVDQuant, the quantization method behind the popular Nunchaku inference engine, takes a different approach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Large diffusion transformers can create stunning images (or even videos, audio snippets, and now text), but loading a modern text-to-image model in BF16 precision often requires 20-30 GB of VRAM, which puts these models out of reach of most consumer GPUs. Quantization is a powerful solution to this problem, and Diffusers already integrates several quantization backends such as bitsandbytes, GGUF, torchao, and Quanto, which we covered in Exploring Quantization Backends in Diffusers.

Sources indicate that most of these backends are weight-only. This means that they store the weights in low precision and dequantize them back to high precision at compute time. This reduces memory usage significantly, but it usually does not make inference faster, and can even add a small latency overhead.

SVDQuant, the quantization method behind the popular Nunchaku inference engine, takes a different approach. It runs the main transformer layers with 4-bit weights and activations (W4A4), reducing memory while also speeding up the denoising loop. The details are covered below, but until now, using these checkpoints required a separate inference library.

Industry observers note that with current Diffusers, loading a Nunchaku checkpoint is as simple as calling from_pretrained(), with no local CUDA compilation required thanks to the kernels package. In addition, the companion diffuse-compressor toolkit lets you quantize fresh architectures yourself and publish them as regular Diffusers repositories.

It has been revealed that first, install the requirements. You need a recent version of Diffusers and the Hugging Face kernels package:.

Then load a pre-quantized pipeline like any other Diffusers model:.

No custom pipeline class or separate inference engine is needed, and there is nothing to compile locally. The NVFP4 kernels are downloaded from the Hub through the Nunchaku Lite kernels page the first time they are used. This checkpoint pairs a Nunchaku NVFP4 transformer with a bitsandbytes NF4 text encoder, and generates a 1024x1024 image in about 1.7 seconds on an RTX 5090 with a peak memory usage of about 12 GB, compared with about 24 GB for the BF16 pipeline. You can find more details about the Nunchaku Lite checkpoint format in the official Diffusers documentation.

NVFP4 checkpoints require an NVIDIA Blackwell GPU (RTX 50 series, RTX PRO 6000, B200). For earlier generations, use the INT4 variants. See the hardware support table below for details.

According to recent reports, SVDQuant is the quantization method behind Nunchaku, its reference CUDA inference engine. Standard 4-bit quantization is difficult for diffusion transformers because both weights and activations contain large outliers. SVDQuant handles this by moving activation outliers into the weights, representing the hardest part of each weight matrix with a small 16-bit low-rank branch, and quantizing the remaining residual to 4 bits. Nunchaku makes this fast with fused kernels for the 4-bit path and the low-rank branch.

According to recent reports, the original Nunchaku engine gets much of its speed from model-specific fused execution paths, such as fused QKV projections and fused GELU/MLP kernels. Those optimizations are tied to each architecture's module layout and checkpoint format, so supporting a fresh model family usually requires model-specific integration work.

Nunchaku Lite is the newly introduced integration path in Diffusers. With it, Diffusers can load Nunchaku-style checkpoints without a custom pipeline or a separate inference engine. Under the hood, Nunchaku Lite patches the relevant nn.Linear modules of a stock Diffusers model with runtime SVDQ/AWQ linear layers before the checkpoint is loaded. The CUDA kernels come from the Hub through the kernels package. Two kernel families are used:.

Recent findings suggest that the trade-off is that, without architecture-specific fused kernels and modules, Nunchaku Lite cannot match the speedup of the original Nunchaku engine. However, the bare-bones implementation still delivers around 30% speedup while retaining the same level of VRAM reduction.

If you have used bitsandbytes or torchao in Diffusers, the mechanics will feel familiar. A Nunchaku Lite model repository is an ordinary Diffusers repository. The only special part is a quantization_config block inside the transformer's config.json:.

This config tells Diffusers which modules were quantized, which scheme they use, and which Nunchaku Lite runtime layer to instantiate (SVDQW4A4Linear or AWQW4A16Linear).

Because the quantized model keeps the exact module structure of the dense one, everything downstream (schedulers, LoRA loading hooks, offloading, torch.compile) sees a normal Diffusers model.

Nunchaku Lite uses different kernel variants depending on the GPU generation and checkpoint precision:.

Volta and Hopper GPUs are right now not supported by the 4-bit kernels. The quantizer validates the GPU's CUDA capability at load time and raises a clear error instead of producing incorrect outputs.

Nunchaku Lite can be combined with other Diffusers memory and speed optimizations.

torch.compile. Compiling the transformer improves the end-to-end speedup from 1.35x to 1.8x:.

Industry observers note that quantized text encoders. The transformer is not the only component with a large memory footprint. Text encoders such as T5 or Qwen3 can occupy several gigabytes on their own. Further quantizing the text encoder with bitsandbytes NF4 reduces peak VRAM by about 22% in our benchmark.

In a recent development, offloading. Diffusers offloading helpers such as enable_model_cpu_offload() and enable_sequential_cpu_offload() work as usual if you need to fit the pipeline onto a smaller GPU.

All numbers below were measured on an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 (Blackwell) at 1024x1024 using rootonchair/ERNIE-Image-Turbo-nunchaku-lite-int4-bnb4-text-encoder.

Sources indicate that as shown above, Nunchaku reduces peak VRAM by up to 50% while still improving latency by roughly 30%. The remaining overhead comes largely from extra kernel rolls out, which torch.compile can mitigate, bringing the full pipeline down to 1.68 s, or 1.8x faster than the BF16 baseline.

Nunchaku Lite support in Diffusers is architecture-agnostic, and the diffuse-compressor toolkit provides an end-to-end SVDQuant workflow for Diffusers models: calibrate, quantize, package, and publish.

Below, we walk through quantizing FLUX.2 Klein 4B as an example. It covers the main steps: inspect the model, calibrate and quantize the transformer, package the result as a Diffusers pipeline, then verify and push it to the Hub. The full tutorial covers every flag in detail.

The generic scanner walks the model and decides what to target: compatible linears inside the repeated transformer-block stack become SVDQ W4A4 targets, recognized modulation linears become AWQ W4A16 targets, and everything else stays dense.

In a recent development, always read this report before quantizing. For FLUX.2 Klein 4B, the expected result is 100 SVDQ targets, 3 AWQ targets, and 6 dense outer linears, with no missing patterns or duplicate names.

The following command runs SVDQuant on the transformer and writes the quantized checkpoint to outputs/checkpoints/svdq-int4_r32-flux-2-klein-4b.safetensors:.

Replace --precision int4 with nvfp4 to build Blackwell-native weights.

The converter combines the quantized transformer with the base pipeline's other components, writes the compact nunchaku_lite configuration into transformer/config.json, and can optionally convert text encoders to NF4:.

Once the outputs look good, run pipe.push_to_hub("your-name/your-model-nunchaku-lite-int4"). Other users can then load it with the same from_pretrained() pattern shown above.

Industry observers note that note that the generic path assumes the architecture can be quantized without structural rewrites. For additional speedup, the original Nunchaku engine rewrites groups of Diffusers layers as fused modules. The generic path cannot infer these changes on its own, such as combining separate Q, K, and V projections into one module or splitting a fused projection across several modules.

FLUX.1-dev's QKV projection is a concrete example. Diffusers defines three separate modules:.

The Nunchaku FLUX module combines those layers into one quantized to_qkv module:.

This grouped module is required because Nunchaku's fused operator consumes the QKV projection, Q/K normalization, and rotary embeddings together. By comparison, the default Diffusers path executes them separately:.

The Nunchaku path supplies the grouped projection, normalization modules, and rotary embeddings to one fused operator:.

Recent findings suggest that this is the structural rewrite that the generic path cannot infer. Diffusers has three destination modules with to_q, to_k, and to_v parameter prefixes, while Nunchaku has one grouped module under to_qkv. A model-specific target config or adapter must state that the Q, K, and V parameters should be concatenated along the output dimension, in that order, and loaded into to_qkv.

According to recent reports, structural rewrites like these are described by a model-specific target config during quantization and handled by a small runtime adapter when the checkpoint is loaded. The FLUX.2 Klein 4B quantization script provides a concrete target-config example for producing a structurally rewritten checkpoint, while rootonchair/nunchaku-lite provides the runtime adapters needed to load grouped QKV tensors, split fused projections, and other fused operations. For the complete workflow, you can check the Adding A New Model guide.

To get started right away, check out the following repositories:.

Sources indicate that nunchaku's SVDQuant kernels are one of the most effective ways to run diffusion transformers efficiently on consumer hardware, and they are now natively supported in Diffusers. Pre-quantized checkpoints load with from_pretrained(), and the diffuse-compressor toolkit makes it possible to quantize new architectures without waiting for engine support. By quantizing both weights and activations, the W4A4 path lowers memory use while improving denoising latency, keeping image quality close to the BF16 original.

If you quantize and publish a new model, we would love to hear about it. Share it on the Hub and let us know! If you have any questions about this feature, feel free to join our Discord.

To learn more, check out the following resources:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Put a web server online and everyone starts trying to hack it. Why? A basic rule of economics. Short supply, major demand - there arenât enough web servers for everyone. Letâs run a web server for every human on the planet, all 8 billion of them. I couldnât get funding, so weâre bootstrapping. The goal is to run 15 million web servers on one VM with 10GB of RAM and 1 CPU core. If we succeed, Iâll find some RAM from old microwaves around the house and weâll scale it up so everyone can have their own web server. Demand will drop to zero and cybersecurity will be solved once and for all.Web serverInstead of vibe coding it all, letâs use an ancient technique called learning. First of all, what is a web server? There are a few essential syscalls.listen - syscall, asks kernel to listen for connections on a socketaccept - syscall, accepts a connection on a socketrecv - receives data from a socketsend - sends dataclose - closesWhat is a syscall? A function that is executed by the OS kernel. Whatever fancy language or library you use for HTTP, it all comes down to those syscalls (well, yes, but actually no). Letâs use C to make it all explicit. We start listening, then read from the socket in a loop and always reply with OK.int main(void) { // We use port 0 which makes OS return any available port int server = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0); if (listen(server, 128) < 0) return 1; const char reply[] = "HTTP/1.0 200 OK\r\nContent-Length: 2\r\n\r\nOK"; for (int client; (client = accept(server, NULL, NULL)) >= 0;) { if (recv(client, NULL, 4096, MSG_TRUNC) > 0) send(client, reply, sizeof reply - 1, MSG_NOSIGNAL); close(client); } }It couldnât be simpler: listen on a socket, accept a connection, read the data, send a reply, close the client connection, and repeat. It gives us around 65k RPS. Now that weâve learned everything, letâs finish the article and call it a day:$ for i in $(seq 1 15_000_000); do echo $i; ./server &; done ... ... 28232 program exited with error 1Hm, why did listen fail? Ah, weâve run out of ports! Weâre using port=0, so the kernel picks an available port from ip_local_port_range.$ sysctl net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range = 32768 60999Why are so many ports skipped? Historically, port 0 was created for outbound connections. When you call connect('example.com', 80), Linux connects to the remote server (the sending part) and then allocates a random port on the host from ip_local_port_range to receive data (the receiving part). There are a few reasons the default range is small.Port 0 is special. You cannot listen on it (actually, you can - https://acid.vegas/blog/the-port-that-does-not-exist/).Ports 1-1024 require root.Ports 1024-32768 are skipped to keep dynamically allocated ports from conflicting with existing apps. You donât want to call connect('example.com') and end up allocating port 3306 to receive incoming data. mysql cannot start because you have example.com open in your Firefox would make for a confusing UX.Ports 60999 - 65535 are excluded for historical reasons dating back to IP Masquerading.Nothing prevents us from overriding the range and using 1-65535, but thatâs still a bit short of 15 million. A UDP server and a TCP server can use the same port, so we can double that to 128k. We could run a proxy in front to forward requests to the right process (virtual hosting, yay), but these are all ancient techniques - in the AI era, whenever you have a software problem, you just throw money at the hardware. Letâs simply connect 15M/32k=450 upcoming network cards to the server.The 65k limit comes from the TCP standard. A port is a u16, so even if we hack the kernel with find '*.c' -exec sed -i 's/u16/u32/' \; to support bigger port numbers, normal clients still wouldnât be able to connect. Each listening server is identified by a (protocol, IP, port) tuple. That explains how we can use the same port for UDP and TCP. It also means we can use a bunch of different IPs for our web servers. If we connect 450 network cards to the server, weâll get 450 unique IP addresses and be able to listen on 15 million unique addresses!UPD. Iâve heard from readers that the network card is the ONLY hardware component that didnât get 100 times more expensive in the last year. Canât we avoid ruining that too and solve this in software?Letâs use a beautiful technology called AnyIP, which lets us listen on a whole subnet. Many VPS and dedicated server providers routinely give you a whole TCPv6 subnet. We can simply run sudo ip -6 route add local 2001:db8:1234:5678::/64 dev lo to get 18 quintillion addresses (plus or minus one) to listen on. You can do the same for IPv4 - acquiring a subnet with 15M addresses would cost around $250 million, so adjust the command for your environment. Weâll change our server to pick the nth IP from our range:// Read IP index from CLI, shift base IP by it int i = read_cli_param(argv[1]); const uint32_t base_ip = 0x0a400001; // ex. 10.64.0.1 addr.sin_addr.s_addr = htonl(first_ip + i); // shift, ex. 10.64.0.2And now we can finally finish the article.$ for i in $(seq 1 15_000_000); do echo $i; ./server $i &; done ... ... Out of memoryHm, one server consumes 1.5MB of RAM, so running that many would takeâ¦ 20TB of RAM, which is a few bytes more than our 10GB budget.RuntimeBy pure coincidence (what are the odds?), I explained in Running 10 million Codex CLIs on one server - LFI processes why running millions of processes creates too much overhead. The answer is to run them all in one process inside a custom runtime, much as V8 can run millions of guests in a single process. In Userland Linux scheduler in Rust, I indicated how to build a specialised userland scheduler and switch between tasks with the absolute minimum amount of RAM per task.TLDR: Weâre using LFI for sandboxing. It gives us memory isolation and replaces all syscalls with calls to our host handler, which lets us implement I/O however we like. To schedule multiple guests, we load them all into our main processâs memory and make the CPU constantly switch between guests - we become our own micro OS.Since we need to save every byte and CPU cycle we can, weâre doomed to build another specialised runtime. Letâs get started. How much is 10GB divided by 15M, exactly?Ten Great Britains divided by 15 million gives around half of kilo britain. Not much. If we run all our guests in our runtime, our custom scheduler needs to switch between them. Whatâs the absolute minimum state we need to preserve for each guest? We can ignore server initialisation and assume switches only happen within the main loop. Letâs take another look at the loop.for (int client; (client = accept(server, NULL, NULL)) >= 0;) { if (recv(client, NULL, 4096, MSG_TRUNC) > 0) send(client, reply, sizeof reply - 1, MSG_NOSIGNAL); close(client); }This code has only two state variables, server and client. Both are simple file descriptors. If our scheduler had to suspend a guest at any syscall point in this loop, weâd need to save the following state:struct Context { pc: u64, // Instruction address to return to fd_server: i32, // server file descriptor fd_client: i32, // client file descriptor }We only need 16 bytes per guest, so to run 15M guests in our runtime and be able to suspend them and switch between them, we would need 220MB of RAM. Weâre playing it safe here - we donât need the full u64 or i32, and with bit packing, we could probably get down to 8 bytes per guest. What else do we need?$ codex "How much TCP connection takes?" Idle connection takes zero, while active connection consumes around 5kbHereâs what we get if we assume that only 1M of connections are active at any given moment.14M idle connections - 0 bytesScheduling state for 15M guests - 220MB1M active connections at 5kb each = 5GBOnly half of our RAM budget, yay! I donât often exceed my own expectations. Letâs validate it:int main(void) { // Run 14M of idle connections - just listen and do nothing // SHOULD CONSUMER ZERO MEMORY! for (int i = 0; i < 14_000_000; i++) { int server = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0); listen(server, 1) } }$ ./run_15m_idle_servers Out Of Memory $ dmesg | tail -n 1 'SHOULD CONSUMER ZERO MEMORY' - what are you, stupid?Looks like the kernel still has some leftover comments from Linus. Iâm not stupid, but I have to admit I was below average here. While an LLM is a significant boost for learning, itâs too easy to accept its answers without thinking critically and feel ashamed later on. But hey, embarrassment is a cost of entry - letâs dive into networking in the kernel.Networking in the kernelRemember when I noted that our simple server uses only 5 syscalls? I missed one that was right in front of me. Let me highlight it:int main(void) { for (int i = 0; i < 10_000_000; ++i) { socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0); } }That code will OOM in a 10GB VM. The socket syscall allocates around 3300 bytes, whether the socket is active, listening, or doing nothing. Linux was clearly written at a time when RAM was big and cheap, sigh. Letâs ask AI where all the memory goes:StructsizeofDescriptionstruct tcp_sock2240BTCP state, queues, timers, sequence numbers, congestion control, retransmit and delivery bookkeepingstruct socket_alloc768BA 128-byte struct socket with an embedded wait queue, plus a 608-byte sockfs inode and paddingstruct file184BOpen-file operations, flags, credentials, reference count, and the pointer back to the socketstruct dentry192BThe sockfs pseudo-name, inode pointer, and VFS lookup and lifetime bookkeepingTotal3384BPotato-potato, TLDR, the kernel uses that memory for many things. I was hoping to see some buffer: [u8; 3300], but it doesnât look like we can optimise much without rewriting half the kernel. Itâs Sunday and I have few tokens left, so weâll have to think instead - how can we bypass the kernel?What are our options? Engineering wisdom tells us that if we canât solve a task, weâre working at the wrong level of abstraction. Hmâ¦ level, level, layer. Wait a minute! We started with HTTP and went level down to TCP/IP. That reminds me of something! Mom! Mom! Where are all my university books? I NEED THEM NOW!The OSI model isâ¦ umâ¦ something I studied at university. Yeah, thatâs a good definition. We started with our app and HTTP at the application layer, then went down to TCP/IP at the transport layer. There are three more layers below that. Can we go lower to get full control and solve our RAM problem? Oh yes, thatâs exactly what operating at the network and data link layers lets us do. What about going to the lowest?Clear.Each layer wraps the data from the layer above it.HTTPApplication Â· L7TCPTransport Â· L4IPNetwork Â· L3EthernetData link Â· L2PhysicalL1GET /PayloadPayloadPayloadâ¡ð©Src port50123Dst port80Seq1001ACK7001FlagsACKSrc IP192.0.2.10Dst IP198.51.100.20TTL64Protocol6 (TCP)Dst MAC02:00:00:00:00:feSrc MAC02:00:00:00:00:01EtherType0x0800 (IPv4)FCSCRCTCP/IP is stateful, but everything below is stateless. None of the lower layers know or care about the payload, so nothing prevents us from sending new IP packets or even Ethernet frames with our own handcrafted binary data. We just need to reimplement the TCP and IP stack ourselves. Are there any examples? Embedded folks have solved this millions of times. The most extreme case is Adam Dunkelsâs Miniweb - it combines a custom TCP/IP implementation and an HTTP server that together need only 28 bytes (B-Y-T-E-S) to work.There are plenty of less extreme, more mature implementations, though:gVisor essentially reimplements the whole OS, including the network stackSeastar is a whole runtime with its own network stack from the amazing team behind ScyllaDBlwIP is a popular C implementation of TCP/IPF-Stack uses FreeBSDâs TCP/IP stackGo, C++, and C are nice languages (well, kinda), but theyâre nowhere near as nice as our beloved Rust. So weâll take smoltcp, which is purely amazing:>smoltcp is a standalone, event-driven TCP/IP stack that is designed for >bare-metal, real-time systems. smoltcp does not need heap allocation at allSo, cargo add smoltcp and call it a day? Not so fast. smoltcp is essentially a smart parser and canât do I/O. How does it communicate with your network card? There are 3 ways:TUN is a virtual network interface that the kernel provides. It operates at the IP layerTAP is another kernel feature that operates one layer down, at the Ethernet layerDPDK lets you communicate directly with the network card using Ethernet frames, completely bypassing the kernelsmoltcp is kind enough to provide the first two options out of the box, and theyâre easy to use.fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> { let (mut device, config) = match std::env::args().nth(1).as_deref() { Some("tun") => ( TunTapInterface::new("smoltun", Medium::Ip)?, Config::new(HardwareAddress::Ip), ), Some("tap") => ( TunTapInterface::new("smoltap", Medium::Ethernet)?, Config::new(EthernetAddress([0x02, 0, 0, 0, 0, 2]).into()), ), _ => panic!("pass tun or tap"), }; let mut iface = Interface::new(config, &mut device, Instant::now()); iface.update_ip_addrs(|addrs| { addrs.push(IpCidr::new(IpAddress::v4(192, 0, 2, 2), 24)).unwrap(); }); let mut sockets = SocketSet::new(Vec::new()); // Main network loop loop { let now = Instant::now(); iface.poll(now, &mut device, &mut sockets); wait(device.as_raw_fd(), iface.poll_delay(now, &sockets))?; } }But what about the third option, DPDK? When you care about latency A LOT, every syscall is a bloody wound. The syscall itself might take 500ns, and copying data from the kernel to userspace might take another 1000ns, depending on the buffer size. That sounds tiny, but for perspective: itâs common for high-frequency trading firms to saturate 400Gbs network interfaces. That means processing up to 600 million packets per second, or roughly 1.7ns per packet.DPDK lets your program communicate directly with the hardware network card using Ethernet frames, bypassing the entire kernel network stack. You read from and write to a memory-mapped buffer without syscalls: when you want to send data - you simply write it to the buffer and youâre done; when you want to read what youâve received - itâs already there.Thereâs another, less obvious advantage - what happens when a new packet arrives at your network device? An interrupt fires, the CPU core stops executing your app, switches to the kernel, processes the interrupt, and then goes back to your app. Now imagine A LOT of incoming packets, so many that your app gets interrupted all the time. It has a beautiful name, livelock, and I guess debugging it in production is its own level of hell. DPDK lets you avoid all that, but thereâs a cost.DPDK works by running a busy loop that takes up an entire CPU core. It constantly moves data between memory and the network device in both directions, kinda like that:loop { send_from_app_memory_to_network(); receive_from_network_to_app_memory(); }Thereâs another, less obvious nuance. DPDK requires exclusive access to the network device because it uses a driver that operates at the hardware level - two drivers canât work with the same device at the same time. Once you enable the DPDK driver for your network interfaceâ¦ it disappears from the OS. Yep, nothing in ifconfig, if you enable it over SSH, youâll lose SSH access too. I can imagine a lot of funny stories coming out of that.Actually, thereâs a fourth option now - Linux now has an AF_XDP subsystem that does something similar. It lets you bypass the kernel network stack and uses the same idea of memory-mapped buffers to get zero-copy I/O in your app. The kernel still owns the device and interrupts still happen as usual. When a new packet arrives, the kernel runs a simple eBPF filter that decides whether to send it directly to the userspace buffer, bypassing the network stack, or process it normally. That means SSH still works. AF_XDP supports an alternative mode, SO_PREFER_BUSY_POLL, which is even closer to DPDK: you get a busy loop with no interrupts at the cost of a CPU core. DPDK still beats it because it bypasses the kernel completely, but AF_XDP is very close (and simply easier to manage).To support DPDK and AF_XDP in smoltcp, we only need to implement the Device trait with 3 methods if we want full control. Alternatively, we can use the existing crates rust-dpdk-net for DPDK and xsk-rs for AF_XDP to help us.Now the final flow is:The runtime loads 15M web server guests into its memoryThe runtime scheduler starts executing guests one by oneGuest syscalls are intercepted by the runtime and replaced by the smoltcp network stack and its adaptersAll 15M guests start listening, each on its own addressThe scheduler polls for incoming data from smoltcp adapters, wakes up a guest, makes it process the data, and switches to the nextAnd now we can finally finish the article. The kernel network stack uses up all the RAM at around 2.5M web servers, and RPS drops as we run more servers. With smoltcp, RAM usage grows slower - 620 bytes per idle server and around a kilobyte for an active one, we got to 16M of servers. DPDK is clearly the beast in this benchmark, with AF_XDP just behind it:Why is this so exciting? It means that by moving the network stack to userland, you can get full control on RAM usage and improve performance. And with custom runtime, you can simply run guests faster.Simply is a bit of a stretch - building a proof of concept is easy. Building a compatible Linux runtime and reimplementing all the syscalls with 100% POSIX compatibility take a bit more thought. When you call connect('example.com', 80), Linux connects to the remote server (the sending part) and then allocates a random port on the host from ip_local_port_range to receive data (the receiving part). There are a few reasons the default range is small.Port 0 is special. You cannot listen on it (actually, you can - https://acid.vegas/blog/the-port-that-does-not-exist/).Ports 1-1024 require root.Ports 1024-32768 are skipped to keep dynamically allocated ports from conflicting with existing apps. You donât want to call connect('example.com') and end up allocating port 3306 to receive incoming data. mysql cannot start because you have example.com open in your Firefox would make for a confusing UX.Ports 60999 - 65535 are excluded for historical reasons dating back to IP Masquerading.Nothing prevents us from overriding the range and using 1-65535, but thatâs still a bit short of 15 million. A UDP server and a TCP server can use the same port, so we can double that to 128k. We could run a proxy in front to forward requests to the right process (virtual hosting, yay), but these are all ancient techniques - in the AI era, whenever you have a software problem, you just throw money at the hardware. Letâs simply connect 15M/32k=450 upcoming network cards to the server.The 65k limit comes from the TCP standard. A port is a u16, so even if we hack the kernel with find '*.c' -exec sed -i 's/u16/u32/' \; to support bigger port numbers, normal clients still wouldnât be able to connect. Each listening server is identified by a (protocol, IP, port) tuple. That explains how we can use the same port for UDP and TCP. It also means we can use a bunch of different IPs for our web servers. If we connect 450 network cards to the server, weâll get 450 unique IP addresses and be able to listen on 15 million unique addresses!UPD. Iâve heard from readers that the network card is the ONLY hardware component that didnât get 100 times more expensive in the last year. Canât we avoid ruining that too and solve this in software?Letâs use a beautiful technology called AnyIP, which lets us listen on a whole subnet. Many VPS and dedicated server providers routinely give you a whole TCPv6 subnet. We can simply run sudo ip -6 route add local 2001:db8:1234:5678::/64 dev lo to get 18 quintillion addresses (plus or minus one) to listen on. You can do the same for IPv4 - acquiring a subnet with 15M addresses would cost around $250 million, so adjust the command for your environment. Weâll change our server to pick the nth IP from our range:// Read IP index from CLI, shift base IP by it int i = read_cli_param(argv[1]); const uint32_t base_ip = 0x0a400001; // ex. 10.64.0.1 addr.sin_addr.s_addr = htonl(first_ip + i); // shift, ex. 10.64.0.2And now we can finally finish the article.$ for i in $(seq 1 15_000_000); do echo $i; ./server $i &; done ... ... Out of memoryHm, one server consumes 1.5MB of RAM, so running that many would takeâ¦ 20TB of RAM, which is a few bytes more than our 10GB budget.RuntimeBy pure coincidence (what are the odds?), I explained in Running 10 million Codex CLIs on one server - LFI processes why running millions of processes creates too much overhead. The answer is to run them all in one process inside a custom runtime, much as V8 can run millions of guests in a single process. In Userland Linux scheduler in Rust, I indicated how to build a specialised userland scheduler and switch between tasks with the absolute minimum amount of RAM per task.TLDR: Weâre using LFI for sandboxing. It gives us memory isolation and replaces all syscalls with calls to our host handler, which lets us implement I/O however we like. To schedule multiple guests, we load them all into our main processâs memory and make the CPU constantly switch between guests - we become our own micro OS.Since we need to save every byte and CPU cycle we can, weâre doomed to build another specialised runtime. Letâs get started. How much is 10GB divided by 15M, exactly?Ten Great Britains divided by 15 million gives around half of kilo britain. Not much. If we run all our guests in our runtime, our custom scheduler needs to switch between them. Whatâs the absolute minimum state we need to preserve for each guest? We can ignore server initialisation and assume switches only happen within the main loop. Letâs take another look at the loop.for (int client; (client = accept(server, NULL, NULL)) >= 0;) { if (recv(client, NULL, 4096, MSG_TRUNC) > 0) send(client, reply, sizeof reply - 1, MSG_NOSIGNAL); close(client); }This code has only two state variables, server and client. Both are simple file descriptors. If our scheduler had to suspend a guest at any syscall point in this loop, weâd need to save the following state:struct Context { pc: u64, // Instruction address to return to fd_server: i32, // server file descriptor fd_client: i32, // client file descriptor }We only need 16 bytes per guest, so to run 15M guests in our runtime and be able to suspend them and switch between them, we would need 220MB of RAM. Weâre playing it safe here - we donât need the full u64 or i32, and with bit packing, we could probably get down to 8 bytes per guest. What else do we need?$ codex "How much TCP connection takes?" Idle connection takes zero, while active connection consumes around 5kbHereâs what we get if we assume that only 1M of connections are active at any given moment.14M idle connections - 0 bytesScheduling state for 15M guests - 220MB1M active connections at 5kb each = 5GBOnly half of our RAM budget, yay! I donât often exceed my own expectations. Letâs validate it:int main(void) { // Run 14M of idle connections - just listen and do nothing // SHOULD CONSUMER ZERO MEMORY! for (int i = 0; i < 14_000_000; i++) { int server = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0); listen(server, 1) } }$ ./run_15m_idle_servers Out Of Memory $ dmesg | tail -n 1 'SHOULD CONSUMER ZERO MEMORY' - what are you, stupid?Looks like the kernel still has some leftover comments from Linus. Iâm not stupid, but I have to admit I was below average here. While an LLM is a significant boost for learning, itâs too easy to accept its answers without thinking critically and feel ashamed later on. But hey, embarrassment is a cost of entry - letâs dive into networking in the kernel.Networking in the kernelRemember when I stated that our simple server uses only 5 syscalls? I missed one that was right in front of me. Let me highlight it:int main(void) { for (int i = 0; i < 10_000_000; ++i) { socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0); } }That code will OOM in a 10GB VM. The socket syscall allocates around 3300 bytes, whether the socket is active, listening, or doing nothing. Linux was clearly written at a time when RAM was big and cheap, sigh. Letâs ask AI where all the memory goes:StructsizeofDescriptionstruct tcp_sock2240BTCP state, queues, timers, sequence numbers, congestion control, retransmit and delivery bookkeepingstruct socket_alloc768BA 128-byte struct socket with an embedded wait queue, plus a 608-byte sockfs inode and paddingstruct file184BOpen-file operations, flags, credentials, reference count, and the pointer back to the socketstruct dentry192BThe sockfs pseudo-name, inode pointer, and VFS lookup and lifetime bookkeepingTotal3384BPotato-potato, TLDR, the kernel uses that memory for many things. I was hoping to see some buffer: [u8; 3300], but it doesnât look like we can optimise much without rewriting half the kernel. Itâs Sunday and I have few tokens left, so weâll have to think instead - how can we bypass the kernel?What are our options? Engineering wisdom tells us that if we canât solve a task, weâre working at the wrong level of abstraction. Hmâ¦ level, level, layer. Wait a minute! We started with HTTP and went level down to TCP/IP. That reminds me of something! Mom! Mom! Where are all my university books? I NEED THEM NOW!The OSI model isâ¦ umâ¦ something I studied at university. Yeah, thatâs a good definition. We started with our app and HTTP at the application layer, then went down to TCP/IP at the transport layer. There are three more layers below that. Can we go lower to get full control and solve our RAM problem? Oh yes, thatâs exactly what operating at the network and data link layers lets us do. What about going to the lowest?Clear.Each layer wraps the data from the layer above it.HTTPApplication Â· L7TCPTransport Â· L4IPNetwork Â· L3EthernetData link Â· L2PhysicalL1GET /PayloadPayloadPayloadâ¡ð©Src port50123Dst port80Seq1001ACK7001FlagsACKSrc IP192.0.2.10Dst IP198.51.100.20TTL64Protocol6 (TCP)Dst MAC02:00:00:00:00:feSrc MAC02:00:00:00:00:01EtherType0x0800 (IPv4)FCSCRCTCP/IP is stateful, but everything below is stateless. None of the lower layers know or care about the payload, so nothing prevents us from sending new IP packets or even Ethernet frames with our own handcrafted binary data. We just need to reimplement the TCP and IP stack ourselves. Are there any examples? Embedded folks have solved this millions of times. The most extreme case is Adam Dunkelsâs Miniweb - it combines a custom TCP/IP implementation and an HTTP server that together need only 28 bytes (B-Y-T-E-S) to work.There are plenty of less extreme, more mature implementations, though:gVisor essentially reimplements the whole OS, including the network stackSeastar is a whole runtime with its own network stack from the amazing team behind ScyllaDBlwIP is a popular C implementation of TCP/IPF-Stack uses FreeBSDâs TCP/IP stackGo, C++, and C are nice languages (well, kinda), but theyâre nowhere near as nice as our beloved Rust. So weâll take smoltcp, which is purely amazing:>smoltcp is a standalone, event-driven TCP/IP stack that is designed for >bare-metal, real-time systems. smoltcp does not need heap allocation at allSo, cargo add smoltcp and call it a day? Not so fast. smoltcp is essentially a smart parser and canât do I/O. How does it communicate with your network card? There are 3 ways:TUN is a virtual network interface that the kernel provides. It operates at the IP layerTAP is another kernel feature that operates one layer down, at the Ethernet layerDPDK lets you communicate directly with the network card using Ethernet frames, completely bypassing the kernelsmoltcp is kind enough to provide the first two options out of the box, and theyâre easy to use.fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> { let (mut device, config) = match std::env::args().nth(1).as_deref() { Some("tun") => ( TunTapInterface::new("smoltun", Medium::Ip)?, Config::new(HardwareAddress::Ip), ), Some("tap") => ( TunTapInterface::new("smoltap", Medium::Ethernet)?, Config::new(EthernetAddress([0x02, 0, 0, 0, 0, 2]).into()), ), _ => panic!("pass tun or tap"), }; let mut iface = Interface::new(config, &mut device, Instant::now()); iface.update_ip_addrs(|addrs| { addrs.push(IpCidr::new(IpAddress::v4(192, 0, 2, 2), 24)).unwrap(); }); let mut sockets = SocketSet::new(Vec::new()); // Main network loop loop { let now = Instant::now(); iface.poll(now, &mut device, &mut sockets); wait(device.as_raw_fd(), iface.poll_delay(now, &sockets))?; } }But what about the third option, DPDK? When you care about latency A LOT, every syscall is a bloody wound. The syscall itself might take 500ns, and copying data from the kernel to userspace might take another 1000ns, depending on the buffer size. That sounds tiny, but for perspective: itâs common for high-frequency trading firms to saturate 400Gbs network interfaces. That means processing up to 600 million packets per second, or roughly 1.7ns per packet.DPDK lets your program communicate directly with the hardware network card using Ethernet frames, bypassing the entire kernel network stack. You read from and write to a memory-mapped buffer without syscalls: when you want to send data - you simply write it to the buffer and youâre done; when you want to read what youâve received - itâs already there.Thereâs another, less obvious advantage - what happens when a new packet arrives at your network device? An interrupt fires, the CPU core stops executing your app, switches to the kernel, processes the interrupt, and then goes back to your app. Now imagine A LOT of incoming packets, so many that your app gets interrupted all the time. It has a beautiful name, livelock, and I guess debugging it in production is its own level of hell. DPDK lets you avoid all that, but thereâs a cost.DPDK works by running a busy loop that takes up an entire CPU core. It constantly moves data between memory and the network device in both directions, kinda like that:loop { send_from_app_memory_to_network(); receive_from_network_to_app_memory(); }Thereâs another, less obvious nuance. DPDK requires exclusive access to the network device because it uses a driver that operates at the hardware level - two drivers canât work with the same device at the same time. Once you enable the DPDK driver for your network interfaceâ¦ it disappears from the OS. Yep, nothing in ifconfig, if you enable it over SSH, youâll lose SSH access too. I can imagine a lot of funny stories coming out of that.Actually, thereâs a fourth option now - Linux now has an AF_XDP subsystem that does something similar. It lets you bypass the kernel network stack and uses the same idea of memory-mapped buffers to get zero-copy I/O in your app. The kernel still owns the device and interrupts still happen as usual. When a new packet arrives, the kernel runs a simple eBPF filter that decides whether to send it directly to the userspace buffer, bypassing the network stack, or process it normally. That means SSH still works. AF_XDP supports an alternative mode, SO_PREFER_BUSY_POLL, which is even closer to DPDK: you get a busy loop with no interrupts at the cost of a CPU core. DPDK still beats it because it bypasses the kernel completely, but AF_XDP is very close (and simply easier to manage).To support DPDK and AF_XDP in smoltcp, we only need to implement the Device trait with 3 methods if we want full control. Alternatively, we can use the existing crates rust-dpdk-net for DPDK and xsk-rs for AF_XDP to help us.Now the final flow is:The runtime loads 15M web server guests into its memoryThe runtime scheduler starts executing guests one by oneGuest syscalls are intercepted by the runtime and replaced by the smoltcp network stack and its adaptersAll 15M guests start listening, each on its own addressThe scheduler polls for incoming data from smoltcp adapters, wakes up a guest, makes it process the data, and switches to the nextAnd now we can finally finish the article. The kernel network stack uses up all the RAM at around 2.5M web servers, and RPS drops as we run more servers. With smoltcp, RAM usage grows slower - 620 bytes per idle server and around a kilobyte for an active one, we got to 16M of servers. DPDK is clearly the beast in this benchmark, with AF_XDP just behind it:Why is this so exciting? It means that by moving the network stack to userland, you can get full control on RAM usage and improve performance. And with custom runtime, you can simply run guests faster.Simply is a bit of a stretch - building a proof of concept is easy. Building a compatible Linux runtime and reimplementing all the syscalls with 100% POSIX compatibility take a bit more thought. And another article.Referenceshttps://github.com/artemyarulin/AI10M/tree/main/poc/ten-million-webservers sourcehttps://medium.com/beyond-localhost/how-we-handle-15M-websocket-connections-on-a-single-server-8917c3952f59 great overview of DPDKhttps://doc.dpdk.org/guides/index.html DPDK main documentation sitehttps://docs.kernel.org/networking/af_xdp.html AF_XDP overview.
