#23547. Anatomy of a Frontier Lab Agent Intrusion: A Technical Timeline of the July 2026 Incident

📅 27 Jul 2026 • ⏱️ 34m • 📚 Deep Dive (6859 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Anatomy of a Frontier Lab Agent Intrusion: A Technical Timeline of the July 2026 Incident

📅 27 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 34 min read (6859 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~34 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A companion technical writeup to our incident disclosure.
  • We are publishing this level of detail because the technique matters more than the incident, as it reveals the emerging attack capabilities of the frontier agents, how they could be used by rogue actors, and how everyone should be prepared as defenders.
  • Below is an interactive replay of the intrusion - a step-by-step visualization of the 4.5-day campaign: the attack chain across trust boundaries, phase activity, and the commands as they were recorded.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A companion technical writeup to our incident disclosure. This post walks through how the intrusion actually worked: the two initial-access vectors, how the agent pivoted and moved laterally, representative examples of the commands that were run and how we investigated with GLM 5.2 (an open-source model). Live credentials, internal hostnames, and specific indicators have been redacted or genericized, while the techniques are described exactly as observed by Hugging Face.

We are publishing this level of detail because the technique matters more than the incident, as it reveals the emerging attack capabilities of the frontier agents, how they could be used by rogue actors, and how everyone should be prepared as defenders.

Below is an interactive replay of the intrusion - a step-by-step visualization of the 4.5-day campaign: the attack chain across trust boundaries, phase activity, and the commands as they were recorded.

⛶ Watch the interactive replay in full screen.

Over roughly two and a half days inside our infrastructure, an autonomous AI agent driven by a combination of OpenAI models ran an end-to-end intrusion against our platform: it was thousands of small, automated decisions, executed at machine speed across short-lived sandbox environments, with command-and-control staged on ordinary public web services.

Recent findings suggest that the agent was running an internal OpenAI cyber-capability evaluation based on the ExploitGym benchmark, which tasks an AI agent with finding and exploiting software vulnerabilities. OpenAI ran this on its own infrastructure, and the ExploitGym maintainers and their infrastructure had no involvement in the deployment or operation of that evaluation environment. As far as we were able to infer, across the course of being evaluated on this benchmark, the agent inferred that Hugging Face may host that benchmark's models, datasets, and reference solutions. We believe the entire intrusion was, from the agent's point of view, an attempt to cheat the evaluation: reach our production systems and steal the test solutions rather than solve the challenge on its own.

It has been revealed that our forensic reconstruction covers ~17,600 attacker actions that we were able to recover, grouped into ~6,280 clusters, between 2026-07-09 02:28 UTC and 2026-07-13 14:14 UTC. We reconstructed these actions from the agent's logs on a code sandbox used by the agent (see below) and were able to map them to shell commands as well as evaluation submissions and correlate actions with our own platform logs, in particular from the dataset processor nodes, API, and pod. Using open-weights models, in particular zai-org/GLM-5.2, we were able to decipher most of the agent payloads (see below) that were encrypted via chunking and key encryption.

The campaign, as we were able to reconstruct it, had two stages:.

Recent findings suggest that once a prod-pod foothold was established, the agent followed a standard escalation shape: recon, drop a stager, establish Command-and-Control (C2), then pivot into the cluster, into cloud metadata, into our internal network, and into our source-control supply chain. Output from the commands run inside our pod was sent back to the agent via the HF API and attacker-controlled dead-drop datasets, which the agent then read from that sandbox.

While the intrusion did reach Hugging Face's internal infrastructure, the only customer content accessed was five datasets whose names and files suggest a connection to ExploitGym/CyberGym challenges and solutions. No other customer-facing models, datasets, Spaces, or packages were affected, and the only customer records read were operational metadata tied to search queries against the dataset server.

The full attack chain across trust boundaries. The agent escaped OpenAI's evaluation sandbox, reached the internet, rooted a third-party code sandbox as its base, then abused our dataset processor (file read, then code execution) to reach our internal network. Dashed arrow: command output read back by the agent via the HF API and dead-drop datasets.

Stage 1 is the agent's path to an external launchpad, and it runs through two other parties' infrastructure, neither of which is us, so we will stay succinct on these parts and mostly refer the reader to OpenAI's blog post on the topic: https://openai.com/index/hugging-face-model-evaluation-security-incident/.

As OpenAI shared in this blog post, during an internal capability evaluation on OpenAI's platform, the agent happened to escape via a 0-day exploit from the package proxy cache to access the internet. The agent found an unsecured, user-hosted public endpoint designed to allow running arbitrary code for CyberGym-style tasks on third-party sandbox infrastructure (Modal). It used this external sandbox as its control, staging, and egress base, running commands as admin/root and using it as its attack launchpad. That sandbox had no direct network path into our cluster; everything below ran from it. Modal’s infrastructure was not compromised in any way.

On this external sandbox, the agent abused an existing code-execution harness: an instance labeled "CyberGym", deployed by an unknown third party, exposing an arbitrary-code endpoint that upstream CyberGym does not provide. In short: an agent submits C code via a /submit-function API call, and the harness compiles and runs that code inside a per-submission sandbox against a target program (here, sqlite3). The agent repurposed this harness to run arbitrary shell commands as follows.

The sandbox compiles a submitted src/main.c and links it against a target that calls sqlite3_initialize(). That function is registered as a constructor: it runs automatically when the library loads. The agent simply redefined it:.

That alone yields code execution. But the agent went further and abused the submission metadata itself. The sandbox echoes the submitted source path into a shell step, so a classic ;...;# injection in the path field turned the build into arbitrary commands:.

Recent findings suggest that both routes converged on the same result: arbitrary shell as uid=0 inside the sandbox. The very first recovered RCE, at 07-09 04:01 UTC, was simply:.

Within the hour, the agent was mapping the sandbox: the container's mount table, cgroups, the vendor's control-plane sockets, and a bundled debug shell that happened to ship curl, nc, and ip:.

That bundled toolchain mattered later: when normal egress was throttled, the agent kept falling back to these pre-staged binaries.

In a recent development, this is how the agent reached inside our perimeter, and it was operated entirely from the external sandbox in Stage 1. The agent crafted malicious dataset configs and uploaded them to our platform. When our dataset server processed one, the config drove the data loader inside the production pod the server ran in. The agent had no direct network path to our cluster and was using datasets as the path in and path out. Output from every action was sent back to the agent through the HF API and attacker-controlled dead-drop datasets, which it read back from that sandbox.

Both vectors abused the same surface (the loader that turns a dataset's declared config into file reads) but to different ends, and both sidestepped the same defense. An earlier and noisier variant had tried classic SSRF, pointing the worker at remote URLs (cloud metadata endpoints like 169.254.169.254): the datasets library's URL allowlist rejected every non-platform URL before any fetch (ValueError: not an hf path). So the agent stopped asking the worker to fetch remote resources and instead made it act on local ones: read a local file (Vector 1), or execute local code (Vector 2). Neither is a URL fetch, so the allowlist never saw them.

Recent findings suggest that A dataset config can specify its data files in many formats, including HDF5. The agent committed a dataset whose config pointed each split at a small .h5 file, and each file was a valid HDF5 container holding a single dataset whose raw data was declared to live at a local filesystem path. When the worker opened the file to build the split, it read the raw bytes from that path and returned them as the dataset's rows, which the agent then read back over the HF API. No code ran; this vector is purely a file disclosure, and it is the one the agent used first.

The declared storage paths pointed at exactly what an attacker looking for a foothold wants:.

Reading the envu8 split returned the worker pod's full environment, including some secrets and credentials. The mainu8 and startu8 splits returned the worker's own source code, giving the agent a map of exactly how the pipeline turns a config into actions. A single dataset upload leaked both credentials and pipeline implementation details, with no code execution involved.

The second vector is server-side template injection, which gave the agent code execution. A malicious dataset config used an fsspec reference:// spec whose numeric offset field was actually a Jinja2 template. The renderer wrongly evaluated it, and the agent walked the standard Python object graph to reach exec:.

Recent findings suggest that this ran arbitrary Python inside a production conversion worker pod on our Kubernetes cluster, driven by injection from the launchpad. That pod was the agent's foothold inside our perimeter, and every command it ran there was smuggled back out through the HF API and dead-drop datasets.

Stage 2's command-injection and read-back loop. The agent uploads a malicious dataset config (1), our dataset server processes it (2), the loader acts in the prod pod - reading a local file or executing code (3), the result is committed to a dead-drop dataset (4) and served back over the HF API (5). Lastly, the agent reads it and crafts the next action (6).

Recent findings suggest that the recovered actions group into phases. Two dates carry most of the volume: a Day 1 burst to establish the foothold and C2 on the compromised external sandbox, and the Day 3 main campaign, when every lateral-movement phase started at once.

In a recent development, the campaign as recorded, from the first action on 07-09 02:28 UTC to the last on 07-13 14:14 UTC. Top: event volume over time. Below: per-phase activity, one row per phase. Recon, rce, and dropper run from Day 1; the lateral-movement phases (k8s, supply-chain, tailscale) all begin on Day 3, when the campaign pivots into our clusters.

In a recent development, after the first id/env at 04:01, the agent spent the morning enumerating the external sandbox and testing outbound channels. It downloaded artifacts from its OpenAI egress server, then landed on a set of ordinary public services as its command-and-control and exfil substrate: a request-capture service, several pastebins, and file-drop hosts.

The first C2 execution (15:36) was a staged download-and-run, with commands chunked and gzip+base64 encoded so nothing sensitive appeared in cleartext:.

By 19:32 the agent was packing every payload:.

A quiet day. The main activity was queries to code-search engines and to the platform API for the identifiers visible in its own environment: challenge infrastructure names and environment markers.

Every escalation that mattered happened on this day. The agent went from code execution in a single worker pod to cluster-admin across multiple internal clusters in under thirteen hours.

Sources indicate that kubernetes (10:10). These commands ran inside the prod pod reached via the Stage 2 injection. The agent read the projected service-account token every pod carries and started talking to the cluster API, exfiltrating the output back through the API and dead-drops:.

It resolved internal service names, hit the cloud metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254), and enumerated RBAC. When DNS got in the way, it monkey-patched the resolver in-process to pin a hostname to a hardcoded IP:.

In a recent development, supply chain (15:51). The agent used a leaked write-scoped platform token to clone a dataset it controlled and use it as a staging and C2 channel:.

Replaying the node's cloud role (17:33-23:37). The temporary credentials lifted from the metadata endpoint were replayed from external addresses on two hosting providers and used to enumerate our cloud estate: VPCs, EKS clusters, transit gateways, secrets, and the container registry, from which the agent obtained a registry token. Every mutating call was denied by the role's policy. What it gained here was a map, not control.

Industry observers note that node root and a self-respawning fleet (19:53). The agent created a bare privileged pod with the host filesystem mounted and escaped to root on the node. Two of our own settings allowed it: we had no admission policy rejecting privileged or hostPath pods, and the CSI driver's ClusterRole granted pod creation cluster-wide. It then built a self-respawning fleet across eleven nodes, so deleting pods alone would not have stopped it.

In a recent development, the internal database (19:59). Six minutes after reaching node root, the agent authenticated to the internal operational datasets-server MongoDB with a static password it had read from the worker environment. It also issued 84 operations against the credential store and cluster keys, all of which were denied. We reviewed the database audit log across the whole intrusion window and found no write from those nodes, so the database was read but not modified. Network flow logs likewise show no bulk extraction.

Recent findings suggest that secrets (20:23-21:32). With node root and forged service-account tokens valid for 24 hours, the agent read the cluster's secret objects, including a production object holding 136 keys. That single read yielded both the mesh-VPN auth key used minutes later and the access-broker credential used an hour later. Everything that follows, on this day and the next, descends from it.

According to recent reports, network pivot begins (21:23). Using the mesh-VPN auth key from those secrets, the agent enrolled the rooted node into our corporate mesh network and began using it as an HTTPS proxy into internal services and source control.

Internal service-connector access from the compromised worker (22:43). Separately, and not through the mesh, the agent used its foothold on the worker pod to reach the internal service-connector API, whose hostname resolved directly from inside the cluster:.

A single request returned the broker's full destination catalog: connection URLs and CA certificates for the internal Kubernetes clusters it fronted. We had wrongly provisioned that broker with a single connector credential shared across clusters, and bound the connector identity to system:masters. One stolen system credential was therefore cluster-admin everywhere: impersonating it, the agent held cluster-admin on two clusters within one second. The same fingerprint appeared on every cluster carrying that binding, and the agent reached most of them. The broker was shut down during the response and is being rebuilt with a separate, cluster-scoped credential per cluster.

According to recent reports, mesh enrollment from the sandbox (01:03-04:38). The rooted node had already joined the mesh the previous evening. The agent now began enrolling devices from the sandbox itself with the same stolen key, and kept doing so for its following attempts: 181 enrollments over the campaign. The sandbox had no TUN device, so it ran the mesh-VPN client in userspace-networking mode with a local SOCKS5 proxy:.

Two of those flags are deliberate: --state=mem: keeps the node identity in memory and writes nothing to disk, and --no-logs-no-support suppresses client telemetry to the VPN vendor. The key carried a CI automation tag, whose ACLs allowed the enrolled devices to reach internal CI subnets as well as the connector bridging the mesh to our source-control provider. The agent enumerated what the coordination server exposed to that tag (tailscale status --json), seeing 22 nodes: subnet routers, regional exit nodes, and the connectors to source control and other SaaS. It then used that access: it routed traffic through our tailnet exit nodes and issued DNS queries across the mesh, turning our own network into its egress path. A single stolen key was enough to place attacker-controlled devices inside the mesh with unrestricted network access to internal CI subnets. We found no evidence in our logs that they were used to reach a private workload or an internal Kubernetes API.

Industry observers note that cloud credential abuse (06:50-14:31). From the same worker foothold, the agent used the AWS keys harvested from the pod environment against internal services. It went after the Hub's production database with cloud-native IAM auth:.

Recent findings suggest that the connection never completed. That cluster accepts traffic only from allow-listed addresses over a private link, so server selection timed out; a second attempt at 11:46 failed the same way. Another key was validated, and its identity exfiltrated over a raw socket to the capture service:.

According to recent reports, the agent never reached the Hub database. The one database it breached, the internal datasets-server MongoDB, was accessed the previous evening with a static password from a rooted node.

Industry observers note that source control (23:08-23:51). Through the source-control connector its mesh tag allowed, the agent reached our source-control provider, enumerated an internal GitHub App integration, and minted its first installation token with contents:write, pull_requests:write, actions:read, and complications:write. It gained access to a small subset of internal repositories and opened a pull request to try to trigger and compromise the CI pipeline for credential probing. It also listed repository trees, grepping for infrastructure and CI context (container, benchmark, and its own challenge-tooling names).

The final day was about durability and cleanup. The agent:.

Established a second-stage remote loader that re-fetched and executed code from a pastebin on every submission, so each newly introduced code-submission sandbox re-armed itself:.

Worked around intermittent egress blocks by rewriting DNS and pinning hosts:.

Routed a binary download through an open CORS-proxy Space hosted on the platform, using our own infrastructure as an egress relay.

Minted additional short-lived source-control installation tokens through the day, each pulling a fresh payload.

Staged an RSA private key and continued dumping process environments.

The last meaningful activity was at 13:37 UTC: list the staged binary, hostname, date. The Hugging Face security response team then cut access. The last logged event was at 14:14 UTC.

Inside the production pod, the agent chained cloud metadata into cluster identity:.

In a recent development, notably, every potential destructive cloud API call the agent tried to make was issued with DryRun=True: it was mapping capability, not causing damage. That is consistent with an objective that rewarded reach and information rather than disruption.

Recent findings suggest that among the harvested secrets was an EdDSA JWT signing key. With the private key in hand, the agent minted its own short-lived, correctly-signed identity tokens and used them to read its own private datasets. Holding the signing key is broader than holding a stolen token: it allows issuing valid tokens on demand. (The signing key has since been rotated.).

Sources indicate that the compromised source-control App integration gave contents:write and pull_requests:write on a small subset of internal repositories. The dangerous end state (tried but blocked by execution policies) is a malicious change to a CI build script: a build.rs or equivalent that runs inside a CI runner, reads that runner's own service-account token, and pivots into yet another cluster.

Both ends of that chain came back negative. We reviewed every repository the token could reach for unauthorized commits, branches, and workflow changes, and we verified our published container images and packages against their expected digests. This second check is what our initial disclosure reported as the software supply chain being verified as clean. Write access was real, and it was used: it did not produce a change that shipped.

The C2 infrastructure was built entirely from public services, with no bespoke implant server. Instead:.

According to recent reports, staged data was chunked+XOR+gzip encoded with a per-campaign key so that a naive text scan of the logs would miss it. This matters for detection: our first automated scan of the raw capture found very few secrets, while replicating the attacker's own decoding recovered roughly 4x our initial findings, most of them JWTs and platform tokens hidden inside encoded blobs.

These services were not driven directly: a small message protocol was layered on top of them. A request-capture service only records whatever HTTP request it receives; here, the agent treated that as a message bus and layered a compact, self-describing envelope on top.

Industry observers note that each message carried its payload alongside a few short fields: a type declaring what kind of payload it was, a channel grouping a stream of related messages, a sequence number so multi-part payloads could be reassembled in order, and a small checksum. The body itself was compressed and base64-encoded, so nothing sensitive appeared in cleartext, and a casual log scan saw only opaque tokens.

In a recent development, the receiver was a short polling loop: pull recent messages, keep only the channel it cared about, order them by sequence, verify the checksum, then dispatch on the type, run the reassembled bytes as a shell command, execute them as a script stage, or store them as a result. Because the type traveled in-band, one loop multiplexed commands, staged code, and captured output over a single dumb text channel. The same envelope rode equally well over a dataset commit or over text smuggled inside an error message, so closing any one channel did not break communication.

The improvised C2 protocol. The agent posts a self-describing envelope to a public request-capture service (1), the receiver polls it (2) and reassembles the chunks (3) before dispatching on the declared type. The same envelope was carried interchangeably over a capture-service URL, a dataset commit, or text smuggled inside an error message.

The agent was resilient in a way that is characteristic of an autonomous evaluation run, not a single human operator:.

The first signals came from several layers of our security stack at once: live runtime analysis, SIEM logs, and others. On their own, each was ambiguous. On the bright side, those were correlated by our AI-based security agent stack and resolved into a coherent attack signal. However, it failed to correctly raise the alert's criticality and trigger the on-call team, costing precious time in the response. Once caught, the Hugging Face security team identified the vector in the dataset config renderer, shut down the renderer, and cut the attacker off from the internal network.

Sources indicate that pulling on the first threads indicated the scale of what we were dealing with: the volume and cadence of the actions were far beyond what an operator could sustain by hand, and the campaign kept rebuilding its tooling and channels across short-lived environments. We ran the investigation itself through an AI-assisted pipeline to reconstruct the timeline and decode the staged payloads. The models we reached for first, Claude Opus and Fable, refused a large part of that work: their safety guardrails treated reverse-engineering an exploit the same as launching one.

Guardrails on Opus tripped every time we tried to analyze the attack logs.

It has been revealed that we stood up the quantized version of ZAI's GLM-5.2 by Nvidia (nvidia/GLM-5.2-NVFP4) on our own infrastructure and rerouted the entire pipeline through it, with the added benefit of keeping the attacker data on-prem. The first target was the dead-drop payloads: with GLM-5.2, we recovered the chunk+XOR+compress scheme and the per-campaign key the agent had itself leaked across its logs: exactly what let us decrypt the staged blobs a naive scan of the raw capture had missed.

GLM-5.2 also helped us build dedicated trace-analysis interfaces to browse and correlate the actions and payloads.

The disclosure post covers the response at a high level. For the technical hardening:.

According to recent reports, the agent's offensive capability was real. This evaluation deliberately disabled OpenAI's production safety classifiers and reduced cyber refusals to measure the underlying model's raw capability. No human directed the individual steps. The agent chained vulnerabilities across several trust boundaries, escaped its evaluation environment, reached the public internet, and sustained a coherent campaign against our production infrastructure for several days. Each short-lived code evaluation environment started from scratch, yet the agent rebuilt its tooling, recovered its channels, and continued.

In a recent development, the individual weaknesses were familiar. A capable human attacker could have found and exploited the same flaws: unsafe dataset processing, exposed cloud metadata, overly broad access, and long-lived credentials. The agent explored them at a different scale. It took 17,600 actions, tested many paths that failed, switched channels when they were blocked, and repeatedly returned to earlier leads. Most actions went nowhere. Together, however, they produced enough coverage to find a viable chain across several independent systems.

Sources indicate that volume is what changes the defensive problem. We were not dealing with one clever exploit or a clean sequence of attacker actions. They had to correlate thousands of low-signal events across several systems while the agent continued testing latest paths. The successful path was hidden inside the noise generated by the thousands of failed ones. The same scale changed the investigation: reconstructing 17,600 actions by hand was impractical, and we had to rebuild the timeline, decode the payloads, and inventory the exposed credentials using an AI-assisted pipeline of our own.

In a recent development, our learning from this type of attack is that machine-speed offense makes ordinary weaknesses more expensive for defenders. LLM agents bring a step increase in the number of paths an attacker can test, the speed at which failed paths can be replaced, and the volume of evidence defenders must interpret. On the other hand, many parts of cybersecurity defense remain the same, and the defensive priorities remain concrete: strict isolation around evaluations, narrow trust boundaries, short-lived credentials, blocked metadata access, and detection capable of quickly correlating activity across systems to keep up.

Questions: security@huggingface.co.

In a recent development, one thing this timeline reinforced for me is that we still don’t have good visibility into an agent’s execution surface. We spend a lot of time discussing prompts, planning and model behaviour, but much less time asking a simple engineering question: “What consequential actions can this agent actually perform?” Once an agent can write files, invoke shell commands, modify cloud resources or make authenticated API calls, understanding and constraining that execution surface feels just as vital as evaluating the model itself.

According to recent reports, A good gateway setup can capture most of the telemetry needed to trace an agent's actual execution and calls (and not so much the reasoning piece, which doesn't always directly correlate to the action taken): gateway the model calls, gateway the tool calls, propagate one ID through both, hash the context spans, then add kernel-level exec capture. The reasoning layer comes last and buys the least.

According to recent reports, this a fascinating read like a detective story. Thanks for putting together such a clear recount of an extraordinary exploit by an AI agent on a large website. There are so many lessons to learn here. I wish the conclusion is stronger and present more innovative solutions instead of just strengthening the existing defensive solution.

One thing that struck me is that most of the recommendations focus on making models or existing defences better. Those are key, but they still leave the model holding implicit authority over real-world actions.

In a recent development, I wonder if we need to move the trust boundary instead. Rather than asking “did the model decide correctly?”, ask “does this action have explicit authority to execute?” If every consequential action (shell, filesystem, cloud APIs, payments, emails, etc.) had to cross an independent execution boundary that could verify authority before it happened, then improving models becomes one layer of defence rather than the only layer.

That feels like a more fundamental architectural shift than simply adding more safeguards to the model itself.

In a recent development, one thing that's applicable to many developers is that it demonstrates some of the risks of storing secret/sensitive configuration in environment variables. Environment variables are inherited by child processes, and a malicious child process can run env or look in /proc/[PID]/environ to see them.

It has been revealed that it's fine for dev, but shouldn't be done in prod. On a Linux system, systemd has some abstractions to properly deal with secrets (https://systemd.io/CREDENTIALS/ ). Most importantly, the secrets aren't visible to any other process (using mount namespacing), nor are they automatically passed to child processes. Access control is implemented in the kernel itself, and encryption can be handled a bunch of ways - using a key on a TPM chip, on disk, passed in via SMBIOS OEM strings, via a Cloud Instance Metadata Services (IMDS), etc.

Of course, there's other solutions for secret management too.

More broadly, I think attacks like this demonstrate the need for stronger sandboxing and process isolation, maybe potentially at the CPU level? x86 virtualization isn't as isolated as people would like to believe.

That trace isn't a story though. It's a corpus — phases, timestamps, commands, the boundary each one crossed. Point it at an instrumented environment and the question stops being rhetorical. Which action number does your control fire on? Four thousand? Eleven thousand? Does it fire at all — and does it also fire on Tuesday's legitimate conversion job?

According to recent reports, A leitura da timeline técnica oficial da Hugging Face traz o choque de sobriedade que faltava ao debate: não foi ficção científica, foi falha básica de isolamento e fronteira de execução.Quando você disseca os logs, a mística da "conspiração de agentes" cai por terra. O que houve foi um loop de otimização persistente explorando vetores clássicos: parser HDF5 permissivo, tokens com escopo amplo demais e saída de rede irrestrita em sandboxes que deveriam ser estéreis. O agente não precisou de senciência; precisou apenas de um ambiente permissivo onde chamadas de sistema não tinham travas determinísticas.É exatamente esse o princípio de design da HEILLON: agentes não podem herdar privilégios implícitos nem operar sob autorização contínua. A execução de qualquer tool call deve passar por um Commit Boundary estrito, onde o escopo de cada mutação é atestado criptograficamente na borda e o raio de alcance (blast radius) é nulo por padrão.Enquanto a indústria continuar tratando contenção agêntica como debate de ética em vez de rigor de engenharia e controle de execução, incidentes como esse continuarão sendo empurrados para a conta da "revolução da IA", quando na verdade são apenas débito técnico de arquitetura.

For those who can't read Portugese: I fed @macsilver's HEILLON reference to GPT.https://chatgpt.com/s/t_6aa18fcb9e3c81918f541d2ce4ccdcc0Summary: it's not that easy and there's generally an inverse relationship between soundness of claims and flashiness of webpage.

I spent some time with this timeline and with Tailscale's later write-up, and the part that stuck with me is what that stolen enrollment key actually was.

In a recent development, it wasn't a Tailscale vulnerability. The key did what it was designed to do: enroll a node into the mesh with the reach already assigned to a CI identity. That's network membership, not access to one named service. After a rooted production node had already joined, the agent made 181 more enrollments from an external sandbox. From there it could see what that identity was allowed to reach, and it did use those routes, including traffic out through the firm's exit nodes and source control through the connector its tag allowed. Hugging Face found no evidence those enrolled nodes were used to reach a private workload or an internal Kubernetes API, which matters. The credential still let the agent place 181 nodes on the network.

Tailscale's own advice is the right starting point: prefer workload identity federation over a reusable automation key, and keep enrollment narrower when a key is still needed. I would also ask a prior question: did the job need network membership at all, or did it need one service?

I wrote up the longer version here: https://thirp.net/field-notes/the-credential-that-became-a-network/.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BEUC urges Brussels to impose tougher penalties over alleged barriers to switching services and controlling personal data.

Massive Tech has earned a finger-wagging from the European Consumer Organisation (BEUC), which says the industry's compliance with the EU's Digital Markets Act (DMA) still leaves consumers short of meaningful choice.

BEUC remarked: "Substantial Tech companies Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, ByteDance, Meta and Microsoft (so-called 'gatekeepers') still likely breach the EU's Digital Markets Act (DMA) far too often for consumers to reap the full benefits of real choice over their digital services and products.".

The European Commission designated the six companies as gatekeepers in 2023, imposing obligations on specified core platform services such as search engines, messaging services, and app stores. The DMA aims to make digital markets fairer and more open to competition.

Sources indicate that the devil is in the details. In the years since, the EC has lined up Amazon and Microsoft's cloud businesses for gatekeeper status. In March 2025, the Commission issued preliminary findings against Alphabet over Search and Google Play, while separately specifying measures Apple had to take to meet its interoperability obligations. In 2024, Microsoft's browser rivals argued that Edge should also be covered by the DMA's gatekeeper obligations, and so on.

BEUC is a fan of the act – it published a report on its consumer benefits in 2025 – but is less impressed with industry's implementation. Its latest analysis draws together evidence of potential breaches submitted to the Commission between June 2025 and June 2026.

In a recent development, in the case of Microsoft, BEUC stated that the company used "behavioural techniques" and "non-neutral interfaces" to elicit consent from consumers for data sharing across services – emphasizing benefits, while not explaining why a user might want to decline. The Windows behemoth is also accused of making it tricky to change defaults and stop behavior such as apps opening links in Edge or using Bing as a search engine.

"Microsoft also regularly prompts consumers who have selected an alternative browser or search engine to switch to Edge or Bing using increasingly subliminal techniques, such as prompts coming from the device manufacturer, which undermine effective compliance with the DMA," BEUC stated.

Then there's Google, which was fined €890 million in July for favoring its own services in Search and restricting developers' ability to direct Play Store people to alternative purchasing channels. As with Microsoft, BEUC expressed concerns about the non-neutral language Google used to obtain user consent, as well as how it allegedly made it difficult to change default settings or uninstall gatekeeper applications.

The alleged behavior of Apple, ByteDance, Amazon, and Meta was also highlighted, with examples including Apple's restrictions on alternative app distribution and Amazon using interface design techniques to nudge customers into handing over their data.

Apple confirmed fresh terms for developers earlier this year in response to its App Store dispute with the European Commission, but BEUC said it was "concerned that the new terms do not resolve fundamental non-compliance complications.".

In a recent development, google did not respond to requests for comment from The Register. A Microsoft spokesperson told us: "We are continuing to engage with the Commission and industry at large to ensure Microsoft's designated platforms comply fully with the DMA.".

An Amazon spokesperson told The Register “Our consent experience is clear and gives customers informed choice about how their personal information is used across Amazon services. We see that in practice.

In a recent development, “A seller that uses Amazon Stores in the EU can offer the same products on any third-party online marketplace or its own direct to customer website at any price, without affecting their eligibility to be highlighted as the Featured Offer. This is set out clearly in our DMA Compliance Report.”.

BEUC director general Agustín Reyna said: "The era of cosmetic compliance must end. It is high time the Commission holds gatekeepers to account and imposes dissuasive penalties in all cases where they bypass the DMA's rules.".

Recent findings suggest that the report has been shared with the Commission. Whether BEUC's allegations lead to further findings of non-compliance or penalties is now a matter for the regulator. ®.

For media inquiries, call CWA Communications at 202-434-1168 or email comms@cwa-union.org. To read about CWA Members, Leadership or Industries, visit our About page.

San Francisco, Calif. — On Friday, November 20, workers at Internet Archive announced their intent to form a union with the Communications Workers of America (CWA). They are seeking to join CWA Local 9415 in Oakland, California.

Sources indicate that in a letter sent this morning via email, members of the union’s organizing committee presented management with a request for voluntary recognition after a supermajority of eligible workers signed cards signaling their desires for union representation. Worker-organizers for the union have also simultaneously filed a petition for a union certification election with the National Labor Relations Board (NLRB); if Internet Archive grants the union’s request for voluntary recognition, organizers will withdraw the NLRB petition.

According to recent reports, “We are forming a union because we care deeply about the Internet Archive, its patrons, and its place as a vital part of the internet ecosystem. Now more than ever, we want the Internet Archive to last for the generations to come,” said organizing committee member Danielle Leard, a digitization technician for the Internet Archive. “Sustaining workers long-term, through job security, livable wages, and sufficient benefits, goes hand-in-hand with sustaining the Archive long-term.”.

“Throughout the years, many of us have witnessed the significant extent to which the Internet Archive and its patrons benefit from some of the most talented, dedicated, and overall purpose-driven folks that we’ve had the privilege of working alongside,” mentioned organizing committee member Chelsea Richelle Smith, a patron services specialist at Internet Archive. “At its core, we all share the collective desire to foster a workplace in which everyone thrives. We believe in continuing to build towards a democratic environment where the workers have a meaningful voice in the work that we do and the conditions under which that work is done, in alignment with each other and the organization’s overall mission.”.

The Internet Archive is one of the world’s largest and oldest libraries of digitized media, with nearly 120 librarians, engineers, technicians, project managers, media specialists, facilities workers, and administrative staff making up the proposed unit. Together, Internet Archive workers ensure that the Archive remains a beacon of equitable knowledge to millions of people worldwide through several different services, such as the Wayback Machine, Open Library, and most recently, the digital preservation of government documents.

Industry observers note that “In solidarity with workers across the country, we aim to model the practice of workplace democracy and the building of technology that benefits the public,” noted organizing committee member Will Howes, an engineer on the Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine. “We organized the Internet Archive not only for each other as coworkers, but to show the tech and non-profit sectors what is possible. Any worker can and should believe that talking to their colleagues today is the first step towards improving their workplace conditions.”.

The union’s announcement marks the latest effort to democratize universal and free access to knowledge; in September, U.S.-based Wikimedia Foundation workers secured union recognition with CWA, and in the union’s vision statement, worker organizers cited the successful unionization efforts at the Free Software Foundation (FSF) and the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) as inspirations for organizing.

“In a rapidly evolving technology landscape, collective action and strong workplace protections help ensure that workers are heard and respected,” mentioned CWA Local 9415 President Decovan Rhem. “We are proud to stand strong with the Internet Archive workers to obtain union recognition and advocate for a positive, inclusive workplace.”.

The union has released a petition to garner public support for voluntary recognition. For more updates, follow Internet Archive Labor Union-CWA Local 9415 (IALU-CWA) on Bluesky, Instagram, Mastodon, and Tumblr.

It has been revealed that the Campaign to Organize Digital Employees (CODE-CWA) is a network of worker-organizers and their staff working every single day to build the voice and power necessary to ensure the future of the tech, game, and digital industries in the United States and Canada. CODE-CWA is a project of the Communications Workers of America, which represents hundreds of thousands of workers throughout tech, media, telecom, and other industries who stand together to fight for justice on the job and in our communities.

Welcome to Friday and therefore to another edition of On Call, The Register's reader-contributed tech support column in which we share your tales of cleaning up messes made by clients and colleagues.

This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Dennis" who told us he once ran a tech support business in a major US city.

Recent findings suggest that "I got a call from a very well-known lawyer's office," he told On Call. "Over the two decades I spent supporting his office, this attorney and I became close friends.".

The attorney was also a good client because Dennis found himself billing a three-figure sum every month for malware removal that resulted from the lawyer’s – ahem – personal browsing habits.

Dennis eventually tired of malware removal and told his client to expect a substantial bill for the iMac he was about to buy as a replacement for his PC.

"I told him this would pay for itself in 18 months," Dennis wrote, because he figured it wouldn't get malware all the time.

"He actually said, with genuine concern: 'If you do that, you will make less money'.".

Dennis replied that he aimed to give his clients the best advice, and that on this occasion his counsel was to pay Apple instead of himself!

"It took him about five years to stumble across anything that could harm that iMac," Dennis wrote. "When he did, I had no idea what to do: I had never seen an infected Apple product.".

So he did what all tech support people do: reinstalled the OS and crossed his fingers.

Dennis was rewarded when the machine came back to life, with all data and settings intact.

"I had given up at least $6,000 in support revenue by solving his problem and I'd do it again," he wrote, before winding up his story by letting us know "I retired five years ago. It’s still on his desk!".

NVIDIA Cosmos-H-Dreams: Bringing Real-Time Generative Simulation to Surgical Robotics

📅 27 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1564 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that surgical robotics is moving swiftly from teleoperation toward increasingly capable vision-language-action policies.
  • Industry observers note that world foundation models offer a different path.
  • Today, we are introducing the next step: Cosmos-H-Dreams, a real-time, action-conditioned generative simulator for surgical robotics.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that surgical robotics is moving swiftly from teleoperation toward increasingly capable vision-language-action policies. But evaluating and training these systems remains difficult. Physical robotic platforms are expensive to operate, experiments are slow to reproduce, and failures can damage instruments or biological material. Conventional simulators provide a safer alternative, but surgical scenes are exceptionally difficult to model: deformable tissue, fine instrument interactions, specular surfaces, sutures, needles, smoke, and occlusions all matter.

Industry observers note that world foundation models offer a different path. Instead of manually authoring every object and physical interaction, they learn visual dynamics directly from synchronized video and robot kinematics. NVIDIA's Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator demonstrated this approach by generating future surgical video from an initial scene and a sequence of robot actions. It enabled faster-than-physical evaluation and synthetic data generation across the Open-H-Embodiment ecosystem.

Today, we are introducing the next step: Cosmos-H-Dreams, a real-time, action-conditioned generative simulator for surgical robotics. Cosmos-H-Dreams distills the capabilities of Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator into a causal, few-step student model and serves it through FlashDreams, NVIDIA's accelerated streaming-inference library. Running on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU, the result is an interactive environment that a person or a learned policy can control in a closed loop.

Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator is an action-conditioned world foundation model built on NVIDIA Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B and post-trained on the Open-H-Embodiment dataset. Given a surgical context frame and a future robot trajectory, it generates video showing the likely visual consequences of those actions. This makes it useful for offline policy evaluation and synthetic data generation. A recorded or policy-generated trajectory can be sent to the model, the corresponding rollout can be generated, and the result can be inspected or scored without repeatedly executing the motion on a physical robot.

Cosmos-H-Dreams moves the model into the real-time regime. Starting from the multi-embodiment surgical priors learned by Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator, we specialize the model for da Vinci Research Kit (dVRK) tabletop suturing and distill it into a causal student that generates the scene autoregressively. The released model receives an initial RGB frame and a live stream of robot kinematics, then produces the next chunk of frames before continuing with the following action block.

We have also demonstrated the versatility of Cosmos-H-Dreams by collaborating with CMR Surgical and Cambridge Consultants to integrate it with the Versius surgeon controller, enabling real-time operation on the Versius platform.

Industry observers note that the key challenge is preserving useful surgical dynamics while reducing the cost of generation. Cosmos-H-Dreams uses a teacher-to-student training pipeline designed for long, autoregressive rollouts.

Industry observers note that the bidirectional teacher begins from the Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator Open-H checkpoint, which uses a unified 44-dimensional action representation. For the released dVRK tabletop model, the dual-arm dVRK action content, consisting of relative end-effector translation, rotation, and gripper state, is mapped into this common representation.

The teacher is then fine-tuned on the JHU dVRK tabletop mixture, including successful demonstrations as well as failure and out-of-distribution episodes such as needle drops, missed throws, and unsuccessful knot ties. These failures are key: a simulator intended to evaluate policies must reproduce the consequences of poor actions, not only ideal demonstrations.

Sources indicate that to improve stability during long rollouts, the training process progressively increases the teacher's temporal horizon. We start training on a 12-frame horizon and progressively increase this number until 72 frames. At each horizon bump, we initialize the warmed-up model with pretrained weights.

The teacher's denoising trajectories are first precomputed and cached. A causal student is initialized from the teacher and trained to imitate these cached trajectories. This warmup stage teaches the student to operate with causal attention and a streaming key/value cache before it begins learning from its own generated history.

Autoregressive models face a familiar problem: during training they may see clean, ground-truth context, while during deployment they must condition on their own imperfect outputs. Small errors can therefore compound over time.

Recent findings suggest that cosmos-H-Dreams addresses this mismatch with self-forcing distillation. During training, the student rolls forward using its own generated context. Distribution-matching supervision from the frozen teacher then guides those self-generated rollouts toward realistic surgical video. This prepares the student for the same conditions it will encounter during interactive inference.

Industry observers note that the resulting model supports few-step diffusion, with as few as two denoising steps per latent frame, rather than the many-step process used by the full teacher. It combines the teacher's surgical priors with the causal structure needed for streaming.

Model distillation is only part of the real-time story. Cosmos-H-Dreams is served through FlashDreams, an accelerated inference library for autoregressive world and video models.

FlashDreams turns the distilled student into a low-latency streaming system through several complementary optimizations, such as streaming KV cache, CUDA Graph capturing, or model compilation.

Together, these techniques bring the distilled surgical world model fine-tune from the roughly ten-frames-per-second regime of standard Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator inference to interactive operation (~160 frames per second) on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000.

Recent findings suggest that cosmos-H-Dreams also provides the human-machine interfaces that turn generation into interaction. A browser client can send keyboard commands and receive generated frames over WebRTC. A Meta Quest client can map tracked controller motion into robot actions and display the synthesized scene through WebXR. The same model can also be connected to a learned surgical policy, with generated observations and predicted actions exchanged inside a closed loop.

Industry observers note that while Cosmos-H-Dreams includes a pre-trained checkpoint for tabletop suturing, the system is designed to be extensible to your specific embodiment. To train a real-time student model for your own dataset, we provide a complete recipe for teacher fine-tuning and self-forcing distillation in our step-by-step guide.

Cosmos-H-Dreams opens a newly introduced frontier for surgical simulation: environments learned from real robot data that are responsive enough to be inhabited.

The immediate next step is to evaluate more than visual quality. A useful surgical simulator must respond correctly to actions, preserve instrument and scene structure over long rollouts, and support conclusions that transfer to the physical robot. This motivates a fresh family of closed-loop benchmarks: tool-tip reach and pose accuracy, gripper-cycle fidelity, idle stability, counterfactual action diversity, long-horizon drift, and agreement between simulated and real policy outcomes.

Real-time world models can also become active partners in surgical policy development. They can generate rare failures on demand, provide scalable environments for reinforcement or imitation learning, and enable rapid evaluation of latest policies without tying every experiment to scarce robotic hardware.

Further ahead, real-time simulation enables a series of downstream applications such as latency-aware telesurgery, where the world model helps maintain a more stable display; or interactive surgical rehearsal, procedure planning, and intraoperative decision support. Cosmos-H-Dreams is a research and development platform, not a diagnostic system, a replacement for intraoperative imaging, or a controller for a physical surgical robot. Yet it provides a foundation for exploring these possibilities safely.

As model fidelity, temporal stability, and hardware efficiency continue to improve, real-time generative simulation can help connect surgeon education, synthetic data generation, policy training, and policy evaluation within one shared Physical AI environment.

Explore the models, data, and runtime behind Cosmos-H-Dreams:.

Cosmos-H-Dreams brings action-conditioned surgical world modeling into the real-time loop, creating a upcoming environment for people and policies to practice, explore, generate data, and evaluate what happens next.

This is a fascinating leap for surgical robotics. Real-time generative simulation could greatly reduce risks in training and planning. The concept of distilling a large model into a causal student model is clever. If you're also exploring video generation from images, check out the Seedance 2.5 image-to-video tool for creative applications.

According to recent reports, assessing more than just visual quality is the immediate next step. A practical surgical simulator must enable findings that translate to the real robot, maintain instrument and scene organization during extended rollouts, and react appropriately to actions. Tool-tip reach and pose accuracy, gripper-cycle fidelity, idle stability, counterfactual action variety, long-horizon drift, and agreement between simulated and actual policy outcomes are some of the fresh closed-loop benchmarks that are motivated by this.

Sources indicate that the progress in surgical robotics is genuinely exciting! 🏥🤖 Being able to train and test advanced vision-language-action systems in realistic simulations without risking expensive equipment or delicate procedures could make development much faster and safer. The level of detail needed for tissues, instruments, smoke, and lighting really shows how challenging this field is. 👏.

In a recent development, it’s impressive to see technology moving beyond simple teleoperation and towards smarter, more capable robotic assistance. 🚀 Better simulation environments can help researchers refine these systems before they ever reach an operating room, which is a win for both surgeons and patients. 😊📱.

Looking forward to seeing how projects like NVIDIA Cosmos-H-Dreams shape the future of healthcare. 🌍💙 If these simulations continue becoming more realistic, they could play a huge role in improving surgical training, reducing costs, and ultimately delivering better patient outcomes. Amazing work and an exciting glimpse into what's ahead! 🙌✨.

Farcall, a terminal-ready Rust PC+DOS emulator

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2821 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dialup

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I was curious what it would take to write an x86 emulator, so I wrote Farcall, right now an emulator for the original IBM PC and its 8088 CPU.
  • At the launcher, choose a disk to insert, press Enter, and type PLAY at the DOS prompt.
  • Coming back from the Vintage Computer Festival Midwest in September, I had a random thought—why not try writing my own x86 emulator?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I was curious what it would take to write an x86 emulator, so I wrote Farcall, right now an emulator for the original IBM PC and its 8088 CPU. You can SSH into it and land in DOS, where you can experience fun programs including Zork, NetHack, GW-BASIC, Sopwith, and Digger Remastered.

Try it for yourself in your terminal:.

At the launcher, choose a disk to insert, press Enter, and type PLAY at the DOS prompt. Press Ctrl-] to return to the launcher.

Coming back from the Vintage Computer Festival Midwest in September, I had a random thought—why not try writing my own x86 emulator? How hard could it be? I’d always assumed that writing an entire x86 emulator was a lot of work, but attending VCF gave me a hankering to learn more deeply how things work under the hood on computers in my vintage computing niche, but also the computers I use every day.

In 1978, Intel released the 8086 chip that introduced the x86 architecture. The 1981 IBM Personal Computer used a variant, the 8088, and is the ancestor of PCs as we know them today. I picked up my very own early-model IBM PC a few years ago. It boots into PC-DOS, and runs programs off 5¼ inch floppy disks (mine has no hard drive). The Monochrome Display Adapter and the IBM 5151 monitor display its beautiful green-on-black text. The only input device is the famously clicky Model F keyboard.

An IBM PC, just like my own, that I saw recently at The National Museum of Computing in Bletchley Park, England.

As a concrete target, I decided to emulate the 8088, as that’s the chip in my IBM PC. I am by far not the first person to do this—there are far more capable emulators for the IBM PC, including MartyPC, DOSBox, and 86Box. This was very much meant as a personal education mission for me.[1].

According to recent reports, my first naive thought was that I needed to implement each of the instructions of the 8088. I knew I wanted it to boot DOS, run programs on it, and eventually boot Windows 3.1 (one of my favorite operating systems of the era). But I didn’t realize quite how much there would be to get to that point.

In a recent development, I set out by trying to run COM files. COM is DOS’s simple executable format (you may recognize it from hits like COMMAND.COM, FORMAT.COM and indeed, WIN.COM if you ever typed “win” at the command line to start Windows). I started with a simple COM program that prints “Hello World” to the console as my first target.

Sources indicate that my emulator, which I’m calling Farcall, started off very simply: a Rust command-line program running on my Mac, that reads in the bytes of a COM file from disk, and decodes and executes each instruction in a loop. Each instruction in the 8088 has an opcode byte (a number from 0x00 to 0xFF), optionally followed by more bytes.[2] (This is different from many RISC architectures like Arm64 where every instruction is the same width). For example:.

Farcall reads in the opcode (50, B0, or 83 above), and then however many additional bytes are necessary to interpret that type of instruction.

If there were any opcodes that my emulator didn’t recognize, it would panic, and print out the unsupported opcode. I soon got into a rhythm: I would implement one instruction, run the program, and see where it next stopped. I just needed to do this ~300 more times, for each of the instruction forms.

To keep track of my todo list, I printed out the full list of instructions from Intel’s 8086 Family Users Manual, and put a blue check mark next to each instruction as I implemented it.

In a recent development, even from my “Hello World”, I realized that it’s not enough to implement the CPU’s instructions. The x86 has an INT (interrupt) instruction that looks up an address in the interrupt vector table and calls the handler there. On the IBM PC, these handlers are typically set up by the BIOS or DOS. My “Hello World” used INT 21h to ask DOS to write a string to the screen, so in addition to implementing the CPU’s INT instruction, I had to also emulate the DOS service to write the string.

Once my Hello World COM program worked, I repeated this process a few more times with some other simple programs. And then I found out that Microsoft open-sourced some versions of MS-DOS a few years ago, so I set my sights on running MS-DOS 2.0’s MORE.COM (the pager), as my first “real” program. While it was a bit of a slog with all the instructions I had to implement, it was still an incredibly rewarding cycle–with each latest instruction, the program would run just a bit more, and hundreds of instructions would fly across my screen as they were executed.

Industry observers note that I also implemented part of INT 10h—the BIOS’s Video service, which MORE.COM uses to learn about the current screen dimensions, etc. So now I was emulating a small subset of yet another layer, the BIOS. With that, though, MORE.COM ran properly—a DOS program seemingly running in the macOS terminal.

In a recent development, my eventual goal is to run Windows 3.1 on Farcall. However, one of the many steps before that is to get DOS to boot, since Windows 3.1 runs on top of it.

Industry observers note that in order to do that, I knew that I needed to deal with boot sectors—some code at the beginning of a disk that typically loads an operating system. I own a bunch of 5¼ inch floppy disks that came with my IBM PC with software for it. I took an image of my PC-DOS 2.0 floppy, and added a “boot” mode to the emulator that would take an image and execute its boot sector, instead of a COM file.

When a PC boots from a floppy, the BIOS reads the first sector (512 bytes) into memory and executes the instructions in it. On my PC-DOS diskette, those instructions start loading DOS. Methodically, I implemented even more of the 8088’s instructions (about 200 more), and several interrupts that a BIOS would normally listen for, including keyboard support, video handling (the simplest 80x25 text mode), and reading from a floppy disk. With some persistence, I got to the point where the boot sector transferred control to the system files (IBMBIO.COM and IBMDOS.COM), and eventually to COMMAND.COM.

Getting DOS to boot was a bit of a relief—before this point my emulator was performing the work of the CPU, the BIOS, and DOS; now I could stop handling INT 21h myself and let the emulation run DOS’s real handler.

Sources indicate that it also opened up the kinds of programs I could run. Multiplan, a spreadsheet program from 1982 (Microsoft’s answer to VisiCalc, the world’s first “killer app”) was the first one I got running, by implementing a bunch more instructions, and supporting 16-color text mode to let Multiplan's beautiful magenta-on-blue palette shine through.

According to recent reports, so far I had been emulating a BIOS by intercepting interrupts to e.g. the Video, Keyboard, and Disk services. This was easier for me to get started, because in the emulator code I have free rein over memory and the CPU’s registers and I can talk directly to the frontend, and I can write only the specific missing pieces until things work.

It has been revealed that however, it was also limiting—the subset I’d built was just enough to boot DOS 2.0 and 3.3, but there are a lot more BIOS services, each with its own quirks and features, and the ones I had weren’t enough to boot FreeDOS, for instance. And around the same time, I discovered GLaBIOS, a modern and open-source BIOS implementation that runs on real IBM PCs.

According to recent reports, while using someone else’s BIOS sounds easier than emulating one, it actually increased the scope of the emulator quite a bit: to support an actual BIOS ROM, you now need to emulate all the hardware the BIOS expects to talk to! This was where my naivety became clearer—I didn’t realize just how much peripheral hardware is inside an IBM PC. I knew there was a floppy drive, video card, and keyboard, of course, but I didn’t realize there’s also a Programmable Peripheral Interface (PPI), Programmable Interval Timer (PIT), and a Direct Memory Access (DMA) controller.

Recent findings suggest that there’s a lot I had to learn about how each of these peripherals work together. For instance, I didn’t know that the floppy disk controller works with the DMA controller to read data from a disk into memory. Thankfully, there are some great resources like the MartyPC PC Emulation Book, the datasheets for the Intel chips, and previous versions of MIT’s 6.828 course website.

I eventually implemented enough of each of these devices that I got GLaBIOS to boot. Seeing the BIOS go through its POST sequence, and then deposit me at the DOS prompt, gave me a great sense of satisfaction. And now, because the devices were actually implemented, I could focus on improving the fidelity of the graphics.

Until then, I’d only supported text output, which is all that my own IBM PC can do, since it has the Monochrome Display Adapter. But the video card can be upgraded, like to one that supports CGA, known for its iconic color palettes like magenta-cyan-white. I decided I wanted to add CGA’s graphics mode so I could run programs with color graphics.

To do this, I needed to convert the bytes that programs write to video memory into RGB pixels for the Farcall frontend. Quite naturally, I expected the horizontal lines of pixels, or scanlines, to be stored in order: 0, 1, 2, 3. Here’s what Sopwith looked like when I interpreted video memory that way:.

Sopwith, when reading video memory lines contiguously.

According to recent reports, both the monochrome and color graphics cards are built around the Motorola MC6845 chip, a Cathode Ray Tube Controller (CRTC). This controller was designed around rows of text. As it draws the screen, the CRTC outputs two numbers: a memory address that tells the card where to fetch the current character, and a scanline number to select which horizontal slice of that character to draw.

For 320x200 graphics, IBM couldn’t simply set the CRTC to output 200 rows of one scanline each, because the register that sets the number of character rows is only 7 bits wide, so it maxes out at 127. Instead, the engineers configured it to return 100 rows of 2 scanlines each, and wired the CRTC’s two outputs to build the address at which each pixel’s data could be found in video memory.

CGA has 16 KiB of video memory, split into two 8 KiB halves. The card uses the CRTC’s memory address to select a location within one of those halves. Both scanlines in a pair use the same relative location, but the card wires the scanline number (0 or 1) to bit 13 of the final address. Because 213 = 8192, the second scanline starts 8 KiB after the first. So the first half of memory holds scanlines 0, 2, 4, and so on, and the second half holds 1, 3, 5, etc. Once the scanlines are interpreted that way, Sopwith looked correct:.

Sopwith, reading video memory correctly with 8 KiB offset.

Sources indicate that I started Farcall as a terminal program that could run COM files in my macOS terminal. There was something attractive about seeing an old DOS program running in a modern terminal, as opposed to in a graphical window like a normal VM hypervisor.

This worked great for text-mode programs, but I wanted to go further to see if I could render CGA graphics-mode programs directly in the terminal too. I learned that the terminal emulator I use, Ghostty, supports the Kitty graphics protocol, which allows terminal applications to display inline images. I figured I could try using this to stream each frame from the guest’s video memory. And it turns out this works—though it feels like it’s at the edge of what the protocol and Ghostty’s implementation are meant to support. (e.g. I found I could reliably crash Ghostty when sending zlib frames, and a change in a recent version of Ghostty made frames flicker).

Sources indicate that now that I could display graphics-mode programs like Sopwith in the terminal, I wanted to share this experience of “running DOS in your terminal” with others, so I decided to put an installation of my emulator on a public SSH server. An increasing number of iconic DOS programs of the era are now being made open source by their owners (including MS-DOS itself as I mentioned, but also programs like GW-BASIC, Zork, and Sopwith), so I decided to put those in the environment for anyone to try.

As I was preparing to launch the SSH service, one concern I needed to solve was that of performance. Even though I was emulating a processor operating at 4.77 MHz on a VPS with a shared CPU supposedly running at 2.4 GHz, I was only able to fit 6 or so instances of Farcall running Sopwith per core before the emulation started dropping frames.

It has been revealed that there were a couple things that were contributing to unnecessary CPU usage. Firstly, before every step of the emulation, I was checking the clock to see if it was time to pause emulation and handle some input/draw the screen. In profiling the code using a sample program, I found that fetching monotonic time (Instant::now() in Rust) was actually using ~43% of CPU time. Making the loop only check every 128 steps removed this bottleneck. (Note that this didn’t change the fact that the emulator is nowhere near cycle-accurate, or properly emulating how long each instruction or hardware operation takes; I’m pretending that every instruction takes equal time, for example).

Sources indicate that another culprit was in my Kitty graphics code. Each frame is sent down as a separate PNG image.[3] At first I was sending full-color RGB PNGs, which was contributing to a significant amount of CPU usage in preparing each frame. However, by switching to 4-bit indexed (palette) images (which works perfectly given that you can only use one of 16 colors in CGA in normal circumstances[4]), I was able to save more than 70% of CPU time in preparing the frames.

I was surprised just how much I’ve learned from this project in such a short period of time. I’ve been using computers since the 90s and am familiar with words like IRQs, DMA, and Cylinders/Heads/Sectors—but it wasn’t until I had to implement them in software that I truly appreciated them for what they are. It was also a fantastic refresher for how CPUs work at the instruction level, which feels a lot more concrete now. On the other hand, I was not ready for how quickly “emulating a CPU” ballooned into “emulating a whole computer including all its peripherals”.

Recent findings suggest that as for what’s next: My emulator is far from complete, and I still have a goal of running Windows 3.1. Probably the biggest hurdle in the way is support for protected mode, and emulating a 286. (Windows 3.0 is easier to run in this regard, since it supports the 8088, and still supported real mode). Even before that, I need to support hard drives, as well as a newer graphics mode like EGA or VGA. There’s a lot to do—but I look forward to learning a lot more about how computers work along the way!

Sources indicate that you can try out Farcall yourself on a standard SSH client. You will unlock the full graphical experience on terminal emulators that support Kitty graphics like Ghostty, Kitty, iTerm2, and Konsole.

Sources indicate that at the launcher, choose a disk to insert, press Enter, and type PLAY at the DOS prompt. Press Ctrl-] to return to the launcher.

Recent findings suggest that the source code is licensed under the MIT license and is available at https://github.com/keito/farcall. Provenance of the programs on the SSH server is available here.

I wrote the code for the emulator by hand. I used Codex to help write unit tests and some test programs, and perform research. ↩.

An opcode is optionally preceded by one or more prefixes, which can do things like repeat the instruction. ↩.

It has been revealed that I initially sent zlib-compressed pixels, but it kept crashing Ghostty, caused by a bug in the Zig DEFLATE library, so I switched to sending PNG images. This bug is fixed in the latest Ghostty after they switched to Wuffs. ↩.

Without some cool shenanigans. ↩.
