GPU Management: Why Idle GPUs Are the Fresh Grounded Aircraft

📅 30 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2665 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, aviation learned this the hard way.
  • It has been revealed that the reason is structural.
  • In a recent development, A bigger fleet still helps.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, aviation learned this the hard way. For most of the industry's history, the number that best predicted whether an airline would survive was how much of the day each aircraft spent on the ground.

It has been revealed that the reason is structural. An aircraft's costs accrue by the calendar hour: financing, depreciation, hull insurance, scheduled maintenance, crew contracts. Its revenue accrues only by the flight hour. Every hour spent on the ground shrinks the output side of that equation while the cost side keeps running exactly as before. Utilization also sits downstream of almost everything else an airline does. Turnaround discipline, network design, maintenance planning, crew rostering, and spare parts availability all eventually show up in that one number, because a broken operation underneath it keeps planes on the ground no matter what else goes right.

In a recent development, A bigger fleet still helps. More aircraft means more available capacity, plainly and simply. But two airlines flying comparable fleets on comparable routes can end up with very different economics, and most of that gap traces back to one measurement rather than fleet size.

Enterprise AI is running into the same structure, on a different piece of hardware. A GPU accrues cost by the calendar hour too, through financing, depreciation, power, and cooling, whether or not it's doing anything useful in a given moment. Its output only accrues by the compute hour. More GPUs helps in roughly the way a bigger fleet helps an airline: real capacity, a genuine advantage, and still no guarantee of the result that actually decides who wins. Two companies with comparable GPU budgets increasingly diverge based on how much of that hardware is doing something useful at any given moment, not on how much of it either one owns. That same number, like an airline's utilization rate, sits downstream of nearly every other infrastructure decision a company makes. Intelligence has carried the industry this far. Utilization is where the next real constraint is forming.

The scarcity didn't disappear as AI scaled. It moved up the chain, landing on a different resource entirely.

The first wave of enterprise AI was won on model quality. Bigger models, trained on more compute, evaluated against tougher benchmarks: parameter count and leaderboard position dominated the conversation, and the race produced models genuinely good enough to run real enterprise workloads. That capability arrives bundled with a dependency, though. Production AI runs on specialized hardware, and today that hardware is almost entirely GPUs.

GPUs are expensive, supply constrained, and in demand far beyond what's available, and this holds even at the very top of the market. In 2020, Microsoft built OpenAI a dedicated supercomputer: over 10,000 GPUs and 285,000 CPU cores, reported at the time as one of the five largest systems in the world, assembled to train what became GPT-3. At the time, it looked like an almost unimaginable concentration of hardware, the kind of number that made compute look like a solved problem for whoever could get access to it. Six years later, that number reads more like a starting point than a ceiling. By 2026, even the best capitalized labs on the planet were treating compute access as a live strategic constraint rather than a settled one. Anthropic alone was running simultaneous multi-gigawatt commitments across four separate hardware platforms, Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and AMD, layered within months of one another, while Meta signed a comparable multi-gigawatt deal of its own. Spreading commitments across four vendors at once is what compute scarcity looks like when a buyer has effectively unlimited capital and still can't get enough from any single source.

Six years apart, both events marked the frontier of what a lab needed just to stay competitive. What changed in between has less to do with AI getting more capable, and everything to do with capability no longer being the binding constraint.

Recent findings suggest that the same pattern demonstrates up downstream of the labs, in a different form. Enterprises consuming these models through an API run into a pricing problem more than a hardware one. Cost scales linearly with tokens used, and that single fact separates the economics of a proof of concept from the economics of production almost completely. A PoC processing a few thousand requests a month looks affordable. The same workload at production volume can turn into a cost line that never quite clears. The alternative gaining ground is straightforward enough: enterprises acquiring their own GPUs and running models locally, trading a variable, linearly scaling cost for a fixed capital one.

It has been revealed that API cost rises with usage, while owned infrastructure stays close to fixed. Past the breakeven point, the trade reverses.

In a recent development, that shift turns the GPU into infrastructure rather than a line item, sized for growth, sized for demand peaks, and therefore sized above what any given week actually needs. Which means the purchase doesn't close the problem. It opens a latest one. The day the cluster comes online, the question stops being can we get accelerators and becomes can we keep them busy, and only the first question had a procurement team assigned to it. Signing for the hardware is the part with a deadline and an owner. Keeping it off the ground is the part that quietly decides whether the deal was worth signing.

It has been revealed that these deals describe capacity commitments, not efficiency. How well that capacity gets used is a separate question, owned by different people, measured far less rigorously, and considerably further from being solved.

According to recent reports, A cluster full of busy GPUs can still be wasting most of its potential, and the reason is almost always the same one. GPUs run continuously, day and night, while the demand placed on them does not. Infrastructure has to be sized for the peak, the moment training runs, batch jobs, and real time traffic all land at once, which leaves a meaningful share of capacity provisioned and unused outside that peak. Better forecasting could solve that on its own if every GPU could absorb every kind of work equally well. Few can, and that turns out to be the harder half of the problem.

The mismatch begins one layer deeper.

In a recent development, in the first generation of enterprise AI, a GPU's job was largely singular: run inference. Today the same hardware supports training, fine-tuning, quantization, real-time inference, batch inference, embedding generation, and model evaluation, often for the same organization, sometimes for the same model, on the same cluster. Each of these workloads wants something different from the hardware, and the differences run deep. Real-time inference needs low latency above nearly everything else, because a slow response counts as a failed one. Batch work cares about throughput and tolerates delay, sometimes for hours. Training can occupy a GPU continuously for a stretch measured in hours or days. Quantization needs a large amount of capacity, but only briefly. A scheduler tuned for one of these will misallocate the other three almost by default. The failure doesn't always show up on a utilization dashboard either. A cluster can report high average occupancy while several queued jobs wait for a GPU shape that happens to be busy running something else entirely.

The exact workload mix varies by organization. The shape of the problem does not. This is also where the aircraft analogy runs into its limit, and the limit teaches something rather than just qualifying the comparison. An idle aircraft can usually be redeployed to any route in the fleet: a 737 sitting in Chicago can fly to Denver instead of Dallas without much penalty. An idle GPU can only absorb a workload whose memory, latency, and duration profile it can actually serve. That difference makes orchestration harder than fleet scheduling, and it's why the question stops being whether GPUs are occupied and turns into which workload should run on which GPU, at what time, with what priority. Buying another rack of GPUs adds capacity and cost, not a fix for the mismatch, and that latest capacity can sit in the wrong shape at the wrong moment just as easily as the capacity already installed.

Maximizing GPU ROI takes more than a one-time provisioning decision. It calls for continuous, active management of the infrastructure itself, running every hour rather than only at procurement time. What's emerging in response is a distinct discipline, GPU Management, an orchestration layer sitting between workloads, models, and hardware. Its job is to decide, continuously, which workload runs, when it runs, how it runs, and on which specific GPU in the cluster. None of this is exotic in concept. It's closer to what a good operations team already does by instinct, just formalized and running continuously instead of depending on someone noticing a problem.

Intelligence doesn't stop at the model boundary. The orchestration layer is making real-time allocation decisions the model itself has no visibility into.

Sources indicate that intelligence used to sit almost entirely in the model: bigger, better trained, more capable, and that was most of the game. Now it also has to sit in the infrastructure, in the layer deciding, moment to moment, which of several competing workloads gets the GPU that just freed up, and at what priority relative to everything else waiting in the queue. Keeping GPUs busy stops being the goal on its own, since busy is easy to fake by running low priority work that could have waited. Maximizing the return generated by each installed GPU becomes the actual target, and that turns out to be a far more continuous problem than the provisioning question that came before it.

It has been revealed that provisioning well doesn't make this go away so much as change its shape. A provisioning decision gets made once, at purchase time. An allocation decision gets made constantly: every time a job finishes, every latest request that arrives, every shift in priority between a customer facing service and an internal training run. That frequency explains why the decision has moved from something a person handles case by case into something that has to run automatically. No engineer is watching a dashboard at three in the morning to decide whether a finished training run should hand its GPU to a queued batch job or hold it for an incoming burst of customer traffic. Something else has to make that call, continuously, and make it correctly often enough that nobody needs to check.

The discipline is latest enough that its tooling and conventions are still forming, and no single playbook has emerged yet for what a mature GPU Management practice looks like. What has settled, at least, is where the constraint moved.

Specialization and orchestration solve different halves of the same problem.

Industry observers note that specialized, smaller models can perform specific tasks at a fraction of the resource cost a large generalist model would need for the same job, without giving up the quality the task requires. That has a direct effect on utilization. Workloads that once required a single, large model, occupying a large share of a cluster's capacity for the full duration of the job, can instead run on smaller, task-specific models occupying a fraction of that footprint. Capacity that used to be entirely spoken for is suddenly free.

How much capacity specialization frees varies by workload and model, but the freed capacity still has to go somewhere or it just sits there. A smaller specialized model only converts into GPU ROI if something is actively deciding what happens next with the space it frees up, reallocating it to another workload, another model, another queue waiting behind it. Left unmanaged, freed capacity becomes a different flavor of idle rather than a win, invisible in a different way than an obviously unused GPU, but no more productive.

Specialization without orchestration frees capacity nobody reclaims. Orchestration without specialization has less capacity worth reclaiming. Neither lever does the whole job alone.

Industry observers note that specialization without orchestration frees capacity that nobody reclaims. Orchestration without specialization has less capacity worth reclaiming in the first place, because the models are still large and the footprint they leave behind is small. Neither lever does the whole job alone; each one raises the ceiling on what the other lever can achieve. Neither is optional if the goal is to actually close the gap between installed capacity and useful output, rather than shifting where the waste happens to sit.

This is why model architecture and GPU management are two ways to address the same problem, approached from two different directions that end up leaning on each other. One shrinks what each workload needs. The other decides, continuously, where the difference goes.

A bigger fleet has always been a real advantage, and nothing here argues otherwise. Among airlines with comparable fleets, sometimes even a smaller one facing a larger rival, the winner was usually whichever one flew what it had more completely, carrying the weight of everything the airline did well underneath it. Enterprise AI is arriving at the same discipline from a different direction. GPUs are already installed, already depreciating, already committed. Specialized models and GPU Management are parallel solutions, or bivalent strategies. Specialization shrinks what each workload needs. Management maximizes the return on infrastructure. Enterprises that master both will set the pace of AI competition for the next decade.

Explore Dharma AI on Hugging Face to try our interactive demos, download our open-source models, and discover how specialized AI systems outperform general-purpose models in real enterprise applications.

The next frontier is managing an entire fleet of agents and there is nothing stopping it.

Industry observers note that agreed. And the part that isn't priced in yet: a fleet of agents makes per-token cost scale linearly with the business. At some point large enterprises stop paying that curve and bring the models in-house — which doesn't remove the cost, it just trades a vendor price list for a utilization number. And agent fleets are brutal on utilization: real-time inference under latency SLAs, batch jobs, retraining, evals — all bursty, all fighting over the same finite pool. Managing the fleet is going to be, in large part, a GPU scheduling problem.

Recent findings suggest that scheduling is the core bottleneck of this problem. A CPU-like isolation mechanism, or a sandbox-based architecture on GPUs, could significantly alleviate this issue.

Recent findings suggest that good point, isolation is a real part of the picture. CPU-style boundaries (and the GPU sandboxing now landing, like the Kata Containers work) are what make it safe to co-locate unrelated workloads on the same card without fault or memory-contention risk, which widens the set of placements a scheduler is even allowed to make.

Taking that a step further: once co-location is safe, we have to decide which workload runs on which GPU, at what time, at what priority, given that each one wants something different from the hardware (memory footprint, latency tolerance, duration). Isolation gives you a bigger, safer decision space; something still has to pick the right point in it. And rigid partitioning can even cut utilization, since an idle slice can't lend capacity to a busy neighbor.

According to recent reports, that's exactly the direction we're taking next: an intelligent solution for job scheduling. We've got a follow-up article on it in the works, which will be published next week. Would be curious to get your read when it's out.

In a recent development, I expect we will see GPU rental systems become a thing. There are a lot of high-end GPUs sitting in consumer computers doing absolutely nothing for 90% of the day. Imagine if individuals could allow a training model to access their GPU remotely and in return pay them something in return. Yes, remote GPUs is not optimal, but with the consumer taking on the maintenance, power bill, and ownership of the GPU, any use the training model gets is a net positive.

Industry News: Presentation: RIIIR: Rewrite It In *Idiomatic* Rust (with AI)

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 42 min read (8443 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~42 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage Presentations RIIIR: Rewrite It In *Idiomatic* Rust (with AI).
  • According to recent reports, nicholas Matsakis shares why AI makes Rust the ideal choice for modern production systems, skipping steep adoption hurdles via compiler guardrails.
  • Niko Matsakis is one of the lead designers of the Rust programming language and co-lead of the Rust language design team.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage Presentations RIIIR: Rewrite It In *Idiomatic* Rust (with AI).

According to recent reports, nicholas Matsakis shares why AI makes Rust the ideal choice for modern production systems, skipping steep adoption hurdles via compiler guardrails. He discusses Symposium - an open-source, agent-oriented toolchain from the Rust Foundation - and demonstrates how the Agent Client Protocol (ACP) standardizes agent-to-tool extensibility across diverse enterprise developer workflows.

Niko Matsakis is one of the lead designers of the Rust programming language and co-lead of the Rust language design team. He is a Senior Principal Engineer at Amazon and a Project Director on the Rust Foundation Board. He is the creator of Symposium, an open-source platform for agent mods built on the Agent Client Protocol.

QCon AI is a practitioner-led event focused entirely on the engineering discipline required to scale these workloads safely. It provides direct access to the architectural playbooks and failure metrics that peer organizations use in production.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness.

Niko Matsakis: My name is Nicholas Matsakis. I am one of the lead designers of the Rust programming language. I've been working on it since 2011. I also am a senior principal engineer at Amazon. I started there about five years ago, in part because Amazon has been adopting tons of Rust, and I wanted to see it firsthand, see how it was going. I'm going to just show my whole cards with you and just tell you all the things I'm going to tell you. Step one, I'm going to try to convince you that Rust and AI is a really great combination, perhaps better than some of the alternatives out there. I have a project I'm curious to get feedback on that I think makes it even better, which I call Symposium, and covers up some of the gaps I see. Next, that actually, if you look at how Symposium works, what you'll find is it reveals something about the way we're currently building all our development tools here, which is that individual vendors, like Anthropic or OpenAI or whatever, everyone's trying to build a complete tool that solves all the problems, and I want to see us do more of an extensibility story where people can plug in and add things and you have a whole bunch of extensions. I think we're only scraping the surface of what is possible, but it's very difficult to do with the way the tools are set up now. Then I'll talk to you about Agent Client Protocol, which is an interesting way to get past that and get to a more extensible model.

Recent findings suggest that how many have heard of Rust? Rust is all about having a language that can go as low-level as you want, as efficient, give you as much control over the hardware. Low-level enough to be used in a kernel, but be productive. High-level enough that you can write application-level software in it, and it's not too bad. It may not be the minimum line count or what have you, but it's not too bad. Low-level enough for a kernel, I mean that quite literally. You have the user, they're typing over on their keyboard, and they're running a program, like a CLI or a GUI. That program is talking to the agent and managing that whole communication. On the flip side, you have a bunch of editors, so Zed, but also all the IntelliJ family ones.

Emacs, still holding on. I still love Emacs. Neovim, we don't talk about Neovim in my household, but I understand people like it. Also, things that are a little different. They're not code editors, like Obsidian. I don't know if anyone here uses Obsidian. It's like a Markdown management information system. They have an ACP connection. Similarly, there's these pretty amazing CLI frontends like Toad and Nori. Toad in particular blew my mind. You just have to try it. You would never believe that it's a TUI. It can do all kinds of things I didn't think were even possible. The nice thing about these CLIs is they're just focusing on the interface. They don't have to worry about the agent.

Sources indicate that then what's really interesting is we're starting to see applications, not surprisingly to me, that go beyond editors. Because once you have something that's extensible, suddenly people start coming up with new, fresh ideas like OpenClaw. How does OpenClaw talk to the agents? I don't know if you all have used OpenClaw. It does a lot of things. Because I think what they did before was they ran an agent in a CLI in like a Pt, Ty and scraped it off, and tried to figure out what it was doing and it was just horrible.

Because that's not really the way that programs like to interact with each other. Now they have something more structured. Something I've been enjoying is building scripts, which is a similar programmatic frontend. This is one I have called retcon, which rewrites your git history, because my git histories are always a total mess. It lets you write kind of LangChain-esque, I was thinking today. I hadn't realized that before. The idea is you'll spin up the agent and then you can send messages to invoke things. Like here, I can send a prompt to it, like I want you to extract changes for this git commit. Then when it comes back, the answer is actually translated into a Rust struct. The way that works is I put in a temporary MCP tool and say, when you're done, invoke this MCP tool with some JSON. I start to interact with the LLM as just a fancy function that I could never have written myself, like extract the changes for step one of this git refactoring.

This gets us to the latest thing that I've been trying to do with ACP and how this connects to extensibility. So far, we've seen that if you put an interface in between a client and an agent, you can have novel kinds of clients or novel kinds of agents. Side note, how many of you remember ELIZA? I wrote an ELIZA ACP, which I think is great. ELIZA is just like a hacky regex that really feels like you're talking to a therapist, even though it's not. 1970s AI resurgence. You have novel clients, agents, but you can also put stuff in between. That's what I call an agent mod. A lot of the stuff I revealed you, or at least some of it anyway, is using some of this. It's still like an unstable part of the spec, but it's like middleware. What's cool about it is that now, unlike all the other extension mechanisms I talked about, it's in charge.

Sources indicate that it can see, what did you type? Should I modify it? Should I add stuff? Should I do context augmentation? What should I do to your prompt before I send it to the agent? It can say, here's the tools I would like the agent to have available to it. It can take the responses from the agent and fork off sub-agents, which is also something you can't, as a program, do, and have parallel work happening, can move to other servers, whatever. It's super cool. It's a little scary. I think this is the thing I'm really interested in exploring. For this to work, of course, we have to get ACP-wise used more broadly and so on. Here's me saying, use Zed, or IntelliJ. They're really good. Plus, they use ACP. Everybody wins. I'm expecting that we will see more things like this, whether it's ACP or something else.

Industry observers note that as agentic coding becomes more mainstream, we're going to need to have some standards that let us build on top of it and build more complex workflows. One of the places we're seeing a lot of interest, actually, is in enterprise applications and so on, where they want to build integrations for their employees to offer a better experience than just a CLI.

Industry observers note that you should use Rust for your next project, especially if you're using AI. If you've tried it and bounced, give it another try because it feels different now. Second, when you do it, use Symposium, cargo agents init. Easy. Third, portability sucks, but I hope it will get better.

Participant 1: For teams that are not familiar with Rust, what's your recommendation on how to start with it? Because with AI, you can really start along with building immediately, and we do, but the fear is that you don't understand the language completely, but then it may end up in production. What's your recommendations for teams that are just starting and they want to ship faster or something like that?

It has been revealed that niko Matsakis: How do you avoid digging yourself into a hole? That is exactly what battery packs are meant to answer, but I'm still trying to make them a real thing. First off, I worry a little less these days because it's so much easier to make changes. Even if you've built stuff, refactoring it is easier. Secondly, what I found really helpful when I'm learning new things is to just really aggressively ask the LLM about its choices. Like it made some choices. You could ask it why. Often, it will give you a good answer. Sometimes it'll say, you're right, that was a bad choice. I'm like, I didn't mean to imply that actually, but ok, go ahead, refactor it. It can go both ways. You don't just have to take the code. You can ask it all about the code and so forth. I think that's the best that I know of. Of course, what I've seen within Amazon, the old advice is still true. Hire someone who knows Rust. That's the surefire way. If you can't do that, then as you get experience, of course, you'll start to have homegrown experts of your own.

It has been revealed that participant 2: I think a lot of us have noticed when writing skills and however much stuff you put in place to try and ensure that the LLM actually uses it or uses it as intended, and so on, sometimes it will just not do it or ignore it. That kind of skills are too loose, hooks are too hard. How do you make it deterministically actually use this stuff? Have you found through this Symposium project any ways to do that better or make sure it actually does the right thing?

Sources indicate that niko Matsakis: How do we nudge the LLM to be more deterministic? This is exactly why I'm so interested in ACP, actually. I'll give you an example, that retcon thing I revealed you, it began as just a giant LLM script where I told it how to rebase and do stuff. What I found was it worked like 90%. Usually, it would forget some parts of the branch. It just would be like, I'm done. I'm like, no, you're not, you've left off a whole thing. Or it wouldn't check that the test pass and everything else. Now when it's written in Rust, like I'm guaranteed every commit passes the test, every commit is formatted because it's got a deterministic backing. I have been toying with similar things for skills where I had experiments where I would detect with some various heuristics and things that I thought a skill was probably good and give it some extra hints to avoid that problem.

In a recent development, I've backed off from a lot of that, partly because models get better, but also because I think we need telemetry first. Ubuntu Core Desktop targets 28.04 debut, with default status in its sights

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1538 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Canonical's stretch goal is to make the immutable OS standard in 30.04 – without retiring the traditional distro.
  • Canonical is targeting Ubuntu 28.04 LTS for the release of its immutable Core Desktop, with a stretch goal of making it the default download for Ubuntu 30.04.
  • Canonical's VP of engineering, Jon Seager, set out the timetable in his opening keynote at Ubuntu Summit 26.10.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Canonical's stretch goal is to make the immutable OS standard in 30.04 – without retiring the traditional distro.

Canonical is targeting Ubuntu 28.04 LTS for the release of its immutable Core Desktop, with a stretch goal of making it the default download for Ubuntu 30.04.

Canonical's VP of engineering, Jon Seager, set out the timetable in his opening keynote at Ubuntu Summit 26.10. Yes, we know, we have heard this before: we reported on his aims last month. But this time, there's the beginning of a release schedule.

Seager stated that Ubuntu Core is already out there in tens of thousands of IoT devices – which seems like a modest estimate to us, and to him too, as he quickly added "maybe more." Despite some noise a few years ago, though, what's still missing is the desktop version.

Seager's slides listed three bullet points: that Core Desktop will be "immutable," "composable," and "attestable.".

As he put it, they are "taking the whole of the Linux operating system, and cramming the whole thing into snaps." Acknowledging that this is going to be wildly controversial, he noted: "This is one for the Redditors.".

In a recent development, he's right. There is a lot of resistance to snap, and in direct response, advocacy of the Red Hat-backed Flatpak instead – but we have seen almost none that is based on either system's technical merits. Much of that opposition concerns claims of one being more open than the other. We've looked at how both systems work, and our impression is that the implementation of snap is cleaner, simpler, easier to use, and more comprehensible. Snap does depend on systemd, which Flatpak does not – but only for now. Flatpak NG is in development and will also need everyone's favorite init system.

Ubuntu Core's immutability is not latest technology: even Core 16 is now a decade old. It has supported in-place version upgrades since Core 22.

We have reported before that Canonical remains strongly committed to its packaging format, and that commitment seems stronger than ever. Seager continued: "Never has a model like snap confinement been more relevant… we're finally in a position where we can bring this to the desktop.".

According to recent reports, the core idea of an immutable OS is that "much more of the system is not writable at runtime," meaning that it "can't be messed with once the system has booted." He talked about the same three use cases we discussed last month. The "browser-centric machine" is the company's analog to Google ChromeOS, and he mentioned that it's essentially ready now, suggesting that everyone listening probably has a family member whose computer is basically just a way to use a web browser.

The second was the dedicated games machine, which we interpret as a response to Valve's SteamOS. This edition, he mentioned, would "boot straight to Steam," with "just enough of a shell to launch games." There's also an immutable "development workstation," and here, he offered the example of developers who need to work on some long-unsupported hardware or software, for whom an immutable OS means that you "can't brick your system by installing some weird old dependencies, unmaintained for 20 years.".

Another vital benefit is "atomic, transactional updates," which he stated "brings enormous stability." The terminology comes from the database world: an atomic operation succeeds as a whole or is not applied. The aim is to avoid leaving the system stranded between incompatible package versions, with rollback providing a route back if an enhancement causes trouble.

Ubuntu VP of Engineering Jon Seager.

The "composable" part means assembling the OS from separately packaged components, from desktop environments to underlying services such as PipeWire and fingerprint-reader support.

Here, Seager used an example that spoke to us. He asked: "Ever installed something and watch as it spewed stuff all over your system?" Yes, we have, many, many times. You install one innocent-seeming little component, and it brings in a database, three newly introduced server components, and about half of a different desktop environment. We mentioned an example when we described how to customize Xfce a couple of months ago. That time around, in Debian, we found it was safe to install all packages starting with "xfce4-" except "xfce4-dev-tools." Most are tiny panel controls taking just hundreds of kilobytes, but the "dev-tools" package also pulls in several hundred megabytes of compilers, linkers, and other programming tools, totally unrelated to desktop layouts – and once installed, they're surprisingly tricky to remove again.

This is part of the appeal of a composable immutable OS: adding a component need not mean tangling its dependencies into the base system. But easier housekeeping isn't the only attraction. Canonical kept snap packages from its cancelled phone and tablet OS because snaps enable it to maintain a single package of, for instance, Firefox, which will work on all of its different OS versions that are still getting updates. Moving such important external dependencies into isolated snap packages makes it easier and safer to upgrade from one version of the OS to another. Complex sets of dependencies are the main point of failure of OS upgrades, especially when the OS has been used for a while.

Industry observers note that this is very much not a solved problem. For instance, Debian version upgrades can be fraught – especially when the installation has decades of history behind it. Debian does at least support version-to-version upgrades. For many years and versions, RHEL did not – which is why we highlighted AlmaLinux's tooling for the task. Zorin OS added version-to-version upgrades in 16.3 just a few years ago. Linux Mint introduced its own upgrade tooling a few years earlier, although it still imposes restrictions.

It's a tough problem to crack. Major enterprise vendors discourage it, and phone OSes are all immutable. Helping with this problem is one of the main reasons snap packaging exists, while Flatpak is almost entirely irrelevant to it.

Seager also stated that Core Desktop would support "multiple desktops from the start." This will not be a GNOME-only project. Indeed, he specifically mentioned a KDE Plasma version, saying: "Plasma is great. People love it. We will have a KDE edition, with rolling Plasma. We will deliver upstream Plasma, as fast as we can." That sounds like a very welcome counterpoint to the LTS version of Plasma 6.6 in Kubuntu 26.04 whose announcement we covered back in August.

For the "attestable" line of the slide, he claimed that Core Desktop was "evolving the way we think about 'trust' on a machine. We have TPM, secure boot, TPM-backed Full Disk Encryption… but they're all bolt-ons." Core Desktop, he added, could "tie this into a hardware root of trust," delivering "verified system integrity." Canonical revived its TPM-backed full-disk encryption system back in 2025, and it arrived in Ubuntu 26.04. Back in January, systemd creator Lennart Poettering launched his startup Amutable, and earlier this month published a technical overview of its new immutable Linux. We suspect Canonical is watching closely, and that this is a hint in that direction.

We were also amused by Seager's mention of another rather niche distro: he noted that Core Desktop would deliver "all of the joy that people derive from NixOS, for those with that perverse habit – but for everybody.".

Daily preview installation images of Core Desktop will, apparently, be available very soon, in both GNOME and KDE flavors, and he warned that "there be dragons." (That may be a veiled nod to one of founder Mark Shuttleworth's other companies.).

Sources indicate that after the promises made in 2023, we'll be watching that timetable closely. "I believe this is the future of Linux," Seager said, promising "a final version by 28.04, released alongside Ubuntu," adding that a "very stretchy stretch goal was by default for 30.04: download from ubuntu.com and you get Core Desktop – unless you ask for the other thing.".

For those alarmed by that prospect, he had reassurance: "Ubuntu as you know it today is not going anywhere. There are no prepares for the existing distro to go away.".

According to recent reports, core Desktop wasn't even the main subject of his keynote. They followed a lengthy excursion into formal logic: definitions, proofs, invariants, and designing software whose behavior can be checked against precisely stated rules. The accompanying slides showed the logos of organizations working in this area, such as Hegel, Antithesis, and the Lean programming language. For now, an entire OS is much too big to formally verify, but subcomponents may be doable – and Canonical is starting with snapd.

According to recent reports, he also expressed his satisfaction with the Stonking release, highlighting that it advanced Canonical's move toward Rust-based components, including Rustls and upki – noting that this proved very timely in the light of recent events. The release also delivered the newest available kernel, OpenSSL 4 – which he called a "huge change" – and official RISC-V images. He also called out the Myna speech-recognition feature, saying that it was all in-house, designed and shipped in six months by a team of "about two and a half people." It will form part of the tech giant's looks for what it calls a context-aware desktop. ®.

#23538. Mutex poisoning is not for everyone

Mutex poisoning is not for everyone

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2118 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bertptrs

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After some recent discussion on the topic of mutex poisoning and notably a blog post that I thought was interesting, thoughtful, exhaustive, yet completely disagreed with, I wanted to comment on the debate myself.
  • In short, I believe that Mutex poisoning is the wrong choice for most applications, as.
  • In theory, a mutex guards a critical section of the code.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After some recent discussion on the topic of mutex poisoning and notably a blog post that I thought was interesting, thoughtful, exhaustive, yet completely disagreed with, I wanted to comment on the debate myself. To me, poisoning-by-default is one of biggest mistakes that were made in the language, next to some others that are a story for a different time.

In short, I believe that Mutex poisoning is the wrong choice for most applications, as.

In theory, a mutex guards a critical section of the code. That code changes the state of a piece of data free from interference of concurrent threads, then releases the lock. That code might then encounter an error, and release the lock in the middle of doing its crucial work. For example:.

It has been revealed that the following code will work fine most of the time, but if the dice roll doesn’t go our way, the always_even mutex gets unlocked in an invalid state. In Rust, today, poisoning exists to handle this. If a guard is released abnormally (while panicking), it records that this happened in a boolean. Any future calls to lock() will return Err(PoisonError), which will trigger a panic when we unwrap it. The bad state is never observed and all is well.

According to recent reports, you might have felt that the example I made up was somewhat contrived. That’s because it is. Real cases of this pattern can and do happen, but most of the use cases that involve mutexes are much simpler. Many critical sections are no longer than a variable assignment, or doesn’t have an invalid in-between state. There are cases in lower level programming where a mutex guards a piece of data that is not directly inside it, or is outside the view of the program entirely. In fact, I’ve written a wrapper for a C library that worked like that. Though I disagree with the notion that this is the common case.

It has been revealed that I do recommend anyone Rain’s blog on the matter, as she has some good examples of how you can cause violations of these critical sections (even without mutexes) and I wholeheartedly support the idea of a Poison wrapper for the use cases that need it. I suspect the domains she works on lend themselves more towards these problems compared to mine. Rust’s default behaviour should make the common case easy and the rare case possible.

This section is only tangentially related to the topic at hand, but I already wrote it and wasn’t ready to kill my darlings.1 Skip to the next section to continue the discussion on poisoning.

It has been revealed that in Rust, for most platforms, mutexes are implemented using the futex2 system call. It allows for operations to remain purely in user-space as long as the mutex in question isn’t contended, which is nice for performance reasons.

Under the hood, a mutex is a simple 32-bit integer on most platforms even though it only holds three unique values:.

It has been revealed that flow chart showing how a mutex acquisition is implemented in Rust, using atomic operations and futex primitives. Note how the uncontended case remains entirely in user-space and does not sleep the thread.

Rust implements this with a few atomic operations and the futex_wait call. Crucially, the path for locking a mutex that isn’t contended is a single atomic operation. The only operation that requires a context switch is futex_wait.

Unlocking is even simpler. The thread that holds the mutex first releases the lock, then optionally, if there was an indication that the lock was contended, wakes any sleeping threads so they can try to acquire the lock.

It has been revealed that flow chart showing how a mutex release in Rust. First, we swap the current value with 0, and depending on whether it was originally 1 (simply locked) or 2 (contended), we optionally wake any sleeping threads.

According to recent reports, as discussed in too much detail above, (un)locking mutexes is cheap as long as they’re not contended, and when contended, they are at least cheap instruction wise. This is where poisoning mutexes get you.

Recent findings suggest that in short, being able to poison is a cost that is always paid, but seldom used. To start, poisoning is essentially implemented by adding an AtomicBool field to every Mutex. Due to alignment, this grows the size of every mutex by anywhere from zero bytes to an additional pointer. This isn’t terrible but for use cases where you have many mutexes guarding small objects, this can add up.

Recent findings suggest that the real issue to me however is in code size. Let’s start with another contrived example, a function that reads its argument, copies it, and returns it. An idealised version of that would be the following.

This compiles down to 2 instructions and a label. Copy the data into the register then return.

It has been revealed that of course, this doesn’t work for any context that needs shared mutation, but we can consider it our baseline. Perfection would look like this. So, let’s ignore that atomic integers exist and add a mutex to this story. We will go over the generated assembly code for each, and you can compare the code in its entirety in this Compiler Explorer overview.

We can patch the code above to actually use mutexes, and simply lock-then-unwrap the mutex.

This compiles to a total of 147 lines of assembly which I’m not going to reproduce here in full.

To divide that up a different way, we have.

According to recent reports, most of this is inlined into the function. This in turn affects performance, as this limits how much of your “real” code fits in the CPU’s instruction cache. The laptop I’m writing this on has a paltry 32KiB of instruction cache. Luckily we can do better.

Most of the code generated in the previous example had to do with setting up the panic, and checking the conditions. But we don’t care about panicking. We can simply acknowledge the PoisonError and continue. That looks as follows:.

In a recent development, this results in only 68 lines of assembly, which is much better, though all of it is inlined to our function. Compared to before, we’ve lost all panic related code. There’s still some unnecessary branching related to whether the mutex is poisoned, as well as a little dance to track poisoning in our function. Our function can never panic, but compiler optimisations currently do not remove the atomic loads and stores involved here. Nevertheless, if you want to target stable Rust and you don’t care about panics, this is what you should do at the moment.

Sources indicate that in the current nightly builds of Rust, there are non-poisoning mutexes that can don’t have any of the overhead. We can optimise our code from above to make use of them.

In a recent development, no unwrapping, and it only results in 34 lines of assembly code. This is short enough for me to walk through it.

I’ve added comments and labels to the assembly so the steps from the (un)locking flow charts become visible. As far as assembly code goes, it’s very readable and simple. Which, of course, is exactly what you want from fundamental library code.

The additional logic checking the poison state, adding a destructor for the mutex guard, and, if you choose ergonomics, even panic machinery, significantly bloats the code of a rather fundamental operation.

In a recent development, besides the purely technical argument that poisoning makes all code larger and slower than it needs to be, there is a different one. As discussed previously, code that doesn’t care about mutex poisoning should generally write:.

It’s reasonably efficient and available on stable Rust. But that whole unwrap_or_else part takes up more than half the line. No worry, you might say, we can make it shorter:.

Industry observers note that this works well enough. It’s less efficient than the previous example, but it’s nice and short. If your code never panics, it’s even perfectly safe. You might have spotted a load-bearing “if” already. It’s kind of hard to guarantee your code does not panic. Array indexing, integer division, and a whole host of other features might panic unexpectedly.

It has been revealed that this is hard for experienced developers, but for those learning it’s even worse. It also trains bad habits. Every time a beginner Rust developer writes unwrap() instead of handling their errors, a puppy steps on a Lego brick. Or causes a widespread internet outage. One of the two, I forget which.

Sources indicate that we should not want to include APIs into the standard library that return a Result that is “expected” to be unwrapped. Infallible operations should not fail.

Poisoning protects against a task panicking in the middle of an invariant violation. But why must this be specific to mutexes? The example from before works just as well with a simple mutable borrow. Panics may still happen, and you may still catch them.

According to recent reports, this is actually a fairly common problem. In a more recent blog post, researchers at Microsoft highlight various places they’ve found where even the standard library gets this wrong.

In most cases however, this is fine, as it is with the mutex example given in the beginning. You don’t need to poison this reference. But for applications where you do, it’s kinda nice to be able to.

It’s not hard to imagine a wrapper that adds poisoning behaviour when you want to have it. Crucially, this needs to be an additive wrapper. You can add a poisoning system to something. You cannot strip out the poisoning system from a primitive that has it. Poison safety is important for the specific use cases that need it, but most do not.

It has been revealed that I don’t believe it’s worth it to saddle mutexes in particular with this overhead when the problem is near universal with any mutable state. State invariants are just hard that way.

According to recent reports, one might draw a comparison between poison safety and buffer safety. In Rust, we always do bounds checking, relying on the compiler to optimise it out in cases it can be proven redundant. Can’t poison safety be the same? And the answer, it turns out, is no.

Sources indicate that the compiler cannot optimise poisoning away. It requires any mutex carry additional data to track it. Maybe the compiler can figure out one particular critical section cannot panic, and therefore it can leave out the setup and clean-up, but in general it cannot avoid checking the state. This is overhead that always applies, and hurts, especially in environments where code size is more restricted.

In C++, there are a few choices in the standard that make certain containers less efficient than they could be4. Because of how standardisation works, the containers can never be “fixed”. This causes third party implementations, such as Abseil and Boost, to become the de facto standard.

In a recent development, mutexes in Rust suffer from the same problem. The standard library has poisoning, but people don’t want poisoning, so instead they opt for crates like parking_lot. I believe this is bad for the ecosystem as a whole. When the standard library offers a feature, it should be an uncontroversially good choice, unless you are doing something hyper specific. We don’t have to be “batteries included” but the parts that are there should be a good fit.

According to recent reports, rain’s blog argued for option 1. I believe we both agree that option 2 is a terrible idea. I think we should do at least option 3. Option 4 would be a good edition improvement, but it is also a significant compatibility issue, and even I find it hard to argue that it’s really worth it.

Which is a roundabout way of saying that we really should stabilise std::sync::nonpoison and definitely should not make std::sync::Mutex panic by default.

Recent findings suggest that it is becoming apparent to me that I just like explaining mutexes and I don’t know what to do about that. ↩︎.

Fast Userspace muTEX. See futex(2) for more on the system call and futex(7) for its semantics ↩︎.

In a recent development, for generic definitions (e.g. Mutex) the compiler must generate code for every unique T that gets used, and for loads of reasons often more than once per T. The compiler development docs have a deeper explanation of monomorphisation. ↩︎.

A famous example is std::unordered_map, which suffers from being over-specified and that prevents more efficient implementations. ↩︎.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We're thrilled to share that Baseten is now a supported Inference Provider on the Hugging Face Hub!

In a recent development, baseten joins our growing ecosystem, enhancing the breadth and capabilities of serverless inference directly on the Hub's model pages. Inference Providers are also seamlessly integrated into our client SDKs (for both JS and Python), making it super easy to use a wide variety of models with your preferred providers.

Baseten is an AI infrastructure platform that covers serverless AI, training and more. With a catalog of many frontier models, Baseten makes it easy for developers to integrate a wide range of AI capabilities into their applications with minimal setup.

Recent findings suggest that baseten supports a broad spectrum of model types - from LLMs to text-to-speech and more. As part of this initial integration, Baseten is launching support for conversational and text-generation tasks on Hugging Face, enabling access to popular open-weight LLMs such as Kimi K3, latest DeepSeek V4 Flash, GLM-5.2, and many more. Support for additional tasks will roll out soon!

See the full list of models supported by Baseten here.

Follow Baseten on Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/baseten.

Baseten is available through the Hugging Face SDKs - huggingface_hub (>= 1.26.1) for Python and @huggingface/inference for JavaScript.

The following examples show how to use the latest DeepSeek V4 Flash through Baseten. Use a Hugging Face token to authenticate - the request will be routed to Baseten automatically.

Industry observers note that hugging Face Inference Providers are integrated in most Agent Harnesses - including Pi, OpenCode, Hermes Agents, OpenClaw, and more. This means you can plug baseten-hosted models straight into your favorite tools without any extra glue code. Browse the full list of integrations here.

For direct requests, i.e. when you use the key from an inference provider, you are billed by the corresponding provider. For instance, if you use a baseten API key you're billed on your baseten account.

It has been revealed that for routed requests, i.e. when you authenticate via the Hugging Face Hub, you'll only pay the standard provider API rates. There's no additional markup from us; we just pass through the provider costs directly. (In the future, we may establish revenue-sharing agreements with our provider partners.).

Sources indicate that important Note ‼️ PRO people get $2 worth of Inference credits every month. You can use them across providers. 🔥.

We also provide free inference with a small quota for our signed-in free owners, but please upgrade to PRO if you can!

Sources indicate that we would love to get your feedback! Share your thoughts and/or comments here: https://huggingface.co/spaces/huggingface/HuggingDiscussions/discussions/49.

Industry observers note that thank you, beautiful work. I’ll take a closer look at it soon!

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Optional patch fixes misleading Android error for versions 25H2 and 26H2.
  • According to recent reports, A Windows 11 passkey bug can leave Android phones announcing that authentication failed even when it succeeded.
  • In a recent development, the problem occurs when customers sign in on a Windows 11 PC using a passkey stored on an Android phone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Optional patch fixes misleading Android error for versions 25H2 and 26H2.

According to recent reports, A Windows 11 passkey bug can leave Android phones announcing that authentication failed even when it succeeded. Microsoft has now released a fix for versions 25H2 and 26H2.

In a recent development, the problem occurs when customers sign in on a Windows 11 PC using a passkey stored on an Android phone. Scan the QR code, and the Android device might display the message: "Something went wrong. Restart the process on your other device and try again.".

Industry observers note that except it might not have gone wrong at all. Microsoft's guidance explains: "In cases where authentication completes successfully on the Windows device, the error message on the Android device is not supposed to appear and can be safely ignored.".

According to recent reports, cross-device authentication lets people sign in on one device using a passkey held on another, without typing a password or copying a verification code. Microsoft claims the matter affects operations using Microsoft Authenticator and Google Password Manager, and can occur in Edge or Chrome – not just when signing in through Microsoft Entra ID.

Cross-device passkey operations with an iPhone aren't affected.

Sources indicate that an authentication system that cries failure after a successful sign-in isn't doing much for user confidence. Nor will it endear itself to support teams fielding the resulting tickets.

According to recent reports, microsoft has included a fix in KB5132057, the optional non-security preview update released on November 19 for Windows 11 25H2 and 26H2. Until affected devices are patched, owners can ignore the Android error if authentication has completed successfully on the PC. ®.

Lisp Game Jam devlog: Polydraw

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1963 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Spritely

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This year's Autumn Lisp Game Jam has just wrapped up!
  • The rest of this post is a daily devlog of how we made Polydraw so you can see what the process look likes to make a game with Goblins and Hoot under a tight deadline.
  • First, we created a Git repository on Codeberg and copied the Hoot game jam template into it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This year's Autumn Lisp Game Jam has just wrapped up! Spritely's contribution to the jam was Polydraw, a peer-to-peer party game that is easy to pick up and play with friends. In Polydraw, players take turns being the artist who draws an image based on a prompt. The catch is that the artist only has 60 seconds and can only draw using triangles. All of the other players are guessers who try to correctly guess the prompt. We're quite pleased with how the game turned out!

The rest of this post is a daily devlog of how we made Polydraw so you can see what the process look likes to make a game with Goblins and Hoot under a tight deadline.

It's go time! First, we created a Git repository on Codeberg and copied the Hoot game jam template into it.

Since the core activity in Polydraw is drawing triangles, the first thing Dave implemented was an interface for doing that on a canvas. This first version was crude and didn't include a color picker.

We took the weekend off to prepare for a busy week ahead.

This is the day that we really got to work on the game jam.

Industry observers note that the first version of the triangle editor stored pixel coordinates of the local canvas, but that wasn't going to be good enough to display on other machines with different sized canvases. So, Dave simply normalized triangle vertices into the [0,1] range so each peer could scale them as needed.

Dave also implemented a basic scene system, a common game programming pattern, to encapsulate the coarse game states such as the title screen, the lobby, and the main game.

A color palette was added along with some additional mockup UI around the canvas.

It has been revealed that with a good enough game engine in place, we turned our attention to the game protocol. Since we are using Goblins, all interactions are modeled using actors. Dave came up with the following actors:.

Player: Used for player identity within the game and contains the player's self-proposed name.

Recent findings suggest that lobby: The place where players gather before the game starts. The player that creates the lobby is the host and all other players are guests.

Game: Holds all of the game state like the player list, whose turn it is, and the scoreboard.

Industry observers note that controller: A player's virtual game controller. Used to speak to the game actor, but all actions are scoped to the individual player.

A test script was written to simulate creating a game, joining the lobby, and playing a round. At this stage, everything was happening in a single process. Goblins makes it easy to start with a single process and then distribute the actors to multiple machines later.

It has been revealed that now it was time to get the actors onto the network and hook them up to the game UI. For networking we used OCapN, naturally. Jessica started up an instance of our upcoming end-to-end encrypted relay netlayer that we set as the default relay so the game would "just work" when we uploaded it to itch.io. In fact, dogfooding the relay was a large part of the motivation behind participating in the game jam in the first place!

Dave got the actors online with OCapN and connected the game UI to the actors, then confirmed that a three player game works. Three players is the minimum number of players needed to trigger OCapN's third-party handoff feature. Handoffs are what enable distributed networking in OCapN: Alice can give Bob a reference to Carol, which causes Bob and Carol to establish a upcoming OCapN session with each other. This is the first application we've made that does handoffs over the relay netlayer and it was nice to see them working as intended.

Industry observers note that unfortunately, we discovered an concern with how Goblins handles two peers connecting to each other concurrently, a problem known as "crossed hellos". OCapN mandates that only one connection may be open between any two peers, so we have to pick which connection wins. The bug is that any promises that were created over the losing connection never resolve. This was observed in the game as an empty lobby player list that should be populated. It didn't prevent the rest of the game from working, though, so we didn't try to fix it (yet).

On this day, Dave discovered that, despite his best efforts, he fell victim to the "identity footgun". We could write a whole blog post series about the many subtle complications of object identity (in the sense of Scheme's eq?) in object capability systems, but instead we'll refer you to the The Grant Matcher Puzzle and just mention that using object references as keys in associative data structures is error-prone. A promise that eventually resolves to a reference to Alice is not identical (again, in the eq? sense) to a reference to Alice. So, if you accidentally use a promise as a key somewhere or use eq? directly you will probably have a bad time, which is exactly what happened to us.

Sources indicate that to deal with this identity crisis, Dave first detected it at runtime by writing a wrapper around eq? called geq?. This latest predicate throws an error when comparing a promise to a non-promise. Then he used the resulting backtraces to find the offending code and change it to resolve all necessary promises before doing identity comparisons.

Christine finally cleared enough other things off her plate where she could start contributing to the game. We thought it would be nice to have the game start with a splash screen of triangle'y animations that would resemble the kinds of art players would make in the game. We decided to use the Blender add-on by Ursula Kurdali named Stop Motion since it gives a great amount of freedom to animate by creating and destroying as much geometry as you like. Christine made the first mockup of a splash screen animation of a "death" type character swinging a scythe.

Recent findings suggest that however, the animation hadn't left Blender yet. We're gonna have to figure out how to get those polygons out and into the game engine!

In a recent development, this was the day to finish implementing the core game loop. We wanted the weekend to be all about fixing bugs and making it look and feel as good as we can. At last, the points awarded at the end of each round were displayed in the UI. The player list on the left side of the screen was transformed into a leaderboard that sorted players by score.

While creating the leaderboard it was discovered that Goblins was not correctly parsing pairs received over OCapN. Christine swooped in with a quick fix and Jessica folowed up with a regression test.

Industry observers note that we also added a small set of emoji reactions underneath the leaderboard. Reactions were not critical to the core gameplay but they were planned from the very beginning of the project. It's good that we had time to add them because it was a lot of fun to spam emojis at the artist to give them an indication of how good or bad they were doing.

Industry observers note that with two days left and the core gameplay loop complete, the focus shifted to bug fixing and adding juice. Up until this point the HTML was mostly unstyled (as you can see in the videos above), so Dave added a little CSS to improve the look and feel.

Recent findings suggest that A playtest revealed that the simple PRNG we were using was implemented incorrectly. We noticed because the artist prompt was always "bus" no matter how many rounds you played. Oops! This was fixed.

Sources indicate that remember that crossed hellos bug from day 7? Dave finally implemented a workaround, which was to simply throw out the first pancake and try again, as suggested by Christine. A simple race against a timeout was all that was needed. We'll be thinking about how to fix this in Goblins so this situation cannot happen in the future.

Christine started work on making more animations for the game's intro. The "death" animation was a good "hello world" for testing the exporter, but being all black it was too simple to make sure everything worked right; draw order, etc, didn't matter. Christine made a "square guys" animation as a kind of Acid2 test equivalent. This file had several tricky properties to it, most especially that draw order would matter, colors would be key, et cetera.

Christine also made this triangle'y duck themed piece:.

It has been revealed that christine wrote a Python script to export the animations from Blender into a custom format encoded using Syrup. The encoded data was then embedded into the Scheme program as bytevector literals using a little script. Dave then started work on a renderer for these animations, but it wasn't working quite well enough by the end of the day to commit and push it.

According to recent reports, up until this point we only had a small number of frequently-repeated words. Morgan Lemmer-Webber curated a word list for us, starting with an existing public domain word list of 5000 words, and curated down to a 621 words, selecting for words that were more feasible to draw (ranging from easy to challenging, but all trying to be feasible).

The game name was changed from the placeholder "Twenty Triangles" to "Polydraw".

The code to render animations was finished. Some final minor bug fixes were made. Some CSS was tweaked. Original music and sound effects by encrypted.whispers were added. Additionally, we used a few CC0-licensed sound effects by Kenney.

In a recent development, A few gameplay improvements were made, such as showing guessers what the prompt was when the round ends and how many triangles the artist had remaining. Little improvements can make a big difference and both of these changes were very helpful for players and made the game feel more polished.

There wasn't enough time remaining to do as much work on resiliency in the face of network partitions as we would have liked, but Dave did squeeze in a commit that allowed the game to survive if a guest leaves. Unfortunately, the experience for the disconnected guest isn't very good as they don't see any message that their connection dropped.

According to recent reports, we did a final playtest to confirm that there weren't any showstopper bugs. Christine added final splash animations.

Finally, Christine added some code (fixed up by Dave) and animations which would overlay over the drawings indicating that drawing was starting, it was time to guess, or the results.

We submitted the game two hours before the deadline! Now it was time to catch our breath and show off the game to everyone we could. Dave even played it live with a couple other people on a stream! Here's a screenshot which gives you a good look of the final result:.

The response was quite positive! The feedback we received closely matched the things we wanted to improve upon if we had more time: better disconnect handling, a way for the host to skip to the next phase instead of being forced to wait for the timer to run out, and invite URLs (rather than URIs) that auto-join the game when visited.

Polydraw ranked 5th overall in the official game jam results.

Try playing it over on itch.io and leave us a comment!

Industry observers note that your support makes our work possible! If you like what we do, please consider becoming a Spritely supporter today!

Meta is back with Muse Glimmer: local, agentic, multimodal, and open source

📅 10 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2173 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Great news from the OGs of open source LLMs!
  • Industry observers note that to celebrate, we are shipping with Meta day-0 support in transformers, llama.cpp, vLLM, Inference Endpoints, and other libraries.
  • Bold indicates the best result among the compared models; ↓ indicates lower is better.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Great news from the OGs of open source LLMs! Muse Glimmer, released today, is Meta’s new multimodal model, especially designed for local agentic use cases. Distilled from Muse to 30B parameters, and released under the Apache 2.0 license, it’s ideal deploying locally for privacy, reducing costs, or just hacking around. It’s intended for privacy-aware applications such as coding, document analysis, personal assistants, Claw- or Hermes-like setups.

Industry observers note that to celebrate, we are shipping with Meta day-0 support in transformers, llama.cpp, vLLM, Inference Endpoints, and other libraries. We built a few cool things and explain our findings in this blog.

Check out the demos below for inspiration.

You can find Muse Glimmer on the Hugging Face Hub.

Scores are reported as published. Bold indicates the best result among the compared models; ↓ indicates lower is better.

Muse Glimmer is a dense 30B parameter model consisting of:.

In addition to the main VLM, there’s also a speculative decoding drafter implemented on DFlash. Usage of this module is optional, and it can provide much faster generation in exchange for some memory cost. We found this drafter to be particularly well suited to structured content generation such as coding.

The language model uses the following architecture components:.

It has been revealed that muse Glimmer uses one image encoder to handle both images and videos. Unlike the relatively small vision encoders used in other VLMs, this is a sizable 2B ViT-like model designed after the Perception Encoder architecture. Perception Encoder was previously introduced by Meta as a backbone for various downstream spatial and multimodal tasks.The encoder patchifies images to a shape of 2 frames x 3 channels x 14 x 14, and passes them through a linear layer for projection. An interpolated absolute position embedding from a learned position table is then added to these embeddings. These are then sent to the vision tower which consist of 50 layers and GELU MLPs. Similar to the language model, the attention pattern consists of three window attention layers followed by one full attention layer. Inside the attention layers, 2D RoPE is applied to the queries and keys.

It has been revealed that after transformer, pixel shuffle concatenates 2x2 groups of neighboring spatial tokens which reduces the number of image tokens 4x without discarding their channels. The merged features are then projected to the shared embedding space of the text decoder.

Videos go through the same encoder frame by frame, where each frame is converted into patches (of shape [batch, temporal groups, grid height, grid width, 2 frames, 3 channels, 14, 14]). The processor targets 2 frames per second and caps the clip at 96 frames sampled evenly across video. The processor creates timestamped video placeholders, interleaving text with frame e.g. “Time: 0.0s <|video|> x N” in which the final video embeddings are replaced before the final projection layer.

Upgrade transformers to the latest version to be able to use Muse Glimmer.

Recent findings suggest that muse Glimmer comes with day-0 support in transformers, both for the main model and the speculative decoding drafter. You can use AutoModelForMultimodalLM and AutoProcessor classes to load the model and the processor.

The same snippet runs unchanged on NVIDIA (CUDA), AMD (ROCm) and Intel (XPU) GPUs, device_map="auto" places the model on whichever accelerator is available.

After loading the model, you can do text-only inference with it as follows.

We would need torchvision to be able to use images and text.

To work with videos we recommend installing torchcodec into the environment.

It has been revealed that muse Glimmer can answer complex questions about videos without audio. You can do video inference as follows, here’s an example from VideoMME2, which is the most popular video question answering benchmark.

Sources indicate that muse Glimmer can do multimodal tool calling, here’s how you can do it. In the example below, we ask the model to call the weather tool based on the city in the image.

Industry observers note that muse Glimmer comes with day-0 llama.cpp support. Meta has distributed calibrated quants in this repo, and Unsloth is releasing optimized quants as well. DFlash speculative decoding is supported as well. You can use a pre-built llama binary to start a llama server or a CLI. To install llama.cpp, run:.
