#23514. Multi-Vector (Late Interaction) Embedding Models with Sentence Transformers

📅 18 Aug 2026 • ⏱️ 28m • 📚 Deep Dive (5566 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Multi-Vector (Late Interaction) Embedding Models with Sentence Transformers

📅 18 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 28 min read (5566 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~28 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for applications like retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, and more.
  • Recent findings suggest that where a regular embedding model compresses a whole text into one vector, a multi-vector model keeps one vector per token and scores query against document with the MaxSim operator.
  • In this blogpost, we'll show you how to use these models: loading the various checkpoint formats, encoding and scoring, plugging them into a search stack, running them on page images, and keeping the index affordable.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for applications like retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, and more. With the v6.0 update, it gains a fourth model type: MultiVectorEncoder, for ColBERT-style late interaction retrieval. Any PyLate checkpoint and any Stanford-NLP ColBERT checkpoint loads straight into it, and colpali-engine models for visual document retrieval can be used too, through the same familiar API you already use for dense, sparse, and reranker models.

Recent findings suggest that where a regular embedding model compresses a whole text into one vector, a multi-vector model keeps one vector per token and scores query against document with the MaxSim operator. That preserves token-level matching information that a single vector has to average away, which usually means stronger retrieval at the cost of a bigger index. It's also the state of the art for visual document retrieval, where a text query is matched against page images directly, with no OCR step in between.

In this blogpost, we'll show you how to use these models: loading the various checkpoint formats, encoding and scoring, plugging them into a search stack, running them on page images, and keeping the index affordable. Everything below runs on a plain pip install -U sentence-transformers.

This blog is about using multi-vector models. If you want to learn how to train them, see the companion Training and Finetuning Multi-Vector Embedding Models with Sentence Transformers blogpost.

Industry observers note that A dense embedding model reads a text and returns a single fixed-size vector. Everything the model noticed has to fit in those 384, 768, or 1024 numbers, and similarity is one dot product between two such summaries. This works remarkably well, but the compression is lossy in a specific way: a rare entity, an exact identifier, or one crucial clause in a long passage all have to compete for room in the same vector. A query with several requirements at once runs into the same wall. For "green sofa with wooden legs and rounded cushions", a single vector has to blend all four into one point, so a green sofa with the wrong legs ends up sitting close to the one you actually asked for.

A multi-vector model (also called a late-interaction or ColBERT-style model, after the ColBERT paper) skips that compression. It runs the same transformer, but instead of pooling the token embeddings into one vector, it projects each token embedding down to a small dimension (classically 128) and keeps all of them. A 9-token document becomes a 9x128 matrix, not a 1x128 vector.

The interaction between query and document is then deferred until scoring time, which is where the name "late interaction" comes from. A cross-encoder interacts early, with both texts going through the model together, which is accurate but leaves nothing to precompute, since every document has to be re-encoded for each new query. A bi-encoder, which is what the dense embedding model above is, barely interacts at all (one dot product between two finished summaries), and that is exactly what lets you encode a collection once and query it fast. Late interaction sits in between. Documents are still encoded independently and can be indexed offline, but scoring compares every query token against every document token, which leaves far more room for the two to interact.

Scoring uses MaxSim: for each query token, take its highest similarity against any document token, then sum those maxima across the query.

MaxSim(Q,D)=∑Qi∈Qmax⁡Dj∈DQi⋅Dj\text{MaxSim}(Q, D) = \sum_{Q_i \in Q} \max_{D_j \in D} Q_i \cdot D_jMaxSim(Q,D)=Qi​∈Q∑​Dj​∈Dmax​Qi​⋅Dj​.

Because the token embeddings are L2-normalized, each of those dot products is a cosine similarity in [-1, 1], so the whole sum lands within [-num_query_tokens, num_query_tokens].

You can read the operator as a soft alignment, where every query token points at the one document token that best explains it, and the score is how well the document supports the query overall.

Recent findings suggest that the alignment doesn't have to be lexical, since the token embeddings are contextualized. Encode "Where do penguins live?" against "Penguins inhabit Antarctica." with lightonai/mLateOn and the query token live finds its best match on inhabit at 0.94, a word it shares no characters with! That is the thing lexical retrieval cannot do, BM25 and its relatives need the term itself, so synonyms and paraphrases slip past them. Dense embedding models bridge that gap as well, of course. What late interaction adds is that it does so without giving up the other direction. When an exact match is what matters (a product code, a surname, a function name), MaxSim still has that token sitting there on its own, where a single-vector model had to average it in with everything else. It isn't one-to-one either, since several query tokens routinely settle on the same document token.

You gain retrieval quality, particularly on queries where one specific piece of a document is what makes it relevant, on multi-requirement queries like the sofa above where each requirement gets to find its own evidence, and on out-of-domain data where a dense model's compression was tuned for a different distribution. That compression is learned from the training queries, so the model learns to keep what they needed and drop everything else, which may include exactly what your production queries ask about. The effect grows with document length, since more text has to fit in the same fixed vector.

The cost is index size. One vector per token instead of one vector per document is a lot more vectors, only partly offset by the smaller dimension. Encoding 4,874 Natural Questions passages with lightonai/LateOn produced 608,414 token vectors, an average of 124.8 per passage:.

That's about 42x the storage of the MiniLM index, or 62 KiB per passage. However, indexes are often compressed, e.g. the same 608,414 vectors take 92 MB as a fast-plaid index, since PLAID stores a centroid id plus a quantized residual per vector rather than the vector itself. For scale, a 4096-dimensional dense model like Qwen3-Embedding-8B would need about 80 MB for these same 4,874 passages, so a compressed multi-vector index sits in the same territory as the dense indexes people already run. Token Pooling cuts the vector count before any of that, and Retrieve and Rerank avoids building an index at all.

It has been revealed that pyLate comes up throughout this post, so here is the short version. Sentence Transformers handled dense and sparse models but not late interaction, so LightOn built PyLate on top of it to close that gap, adding the training, inference, and retrieval pieces these models need. Much of what you'll load below was trained with it, and LightOn built an ecosystem around it too, including fast-plaid, the late-interaction index that turns up in Indexing. With v6.0 those capabilities live in Sentence Transformers itself.

With the tradeoff in mind, let's get a model running.

Multi-vector models work with a plain install:.

For ColPali-style visual document retrieval, you also need the image dependencies (see Installation for all extras, and Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models for multimodal support in general):.

Sentence Transformers v6.0 requires transformers v5.x, torch 2.2+, and huggingface-hub v1.x. If you pin any of those lower, plan the upgrade first. See the Migration Guide for the full list of breaking changes.

Loading a multi-vector model looks exactly like loading any other Sentence Transformers model:.

Recent findings suggest that to find models that work, look for the multi-vector and sentence-transformers tags on the Hub. Any model with those tags loads with the line above, whether it started life as a PyLate checkpoint, a Stanford-NLP ColBERT checkpoint, or a ColPali-family model for visual document retrieval. We're working through the ecosystem to get that tag onto every model that works, so the list keeps growing.

Underneath, MultiVectorEncoder reads each of the formats these checkpoints have been published in over the years, so PyLate and Stanford-NLP checkpoints load directly even where the tag hasn't been added yet:.

Industry observers note that visual document retrieval models are the exception. ColPali-family checkpoints ship in colpali-engine's own format, which carries no information Sentence Transformers can use, so each one needs a small configuration added to its repository before it loads. Most of that work is done and waiting to be merged. See Supported Models for the current state and how to load them today.

Multi-vector models carry a handful of recipe knobs that differ per checkpoint: marker prefixes for queries and documents, length caps, whether queries are padded out with [MASK] tokens, and which tokens are skipped when scoring documents. All of them live in the module configs, so print(model) shows you exactly what you loaded. Here's the original ColBERTv2 checkpoint, which pads every query to exactly 32 tokens and truncates documents at 180:.

That's the classic ColBERT pipeline: a Transformer producing contextualized token embeddings, a token-level Dense projecting each of them to 128 dimensions, a MultiVectorMask deciding which tokens count during scoring, and a token-level Normalize. Other checkpoints fill in different values. lightonai/GTE-ModernColBERT-v1 uses the same four modules with [Q] and [D] prompts, no query expansion, and caps of 48 and 300.

You rarely need to touch any of this, since every released checkpoint configures its own. It matters when you build a model from a bare backbone, which is covered in Creating Custom Models.

One value is worth checking against your own data, though. document_length truncates, so anything past it never reaches the index. For example, a 662-token passage through LateOn's cap of 300 comes back as 273 vectors, with the rest of the passage simply gone. Most of these checkpoints were trained on short passages, so if your chunks are longer than the cap, you can lift it for a single call with encode_document(..., processing_kwargs={"text": {"max_length": 512}}), keeping in mind that you would be running the model past the length it was trained on and that the index grows roughly in proportion. Multi-vector models tend to tolerate that well. On MLDR, a long-document retrieval benchmark, the multilingual siblings of the pair above show the gap clearly: mLateOn scores 77.92 against mDenseOn's 51.59.

Industry observers note that multi-vector models are asymmetric, so queries and documents go through different prefixes, different length caps, and different scoring masks. Unlike many dense models, where the two are interchangeable, encode_query() and encode_document() are required to get correct embeddings:.

What you get back is a list of 2D tensors, one per input, each of shape (num_tokens, embedding_dim). Unlike dense embeddings, you can't stack these into one rectangular tensor, because every input has its own token count. The second document is longer than the first, so it comes back as a taller matrix.

Recent findings suggest that each call applies the model's own recipe for you. encode_query prepends the query marker, expands the query to a fixed length if the checkpoint asks for it, and caps it at the query length. encode_document prepends the document marker, caps at the document length, and drops any skiplisted tokens (punctuation, for most checkpoints) from the scoring mask.

The usual encode() arguments all still apply, so batch_size, show_progress_bar, convert_to_numpy, device, and multi-process pools work the way you'd expect:.

model.similarity() computes the full all-pairs MaxSim matrix:.

Mars wins, as it should, though the runners-up are close behind. Saturn also contains the literal phrase "the Red Planet", and Jupiter is a planet with a red spot, so a token-level operator has plenty to latch onto in all three. The ordering is what matters.

Scores often sit this close together, as GLInt shows by measuring the spread across a full candidate pool. MaxSim takes a maximum per query token, so a document will usually give every query token some decent best match, and scores start from a floor. Contextualized token embeddings are also anisotropic, clustering in a narrow cone rather than spreading out, so even arbitrary token pairs tend to score high.

There is also model.similarity_pairwise(), for when you already have matched pairs and just want the pair scores instead of the full similarity matrix:.

MaxSim sums over query tokens, so its magnitude scales with how many query tokens there are, which means you can't compare scores across models with different query recipes. LateOn encodes the Red Planet query above as 12 tokens. Run that same query and those same documents through ColBERTv2, which pads and truncates every query to exactly 32 tokens, and the scores land in a completely different range:.

Recent findings suggest that within one model the ordering is all you need, but if you want scores on a bounded scale, switch the model's similarity function to MeanMaxSim, which divides by the query token count. Back on LateOn:.

Now every score is an average cosine similarity in [-1, 1], although you'll only see [0, 1] in practice.

In a recent development, if your corpus is small, exhaustive MaxSim over all of it is the simplest thing that works. Encode the corpus once, then score each query against everything:.

Those 4,874 passages encoded in 20 seconds on an RTX 3090, and each search takes about 120ms end to end, most of that the MaxSim scoring against all 608,414 token vectors. This is exact, but it scales linearly in total corpus tokens and keeps every token vector in memory, so reach for it when you have a few thousand documents rather than a few million. The runnable version of this script is semantic_search.py.

It has been revealed that past that size you want a real late-interaction index, which Sentence Transformers doesn't ship. It doesn't need to, because these indexes store whatever encode_document produced, so you encode here and hand the token embeddings to something built for them. Indexing has working snippets for four of the options, and the section directly below covers how to skip the index entirely.

You can also get late-interaction quality without maintaining a late-interaction index, by using a multi-vector model as your reranker. A fast bi-encoder narrows a large corpus to a handful of candidates, then the multi-vector model rescores only those:.

In a recent development, only the 50 candidates are ever encoded as multi-vectors, so your index stays a normal dense index and the token vectors are transient. This is the same role a cross-encoder plays in a retrieve-and-rerank stack, but a multi-vector model is considerably cheaper per candidate. You encode the documents in one batch and score them with a matrix multiplication, instead of one forward pass per query-document pair. The runnable script is retrieve_rerank.py, which prints the timings of both stages.

Several vector databases index and score multi-vectors natively: Qdrant since v1.10, Weaviate since v1.29, Vespa for years now, LanceDB since v0.15.0, and VectorChord, which adds a MaxSim operator to Postgres that plain pgvector doesn't have. Milvus joined them in v2.6.4, under array-of-structs rather than the unrelated feature it calls multi-vector search. If you would rather not run a server at all, LightOn's fast-plaid is a pip install away and implements PLAID directly, and PyLate wraps it in a fuller retrieval stack.

Industry observers note that A few others get you partway. OpenSearch and Elasticsearch can rescore candidates with MaxSim but not retrieve on it, and the Elasticsearch field is additionally in technical preview and Enterprise-tier. turbopuffer has late-interaction indexing in private beta.

The snippets below index text, but nothing in them is text-specific. encode_document hands back the same list of token-vector matrices whether the document was a passage, a page image, an audio clip, or a video, so the ColPali-style models from Visual Document Retrieval go into any of these unchanged. There are simply more vectors per document, which is what makes Token Pooling worth reaching for sooner there.

It has been revealed that fast-plaid, Qdrant, Weaviate, and Vespa all take exactly what encode_document returns, so the code is the same up to the client library. Here's a working snippet for each, run against the 4,874 passages and 608,414 token vectors from the Semantic Search example. Each one carries the ingestion and query times it produced on one machine (RTX 3090, i7-13700K), with no tuning beyond what the code indicates, to give a sense of the shape of the work. All four answer the query faster than the 98ms model.similarity took in that section, and three of them do it on the CPU, since fast-plaid is the only one here using the GPU.

Industry observers note that all four returned the same three passages in the same order as the exhaustive PyTorch MaxSim earlier in this post, and the three databases reproduce its scores to four decimals! That is because their snippets score every document, which is affordable at this size and removes approximation as a variable. fast-plaid is approximate by design, so its scores differ slightly. The notes under each one say what changes when you switch to an approximate index, which is where rankings start to drift.

fast-plaid is LightOn's Rust implementation of PLAID, the index ColBERT was originally built around. There's no server to start, and it reads the tensors encode_document hands back without any conversion.

Industry observers note that the index argument is a directory, not just a label, so the index is written to disk as it is built. Pointing a upcoming FastPlaid at the same path reopens it for searching or for adding more documents, instead of rebuilding from the embeddings each time. On this corpus it occupies 92 MB, against 311.5 MB for the raw float32 vectors.

Sources indicate that this is the only one of the four that is approximate, and it is the one place in this section where the scores do not match the exhaustive MaxSim. PLAID prunes with centroids and stores quantized residuals, so the three scores drift by a few hundredths in both directions against the 11.9192 / 11.7591 / 11.6710 computed earlier. The ranking is unaffected here, and that is the trade PLAID is making. It was designed for corpora far larger than this one, where scanning everything is not an option.

Recent findings suggest that qdrant needs a server: docker run -p 6333:6333 qdrant/qdrant. The client also has a local mode (QdrantClient(":memory:")) that needs no server, but it's a pure-Python reimplementation, so use it for trying things out rather than for timing them.

MAX_SIM is the only comparator Qdrant offers, and hnsw_config=HnswConfigDiff(m=0) is their recommendation for late-interaction fields, since the vectors are used for rescoring rather than graph traversal. Note that Qdrant themselves suggest reserving late interaction for reranking a few hundred candidates rather than scanning a whole collection, which is the Retrieve and Rerank pattern. At 4,874 documents the full scan costs 18ms and is exact, but that doesn't extrapolate.

Industry observers note that weaviate needs a server too: docker run -p 8080:8080 -p 50051:50051 cr.weaviate.io/semitechnologies/weaviate:1.34.0. Multi-vector support needs 1.29 or newer, and the embedded mode isn't available on Windows.

Recent findings suggest that defaults are enough here. Weaviate's dynamic ef resolves to 100 for a top-3 query, and this ranking is already exact from about 32 upward. That margin is a property of the embeddings rather than of Weaviate, so it's worth confirming on your own model instead of assuming the defaults hold.

Weaviate also supports MUVERA encoding, which made ingestion 3x faster and queries 1.8x faster in our test. It cost far more accuracy than that speed is worth at this size though, since the correct third passage didn't appear even in its top 50.

Vespa also runs in a container, but pyvespa starts it for you, so there's no separate docker run.

Industry observers note that vespa asks for the most upfront structure of the four, because you're declaring a ranking pipeline rather than just an index. In exchange you get to write MaxSim out as a tensor expression and see exactly what it computes. This version puts MaxSim in first-phase over where true, which scores all 4,874 documents and is why the output matches exhaustive MaxSim exactly. It's deliberately not what Vespa recommends at scale. Their ColBERT sample app stores int8-binarized vectors and moves MaxSim into second-phase to rerank a cheaper first stage.

Moving to that phased setup needs care, because second-phase rescores only the best 100 candidates by default, and here that window left two of the three correct passages unscored entirely. Raising rerank-count to cover your candidate set fixes that, though at this size the phased version still came out slower than simply scanning everything.

Late interaction is the state of the art for visual document retrieval, matching a text query against page images, with charts, tables, and layout intact, and no OCR step. This is what the ColPali family of models does, and those checkpoints load and run through the same API, with the revision pinning the open pull request that adds this one's Sentence Transformers configuration (Supported Models has the full list). Image documents are passed as URLs, local paths, or PIL images:.

Each query retrieves its own page (the diagonal), and the second query separates much more cleanly than the first, since only one of the four pages is about outlay over time.

The code is unchanged. Underneath, the processor handles the visual prompt and the image patches, and MaxSim scores query text tokens against document image patches. A page holds many separate regions, which is exactly what makes late interaction a natural fit here, since a single vector would have to average a chart, a table, and three paragraphs into one summary. That fidelity costs index space, though. The shapes above are 755 token vectors for one page against 25 for the query, where a Natural Questions passage from earlier averaged about 125, so token pooling is worth reaching for earlier here than it is for text.

These are VLMs, so plan for the memory they need. The table in Supported Models runs from 252M to 8.8B parameters, and the small end of it stays practical on CPU where the multi-billion ones don't.

Page images are the common case, but they're not the only non-text modality. Sentence Transformers accepts text, images, audio, and video, and a checkpoint supports whichever of those its processor does, which model.modalities reports. A single document can combine modalities too, by passing a dict like {"text": ..., "image": ...} in place of a bare value. Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models covers multimodal models in Sentence Transformers more broadly, and the Usage documentation lists exactly which input formats each modality accepts.

vidore/colqwen-omni-v0.1 is built on Qwen2.5-Omni and takes all four modalities. Retrieving a recorded conversation with it is the same two calls as retrieving a page:.

In a recent development, colQwen-Omni was trained purely on image-text pairs, so its audio retrieval is zero-shot. It never heard a training example, and there is no transcription step anywhere in the pipeline. The query says nausea where the recording says carsickness, and it still picks the pharmacy conversation out of twenty by a wide margin.

Video works the same way, but sample the frames or it will eat your VRAM. Its release blogpost is blunt about this, that video "is very memory-intensive, so it's best suited for short clips":.

At 1 fps and full resolution the same pair of videos produces 8,426 and 5,137 token vectors and peaks at 20.8 GB of VRAM, against 4,240 and 2,446 vectors and 12.5 GB here, for a model that occupies 9.0 GB on its own. The ranking is identical either way. Long audio wants the same treatment, and the release blogpost recommends 30-second chunks, which come to roughly 800 tokens each.

Because MaxSim is a sum of per-query-token maxima, a ranking decomposes exactly, so every point of a document's score belongs to one query token and one document token. That lets you answer "why did this rank here?" precisely, rather than by eye.

Industry observers note that for image documents, sentence_transformers.multi_vector_encoder.interpretability overlays that decomposition onto the page as the standard ColPali heatmap, either aggregated over the query or one map per query token. Asking "How much was spent on water resources and power?" against the outlays page from above, this is where the water token went:.

heatmap.py is the runnable version, including the masking step that lines the document embedding up with the patch grid.

Text documents have no patch grid to overlay, but the same decomposition applies. text_similarity_map.py ranks a corpus and then attributes the top hit's score token by token, here on the Natural Questions corpus from earlier with the 32M-parameter mxbai-edge-colbert-v0-32m:.

According to recent reports, rich, mond, preliminary, and final matched themselves, while when settled on since and play on game. Three special tokens contribute 22.7% of the score while carrying none of the query's content. Below this table the script prints the passage itself, with the winning tokens highlighted in place.

Recent findings suggest that if the index footprint worries you, the most effective knob is to store fewer token vectors. HierarchicalTokenPooling implements the token pooling technique from Clavié, Chaffin, and Adams by clustering each document's token vectors with Ward linkage on cosine distance and replacing each cluster with its mean, keeping roughly 1 / pool_factor of the tokens. Within one document a lot of token vectors end up close to each other, so much of what you drop is redundancy rather than signal:.

There are three places to apply it, depending on when you want to pay for it:.

By default, pooling applies to documents only, since queries are short and are the side you can't afford to distort. On the Natural Questions corpus from earlier, the reduction tracks pool_factor closely, and pooling all 608k token vectors took about 6 seconds:.

According to recent reports, A cluster mean is a worse match for a query token than the best of its members was, and the coarser the clusters, the more that demonstrates. The original experiments measured that cost on BEIR and found very little of it, at 100.6% of the unpooled retrieval performance on average at pool_factor=2, and 99.0% at pool_factor=3. Halving your index for free is a good deal, so 2 is a reasonable place to start. How much it costs on your data is corpus-specific though, so measure it with an evaluator before you settle on a factor. The runnable comparison is token_pooling.py.

Industry observers note that how far you can push pool_factor is also partly a property of the model. LightOn's hierarchical pooling regularization trains for exactly that, shaping the embedding space so pooling costs less and reporting 99.4% retention at 5x compression. Training with that regularizer isn't in Sentence Transformers yet, but the resulting checkpoints are ordinary PyLate models, so lightonai/LateOn-hpool-regularized loads and pools like any other.

Multi-vector models run through the same backend machinery as the rest of Sentence Transformers, so you get torch (default), onnx, and openvino, alongside half precision, Flash Attention, and torch.compile.

On GPU, fp16 with Flash Attention is the best configuration we measured, at 2.44x the throughput of fp32 with no measurable retrieval quality loss. Flash Attention helps multi-vector models more than most, because documents are only truncated and never padded to a shared length, so your batches have widely varying sequence lengths that unpadding can exploit:.

Recent findings suggest that models with non-attend query expansion (attend=False, which covers the Stanford-NLP checkpoints like colbert-ir/colbertv2.0 and answerdotai/answerai-colbert-small-v1) reject Flash Attention at load time. Flash Attention strips attention_mask=0 positions, so the [MASK] expansion tokens that MaxSim scores would never receive an attention update. Use "sdpa" for those models.

On CPU, OpenVINO is your better bet where the architecture is supported, and int8 quantization buys a further speedup at a cost of about 0.4% accuracy. See Speeding up Inference for the full benchmark details, the export and quantization helpers, and a flowchart for picking a backend.

MultiVectorNanoBEIREvaluator runs the NanoBEIR suite of 13 small BEIR subsets with MaxSim scoring, and needs no data preparation on your side:.

According to recent reports, this also makes it easy to check the claim from the top of this post. lightonai/LateOn and lightonai/DenseOn were trained by LightOn on the same data with the same ModernBERT backbone and the same 149M parameters, differing only in whether they keep one vector per token or pool down to one per document. Running both over all 13 NanoBEIR datasets isolates what that choice buys:.

Industry observers note that late interaction wins on 9 of the 13 datasets and on the mean, by roughly one NDCG point. The four it loses (ArguAna, FiQA2018, SCIDOCS, and SciFact) are the shape of the tradeoff you should expect, a real gain in retrieval quality at the same model size, paid for in index footprint, rather than a universal win on every dataset. The same pair scores 57.22 against 56.20 on the full 15-dataset BEIR, a comparable gap, so the margin is not an artifact of the small benchmark.

In a recent development, alongside NanoBEIR, MultiVectorInformationRetrievalEvaluator, MultiVectorRerankingEvaluator, MultiVectorTripletEvaluator, and MultiVectorDistillationEvaluator cover the usual evaluation setups on your own data. They're documented in the Evaluation API Reference.

Sources indicate that multiVectorEncoder absorbs the modeling, inference, training, and evaluation of both libraries. Every PyLate checkpoint loads directly, and Supported Models lists the colpali-engine checkpoints along with the revision to pass where one is still needed. If you're migrating, these are the calls that change:.

Industry observers note that the difference worth knowing about is on bare (non-ColBERT) checkpoints, where PyLate's ColBERT("bert-base-uncased") applies the classic recipe by default while MultiVectorEncoder("bert-base-uncased") builds a plain stack, leaving the prefixes, query expansion, and skiplist as explicit choices. The training loss and evaluator equivalents, and the data-handling differences, are in the Migration Guide.

Save compatibility is one-way in every case. PyLate, Stanford-NLP ColBERT, and colpali-engine checkpoints all load into MultiVectorEncoder, but MultiVectorEncoder.save_pretrained output isn't loadable by any of them.

Models carrying the multi-vector and sentence-transformers tags on the Hub are the list that stays current, and we're working to get those tags onto every model that works. The tables below are what we test against directly, so treat them as a starting point rather than the full set. For text retrieval in particular, any PyLate or Stanford-NLP ColBERT checkpoint loads whether or not it carries the tag yet.

Some entries need a small Sentence Transformers configuration added to their repository first, and several of those are still open pull requests at the time of writing. Where a revision is listed below, pass it until that pull request is merged, after which the plain model name is enough:.

These load with their trained prefix tokens, query expansion, and punctuation skiplist recovered from the saved configuration.

Sources indicate that the NanoBEIR column reports the mean NDCG@10 (higher is better) across the 13 NanoBEIR datasets, each a 50-query subsample of a BEIR dataset, as a fast proxy for English text retrieval quality. We used the MultiVectorNanoBEIREvaluator to compute the scores for the primarily-English models. A - means the model was not evaluated on it. Note that NanoBEIR is a small benchmark, and its scores aren't a substitute for evaluating on your own data, which is always the right way to pick a model.

ColPali-style models embed page images as documents and text as queries.

According to recent reports, the NanoViDoRe column reports the mean NDCG@10 (higher is better) across NanoViDoRe v3, a compact visual document retrieval benchmark spanning 8 subsets (computer science, energy, finance in English and French, HR, industrial, pharmaceuticals, and physics). Like with NanoBEIR, NanoViDoRe is a small benchmark which shouldn't replace evaluation on your own data.

In a recent development, most of these are LoRA adapter repositories, with the adapter applied directly onto its base at load time. Some also have a -merged sibling on the Hub (e.g. vidore/colpali-v1.3-merged) with the adapter already folded into the weights.

Industry observers note that the three -hf entries are the transformers-native *ForRetrieval ports. They load without any configuration, but use more modeling from transformers and less from sentence_transformers. Generally, it's preferable to use the original models instead, as the ports score approximately the same.

Recent findings suggest that late interaction in Sentence Transformers rests on a lot of earlier work. Thanks to Omar Khattab and Matei Zaharia for ColBERT, which everything here descends from, and to the LightOn team (Antoine Chaffin, Raphael Sourty, Paulo Moura, and Amélie Chatelain) for PyLate and fast-plaid, which carried late interaction for years and shaped a good deal of the API described above.

Thanks to the ColPali team (Manuel Faysse, Hugues Sibille, Tony Wu, Bilel Omrani, Gautier Viaud, Céline Hudelot, and Pierre Colombo) for ColPali and colpali-engine, which brought late interaction to page images, and to Benjamin Clavié, Antoine Chaffin, and Griffin Adams for token pooling.

Thanks as well to the core MTEB team, Kenneth Enevoldsen and Roman Solomatin among many others, for MTEB and for the kind of hidden work that keeps information retrieval research running.

Industry observers note that and thanks to everyone who trained and released the checkpoints in Supported Models. Without them this post would have had nothing to measure.

To learn how to train or finetune these models on your own data:.

See the companion blogpost: Training and Finetuning Multi-Vector Embedding Models with Sentence Transformers.

The guide's distinction between first-stage retrieval and late-interaction reranking is useful for comparing complete systems. A practical baseline is BM25 candidate generation followed by a reranker, measuring recall at the candidate cutoff as well as final nDCG and end-to-end cost. We evaluated that pattern on a small English corpus here: https://huggingface.co/blog/ironbcc/bm25-seb-rag-retrieval (I'm an author). We haven't benchmarked the multi-vector models in this guide, especially on long or visual documents, so a matched evaluation would be needed.

Design for Understandability

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 28 min read (5569 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jschuster

⏱️ ~28 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a talk I gave at Google’s internal Code Health Summit in November of 2025.
  • Recent findings suggest that in a world where LLMs generate much of our code, understanding that code is more important than ever.
  • There’s a better way to go about this.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a talk I gave at Google’s internal Code Health Summit in November of 2025. I’m sharing it here in the hopes that it sparks further learning and discussion.

Recent findings suggest that in a world where LLMs generate much of our code, understanding that code is more important than ever. But with a system as large and complex as Google’s codebase, SWEs can easily fall into a pattern of learned helplessness where the best you can do is tweak the code and pray that it passes the tests. Without understanding, LLMs are little more than complexity-generating machines running at top speed.

There’s a better way to go about this. Just as our industry has learned to design software for testability, we can also design it for understandability. We can use ideas like design by contract, class invariants, modularity, and more to create systems that we can understand one piece at a time, rather than piling more onto the significant ball of mud and hoping it doesn’t all collapse.

Is it easy? No. But is it worthwhile? Absolutely. These ideas aren’t fresh, but they’re not nearly as widely taught or well understood as they deserve to be, and mastering them leads to a world where we can have more confidence in our code and increase velocity at the same time.

According to recent reports, hi everyone, thanks for having me! Let’s get started.

I’d like to start this talk with a question: If LLMs can code, then what is left for human SWEs?

The tech industry is swiftly looking to large language models to write all of our code. But you might say: isn’t writing code our job as software engineers? Where does this leave the responsibility of SWEs? What is the essential human element that SWEs add on top of LLMs?

Every one of you is going to have a different answer to this question, and that’s fine. But here’s my take.

That necessary human element is judgment. Judgment of whether the code is maintainable. Judgment of whether it is healthy.

In a recent development, LLMs can follow patterns and generate code that looks like what it was trained on. Sometimes they can produce useful tips and critiques for a piece of code. But that critical piece of judgment, of deciding whether some code is suitable for the task it was designed for, is still up to you, the human.

According to recent reports, because here’s the thing: LLMs today are still a sloppy intern. Sometimes the code they produce is good, but sometimes it’s completely off-track and needs correcting. You wouldn’t incorporate a sloppy intern’s code into your system without a close review first, so you shouldn’t do so for an LLM’s code either.

YOU are responsible for the quality of your code, regardless of whether you had an LLM generate it for you or wrote it the old-fashioned way with fingers on a keyboard.

So where does that leave us? If LLMs are going to write a lot of the code for us, then we’re looking at a future where we humans are going to spend less time writing code, and more time reading code and understanding it, in order to make sure it passes our quality bar.

This means it’s more key than ever to get better at understanding code, and to speed up that reading and understanding process.

Sources indicate that now: if you want to get better at something, it’s helpful to set an aspirational goal for yourself. Something that’s above your current skill level, and drives you to get better and better every day.

Here’s the goal I propose: we should be able to predict the behavior of every line of code, without running a single test.

Let me say that again: We should be able to predict the behavior of every line of code, without running a single test.

Now, I know you may be thinking: “Understand every line of code? Without testing? Are you serious?! There’s way too much complexity and legacy code for me to ever be able to do that!”.

You might think so. And if we take our hands off the wheel and relinquish all control, you might be right. But I’m here to tell you there’s a better way.

We can design our code to be understandable.

Consider that a decade or two ago, we used to think that writing multiple tests for every public method in an API would have been infeasible. It wasn’t because we didn’t want to, or that we weren’t trying. It was because we hadn’t designed our code to make testing possible at that level. But gradually, across the software industry, we changed our practices to design for testability. Today, designing our code for testability is so ingrained into our culture that doing anything else is practically unthinkable. We can do the same for understandability, so that our code enables us to understand it better.

Our own Code Health guide makes a strong case for understandability. It says “For code to be sustainable, it must be understood. Change cannot be made unless a developer knows what the system right now provides, and what needs to change to adapt to newly introduced circumstances. As a result, key components of code health include good documentation, easy to understand error messages, and clear, simple code”.

According to recent reports, not only is designing for understandability notable, but it’s a learnable skill. It’s not some magical ability that you either have or you don’t. There are specific, concrete actions you can take to improve the understandability of your code.

I’m going to introduce you to a few of those today. Think of it as a “starter kit” for designing for understandability. We’ll also talk more about a general theme that runs through all of these practices, so that at a certain point you can find even more ways to design your code for understandability.

It has been revealed that the ideas I’m going to show you today are not latest. But they’re not taught as well as they should be, when they’re taught at all, and most of us have only a rough understanding of how to apply them. My goal today is to sharpen that understanding just a little bit, and make it just a little more practical, so we can kickstart a process of making our code more understandable over time.

So let’s get started on each of these Design for Understandability practices.

The first one is Design by Contract.

To motivate the idea, let’s ask the question: when calling a method, what behavior should you rely on?

Let’s say we have this binary search method, but its documentation is not terribly helpful (you’ve probably seen something like this before).

Binary search is reasonably well understood, but as a caller of the method, we have some questions we want to ask about this specific implementation. Such as:.

The documentation doesn’t answer these questions. So what can we do?

Recent findings suggest that first, we could guess. But we’ll probably be wrong.

Sources indicate that second, we could read the code. But that might take a long time, especially if the particular behavior we care about is buried several levels deep.

Third, we could test the code on some examples and see what happens. But just because it works a certain way on some examples doesn’t necessarily mean it works that way for all such inputs. Furthermore, even if it works that way now, there’s no guarantee that it will continue to work that way in the future.

The point is that without a clear statement of what this code is intended to do, there’s no distinction between implementation and intent. The SWE who wants to use this code has to guess at which behavior the method commits to, versus which behavior is an implementation detail that might change over time.

This is where contracts come in.

There are many ways to define a contract, but for the sake of this talk I’m going to define it as a formal-ish description of the observable behavior that each participant in an interaction commits to.

In the real world, a basic contract is something like “If I cook dinner, then you will wash the dishes”.

In programming, an example might be: “If the caller provides a non-negative integer n, then the square-root function returns the square root of n”.

Let’s see how contracts can help us with our binary-search example.

Here’s a possible contract for this function. It says, “If the list is sorted, binarySearch returns the index of the first occurrence of t in the list, or -1 if not found. Behavior is undefined for unsorted lists.”.

We can see that this contract answers the questions we asked about it:.

It has been revealed that the power of a contract is that it defines a clear boundary between the author’s intent and the implementation. The caller doesn’t have to guess at the behavior anymore: they can just read the contract, and if a specific detail of the behavior isn’t there, they will know that it’s unspecified.

In reality, this isn’t always perfect. Whether intentionally or accidentally, we still tend to end up with code that relies on implementation details rather than specified behavior. But contracts at least give us a way to minimize this behavior.

Now that we understand what a contract looks like, let’s talk about how contracts can help us reason about and understand our code better.

Suppose you just wrote a method. I’m going to draw that method as a little circle here.

You want to know if it’s correct.

I’m going to use a purple circle to stand for methods we’ve read the code for.

Now, our method doesn’t live in isolation: it calls some other code.

In a recent development, so, you think “Okay, well, I need to understand what those do. I’m going to read the code for those methods.”.

Well, those methods call other methods, and we start thinking about this, and figure out how we’re going to reason about those. And at this point you can maybe see where I’m going.

Oh no. Now we have lots and lots of code we have to read across our entire code base.

Why do we need all this reasoning just to reason about one single method? That’s all we’re trying to do! How did we get so out of control?

So, let’s back up and try again, using Design by Contract this time.

You still have to read your own code. We can’t get around this part; that’s the change we just made.

It has been revealed that and we haven’t changed the code. It still calls those other methods.

But now, the trick is that we can read just the contract on those called methods, not the code.

It has been revealed that and that’s it! We can stop here. We don’t need to worry about all of that other code. The contracts tell us all we need to know about calling these other two methods.

The rest of that code still exists, but we don’t have to think about it. The contract abstracts away all that other behavior that doesn’t matter to us as the caller of these two methods.

So that is the power that contracts give to us to reason about our code.

Finally, I’ll wrap up this section with a few tips for writing contracts:.

First, document the behavior that you’re willing to commit to. This is usually the same as what you want your callers to rely on. For example, you probably want to document the return value of your method. But the exact human-readable text in your error messages? Not so much.

Second, describe your error handling in your contracts. A contract does not and should not be just about the happy path. If your method might go wrong in some way, tell the caller under what conditions it might go wrong, and how you’re going to signal that to the caller, whether it be through a special return value, or an exception, or something else.

Sources indicate that finally, keep in mind that the more callers your method has, the harder it is to change the contract. If it’s a private method used only by your team? Sure, that’s probably an easy case to change both the contract and change the callers to match. If it’s a public method on a popular framework used by hundreds of other projects? Then renegotiating the contract is a much more expensive effort, so you should evaluate the costs and benefits carefully before deciding to do that.

So that was the first element in our Design for Understandability starter kit.

The next one is data invariants.

Let me explain this idea with a little story.

Sources indicate that early in the COVID-19 pandemic, when my wife and I started working from home, we missed having free soda at work. So we got in the habit of keeping cans of Diet Coke in the fridge.

But there was a problem: we were great at taking cans out of the fridge, but not so great about putting new ones back in. So if you’re working hard and looking forward to taking a break with a nice cold beverage, it was a substantial disappointment to open a Coke-less fridge and resort to drinking room-temperature soda from the pantry instead.

The problem was that we hadn’t set any rules on how we retrieve Diet Coke and how we replenish the fridge. Without any rules governing access to the fridge, we eventually got into an unwanted state: in this case, an empty fridge.

According to recent reports, this happens in code, too. For example, let’s say you have this proto to represent a customer’s order [Note: “proto” is Google jargon for a Protocol Buffers message, similar to a JSON object]. If you receive this proto, how much do you trust that the total actually indicates the total amount on the items?

Recent findings suggest that probably not much, right? This proto could have come from any part of your code, so it’s easy to imagine that someone forgot to set that field appropriately.

Protos give you completely uncontrolled access to the underlying representation of your data. Protos are great for transferring data back and forth across the network, but they’re poorly suited to situations where you want to rule out certain states.

In a recent development, to solve these kinds of problems, we can use data invariants. A data invariant is a statement about a piece of data that is always true.

It has been revealed that data invariants are a principled way to enforce these kinds of valid states in your data. If you use them well, you can avoid a lot of bugs in your code.

Let’s see how we can use invariants to solve the Diet Coke problem, and similar problems you might come across in your own code.

First, identify the invariant you want to maintain.

Ask yourself: What’s the property you want to rely on for this piece of data? Where are the places in the code where you explicitly validate and return an error if invalid? Alternatively, where do you make the assumption that it’s invalid, but you’re not actually sure?

In this case, the invariant we want is “the fridge always contains a Diet Coke”.

Second, you need to document the invariant.

It’s vital to note this is a separate step. It’s one thing to have an invariant in your own head. It’s another thing to write it down so that you communicate it to everyone else who might touch this code. Not to mention that if you come back to this code months or years later, you yourself might have forgotten which exact invariant you meant to maintain.

Write it down where people will see it: probably close to the relevant data members, or maybe in a class-level comment at the top.

In a recent development, third, establish the invariant at creation time. Usually this will be done in a constructor or factory method. In this case, we’re constructing the fridge with a few drinks already added.

Fourth, every time you change your the data, make sure you maintain the invariant.

This is the part my wife and I didn’t do for our fridge. What we should have done is established a rule where if you take a Diet Coke, you put another one back in the fridge to make sure there’s another for the next person.

Industry observers note that you can maintain the invariant many ways – that part is up to you. The key thing is that you always maintain it. Without that, you have to think to yourself “Wait, are there going to be Diet Cokes in the fridge? Did I already take them out earlier? Let me go back and check all my callers to see if they did that already”. With an invariant, though, you just know: If I have a Fridge object, then it definitely has Diet Cokes, regardless of the sequence of operations that led to this point.

Sources indicate that finally, one last step, and this might be the hardest one: you need to maintain the invariant as the code evolves. It’s relatively easy to maintain the invariant for a single version of code. But over the weeks, months, and years, complexity will creep in, fresh requirements will force you to change the code, and you might accidentally break the invariant or forget you even had one.

According to recent reports, establish the culture on your team that maintaining invariants is just a thing you do. If you have a mental checklist of things you look for in code review, make sure that maintaining the invariants is on that checklist.

So how do data invariants help us design for understandability? Let’s first consider what we have to do when we don’t have an invariant.

Recent findings suggest that recall this representation of all the methods in your codebase, calling each other in various ways. Suppose you have a proto-based version of the fridge, and you want to know if it has any Diet Cokes in it. Because it’s a proto, you don’t have a way of knowing what state it’s in.

So, you need to check all the callers of the current method.

And you do the check, crawling across the codebase, and you find that there’s one particular case where you didn’t enforce it.

It has been revealed that of course you can fix these challenges one at a time as they crop up, but all that searching sounds like a lot of work, right? What do you think are the chances you’re always going to find that one particular buggy spot? What are the chances that upcoming methods added to this web of code are going to maintain that condition?

In contrast, let’s try the version with our Fridge class and its invariant.

Recent findings suggest that in this case, the class has an invariant: the Fridge always has at least one Diet Coke, no matter what operations have been done previously or where we came from. By maintaining that invariant, we’ve removed the need to check what every single caller does.

This is what data invariants do for you: they let you focus on the state you’re in now, and not how you got there.

That wraps up the section on data invariants.

The final practice I want to discuss today is isolating side effects and dependencies on global state.

In a recent development, to motivate this idea with an example. Let’s say there’s a supermarket point-of-sales system with this method to compute sales tax. Now ask yourself: what are the inputs and outputs for this method?

It has been revealed that seems pretty obvious, right? It takes in a customer’s grocery order and returns the sales tax as an integer.

According to recent reports, but that’s not the whole story. If you dig into the implementation of this method, you’ll find that it reads in a set of sales tax rates from a separate file. That’s effectively a new input channel! The code depends on that data to compute the tax just as much as it depends on the content of the grocery order itself.

It has been revealed that and if you look further, you’ll find that the method also records the computed tax in the store’s account database for bookkeeping purposes. That’s a new output, but it’s nowhere to be found in the type signature!

So functions have two kinds of input and output: the ones that are visible in the type signature, like the order and the computed sales tax, and the ones that are hidden, like the tax rates file and the entry in the accounting database.

Sources indicate that the hidden outputs are more commonly known as side effects. Side effects generally come in two flavors: mutation, so modifying something like a global variable or one of your input arguments, and outputs outside of your process. That would be things like database writes, remote procedure calls, printing to the console, etc.

I don’t know a common term for the hidden inputs, but I would call these dependencies on global state. Again, there are two flavors: dependency on the state of some global variable, or a dependency on the state of the system your program is running in. That’s things like permissions to access the database, the existence of a given file on the file system, and even the ability to read the system clock.

Industry observers note that so why are these hidden inputs and outputs a problem? They make code hard to test, hard to reuse, and hard to reason about.

Industry observers note that hard to test because you have to make sure you have all the necessary dependencies are set up before you can even run the method in your test. And then once you do run the method, side effects often force the test to rely more on interaction verification than state verification, which can be brittle.

Hard to reuse because the code now makes assumptions about what kinds of resources you have available to you. If you need to reuse some method in another part of the codebase, but the input data needs to come from a different source, or you need to store the results in a different place, those side effects and global states are going to create a tight coupling between your computation code and the specific sources and destinations for that computation, which will make your life harder.

Recent findings suggest that hard to reason about because, by definition, these inputs and outputs are hidden! If you don’t even know that your method is making these kinds of assumptions on the system that it’s running in, then you’re going to make some faulty conclusions about how your code will behave.

Now I’m not saying all side effects or global state are bad. And I’m not saying we should all immediately switch to a pure functional programming language like Haskell.

Industry observers note that effects have to happen somewhere. Without side effects, computation is just the process of making a metal box hot for a little while(and even that heat is a side effect! although not usually one we care about).

But by default, we tend to sprinkle them everywhere throughout the code. Need some input? Just read the file at whatever point you happen to be at in the code. Need to store your result? Go ahead and do it 4 layers deep into your business logic.

Without a principled approach to side effects and global state, we’re constantly running into the kinds of problems we just described.

It has been revealed that there’s a better way, which is to isolate the side effects and the dependencies on global state. Much of our code is just logic on top of the data (once we get it) and creating fresh data based on that. Divide your code into the computational parts on one hand, and the parts that deal with side effects and global state on the other.

There are a few common patterns for this.

Sources indicate that one of them is Command/Query Separation. It’s a pattern where each method is either a command, which performs some side effect, or a query, which is a pure function that returns its output as the return value. But you maintain a strict separation so that no function does both of those things.

In a recent development, another pattern is called “Functional Core, Imperative Shell”. This is a pattern at the architectural level. You focus the inner modules of your system on the business logic and computation, not performing side effects – this is the “functional core”. The outer modules coordinate the effects of your system with that computation, so that the complexity of the side effects is isolated to just that outer layer, and the majority of your system is simpler due to the functional purity.

As with the other two practices, side effects and global state have a big impact on how we think about code.

For example, you might be working on a method and need to delete a file. Your assumption is that it should be okay, you think no one is using it.

Sources indicate that but then it turns out, some other part of the codebase was relying on it, and you just broke them. The code was so far away and unrelated that you didn’t even think to check there.

On the other hand, if you isolate your side effects and global state such that they only happen in a known region of the code, then you can have confidence that you really aren’t going to break anyone else.

So, those are the three starter practices for Design for Understandability: Design by Contract, Data Invariants, and Isolating Side Effects and Dependencies on Global State.

According to recent reports, now, I’ve presented these as independent practices, but in fact they’re not so distinct. There’s a unifying theme to them. That theme is local reasoning.

What do I mean by local reasoning?

Local reasoning means you can come to conclusions about some chunk of code by looking only at that chunk of code, plus just a small amount of the neighboring code, like the specifications or contracts of the components that you directly interact with.

This is as opposed to global reasoning. That’s the kind of reasoning where to answer even a simple question, you have to read a large chunk of the codebase, because the answer could be in any method, at any level of the call stack.

The benefit of local reasoning is that it puts a hard boundary on how far you have to look in order to figure something out about your system: there’s always a limit to how far you have to search.

So let’s talk about how each of the practices we talked about enables local reasoning. You may have noticed we covered this already, but let’s review.

According to recent reports, design by Contract defines the expected behavior for a caller and a called method. That means that to understand what behavior a caller can rely on, or what behavior a called method is obligated to implement, the only place we need to look is the defined interface for that called method. Without that, we would revert to global reasoning to find all the parts of the code that might depend on some aspect of this method’s behavior.

Data invariants often go hand in hand with contracts, but they usually say something about an entire object rather than a single method on that object.

If you have a piece of data and you want to know something about its validity, like “does this fridge have any diet cokes?”, an invariant is what lets you immediately conclude yes, without looking at the callers that produced that data.

It has been revealed that finally, by isolating side effects and global state, you minimize the number of places in your code where a change in one part of the code can cause a problem in a completely unrelated part. So it lets you say things like “this is the only part of the code that’s allowed to touch this file, so I know for sure that it’s safe to delete”.

Another way of looking at local reasoning is to say that it minimizes the amount of context we need in order to reason about the system.

With global reasoning, you might need to know about any arbitrary part of your codebase, because the part that breaks your assumptions could be anywhere. You need to have the whole system loaded into your head in order to understand it.

Local reasoning keeps the amount of stuff you need loaded into your head to a reasonable size.

And guess what else benefits from small contexts: LLMs!

Sources indicate that A key portion of making an LLM useful for your work is giving an LLM the right context to give good suggestions. But contexts costs tokens, and your tokens are limited. So LLMs give us another great motivation to use local reasoning and minimize our context.

Sources indicate that in other words, if you want your LLMs to be useful to you, then design your systems for understandability. Keep the necessary context small to make it easier for both you and your LLM to work with your code.

At the beginning of this talk, I compared “Design for Understandability” to “Design for Testability”. I’d like to revisit that for a moment.

Industry observers note that before designing for testability was the norm, the default testing approach was application-level testing. Our code wasn’t set up for practices like dependency injection, so there was no way to run your code without setting up a huge set of dependencies as well. It wasn’t until we started designing and building our systems with testability in mind that we were able to make unit testing practical.

Sources indicate that that’s how it is with understandability and local reasoning, as well. If you don’t design for it ahead of time, it’s somewhere between hard and impossible to use local reasoning. But if you design for it along the way, you can make it work.

If you’ve never heard of unit testing, then application-level testing seems obvious, and straightforward. But it’s not sufficient for modern software engineering. The same is true for global reasoning. I say it’s time we made designing for understandability a required part of our work, just like we did for testability.

So you may be thinking: that all sounds good, and these practices sound good on paper, but is designing for understandability feasible in practice? You’re probably not working in a brand-latest greenfield project. You’re probably working on old code, with lots of old warts and complexity, and the situation may seem hopeless. Can you really do this?

It has been revealed that I’m here to say yes, this is feasible, if you take it one small step at a time. I’ll share some tips for getting started.

First off, take little bits at a time. Don’t try to boil the ocean. Don’t say “We’re going to take two weeks off from our normal work, make all of our code perfectly understandable, and then we’re done!”. That’s not going to work; you’re going to have a bad time.

Instead, try applying some of these practices to just latest methods that you write. You might have some old code out there that’s hard to change. So be it. Start with just the new methods and build some momentum.

Teach your teammates, as well. Maybe share this talk, or find other ways to help your teammates design for understandability.

And finally, you might consider group programming sessions where you all get together and discuss: what does designing for understandability mean in your context? The Monarch team at Google did this with their Design by Contract practice and it worked well for them.

Here are some further resources to learn more about Design for Understandability. I’m not going to go into them in detail, but please feel free to go revisit the slides after the talk and check these out.

[Public links reproduced here for the blog post:].

According to recent reports, in conclusion: design your code for understandability. Whenever you’re working on some code and realize that you’re falling back to global reasoning, pause for a moment. Ask yourself: can I do this with local reasoning instead? Would a contract or an invariant help here? Or what if I moved the side effects and global state somewhere else? Or, maybe you’ll think of some other practice that fits here – you probably know a lot of local-reasoning practices, even if you didn’t have the terminology to call it that until today.

Sources indicate that it’s time to make design for understandability just as much a part of software engineering as designing for testability is today. Understandability is not just helpful – it’s crucial, especially with Google-size systems. And not just that, but making your code understandable is doable if you design for it along the way.

Trust me: you’ll be glad you did.

How Much Memory Does Your Agent Actually Need?

📅 18 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1595 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In our previous post, we compared ALTK-Evolve with ACE and highlighted that how you deliver an agent's self-distilled guidelines — a few retrieved per task vs.
  • Industry observers note that equipping an agent with agentic memory sounds simple: distill lessons from its past work, put them back in context, and more experience should mean better performance.
  • Agentic memory is not a feature you switch on.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In our previous post, we compared ALTK-Evolve with ACE and highlighted that how you deliver an agent's self-distilled guidelines — a few retrieved per task vs. the whole set injected — drives both accuracy and cost. This post steps back to the question that comes before it: how much should you give it?

Industry observers note that equipping an agent with agentic memory sounds simple: distill lessons from its past work, put them back in context, and more experience should mean better performance. It doesn't always work that way. When we scaled the evaluation to eight models — from a 30B dense model to frontier proprietary systems — one finding stood out:.

Agentic memory is not a feature you switch on. It's a dose you calibrate to the model.

ALTK-Evolve lets an agent learn from its own past trajectories: distilling reusable guidelines and injecting them back at inference time, with no weight updates and no human annotation.

The right dose differs by model tier: strong models with headroom want the full guideline set, weaker models do best with a compact core plus per-task retrieval, and saturated models show no measurable gain.

Curated retrieval can be both the most accurate and the cheapest option: gpt-oss-120b gained +16.1pp task completion at only +5% tokens — and prompt caching keeps even the full guideline set affordable in production.

Recent findings suggest that not every model benefits from the same amount of memory. Across eight models spanning the capability spectrum, we saw three recurring patterns:.

Industry observers note that strong models with headroom want the full guideline set — every guideline, including rare edge-case lessons. They have the capacity to absorb and apply all of it. DeepSeek-V3.2 (671B MoE) climbed +9.5 percentage points in task completion when given its full self-mined guideline set.

Sources indicate that smaller or weaker models get drowned by a large guideline set. For these, a tight, high-confidence core plus a handful of task-relevant guidelines retrieved per task works best. gpt-oss-120b (117B MoE) gained +16.1pp with this selective approach — while the full guideline set gained less and cost ~50% more tokens.

Already-saturated models show no measurable gain. We call this the saturated pattern — the label describes what we observed, not a proven cause. The model may already have been near its ceiling on these tasks, the guidelines may not have addressed its remaining failures, or it may not have applied the guidance effectively. GLM-5 (745B MoE) sat here in our runs.

In a recent development, what puts a model into one pattern rather than another isn't simply parameter count. Benchmark headroom, context-window size, architecture, guideline quality, and task distribution all appear to shape where a model lands, and separating those factors is ongoing work. The practical takeaway holds either way: the right dose of memory depends on the model, and we can calibrate it.

"Memory" here doesn't mean replaying a past transcript. It means a guideline set — strategies that worked, mistakes to avoid, and edge cases — distilled from the agent's own prior trajectories. The loop is straightforward:.

The agent attempts tasks and produces trajectories.

ALTK-Evolve extracts behavioral guidelines from both its successful and unsuccessful runs.

It consolidates those guidelines into a reusable set.

At inference time, the agent receives either the full guideline set or a task-relevant selection of it.

No model weights are updated. The learning loop changes the guidance available to the agent, not the underlying model — which is exactly why it's cheap to adopt and portable across the eight models we tested.

We evaluated on AppWorld — 585 multi-step tasks (168 test_normal + 417 test_challenge) across 9 simulated apps (calendars, messaging, payments, and so on). Tasks are scored two ways: whether the agent fully completes each task (TGC — Task Goal Completion) and whether every variant of a scenario passes (SGC — Scenario Goal Completion, a stricter, all-or-nothing bar). Full definitions are in the appendix.

Because the confusing part of any memory study is what's actually in the context window, we define the configurations up front.

Both memory configurations draw from the same guideline set, mined once (via the loop above) from AppWorld's training split only. What changes between them is only how that one set is delivered — the full guideline set injects all of it every step, while curated retrieval delivers a selected subset — never how the guidelines were produced, and no test-split data ever goes into building it.

The number of guidelines a model mines depends on its own capability, so we report configurations by strategy — "full guideline set" vs. "curated retrieval" — rather than by raw counts, which aren't comparable across models.

Representative models from the eight-model sweep, measured by task completion (TGC) on test_normal:.

Figure 1. Representative models in the three observed patterns. Bars show TGC on AppWorld test_normal for baseline vs. the best-memory configuration; the x-axis begins at 40% to make differences visible. TGC alone understates the larger SGC gains — see the SGC columns in the table below.

The figure plots TGC to keep it readable; the table adds the stricter SGC metric, where the gains are often larger:.

Reading the SGC column, the stricter metric usually moves more than TGC — DeepSeek's SGC jumps +16.1pp against a +9.5pp TGC gain — because good guidelines especially help an agent clear every variant of a scenario, not just the average case. And the effect doesn't disappear at the top of the range: GPT-5.5 and Opus, both near the ceiling on TGC, still gain +7.2 and +7.1pp SGC respectively. Memory keeps paying off as long as a model has a remaining failure mode to target.

Recent findings suggest that A practical concern: injecting a full guideline set inflates every ReAct step's input, because the guidelines are re-sent each turn. Here's what we observed:.

Table 1. Average token use per task, accumulated across agent steps, measured against the no-memory baseline.

Curated retrieval keeps cost near baseline. For weaker models, where selection wins on accuracy, it also wins on cost — the best of both worlds (+16.1pp TGC at only +5% tokens for gpt-oss-120b). Better performance here does not require more inference cost.

It has been revealed that memory doesn't blow up the reasoning loop. DeepSeek runs about the same number of ReAct steps with memory as without (≈18–19 on average), so the added cost is input-token inflation, not longer trajectories.

The real efficiency lever in production is prompt caching: the static portion of the guideline set is identical across steps and can be cached, cutting effective cost substantially. Cache-aware prompt design — keeping the shared guideline-set prefix stable so it stays cacheable — is worth engineering for. We also hypothesize that context-window size plays a role: models with larger windows may absorb the full guideline set more effectively, while smaller-context models benefit more from retrieval that keeps injected content compact. We have not yet run controlled experiments isolating this factor.

In a recent development, the lesson isn't to give an agent everything it has learned. It's to give it the amount of experience it can actually use.

For weak models, that means a compact core plus a few task-specific lessons — which, conveniently, is also the cheapest option.

For strong models with headroom, it means preserving the full guideline set, kept affordable in production via prompt caching.

For saturated models, it means spending no extra context until their remaining failure modes are better understood.

The gains are real across the board — automatic, leakage-free, and requiring no human annotation — but only when the dose fits the model.

This is a starting point, not the finish line:.

A learned selector. Our current retrieval ranks guidelines by cosine similarity, which we've shown doesn't perfectly predict which guidelines help a given task. A selector trained on outcome signal is the natural next step.

Memory for very weak models. Below a minimum capability baseline, self-distillation lacks signal. Teacher-distilled memory for very weak models is a separate problem we're exploring.

Beyond AppWorld. These results are validated on AppWorld — a rigorous multi-step benchmark, but a single one. Broader agent benchmarks and real-world deployments are in progress.

Isolating context window. As above, we want controlled experiments that separate context-window size from raw capability.

Try the ALTK-Evolve library — which includes the extraction, consolidation, and retrieval pipeline used here — or read the full technical report for the complete method and ablations.

AppWorld tasks are graded by two metrics, both reported as percentages (higher is better):.

Recent findings suggest that TGC — Task Goal Completion. The share of individual tasks the agent completes fully and correctly. This is the headline "did it get the job done" number.

SGC — Scenario Goal Completion. A stricter, all-or-nothing metric. Each scenario bundles several variants of the same task (the same request with different data, phrasing, or edge conditions). SGC counts a scenario as passing only if the agent succeeds on every variant. It measures reliability — an agent that solves a task most of the time but fails on one variant scores on TGC but not on SGC.

Recent findings suggest that really interesting take on agentic memory. The idea that memory needs to be calibrated to the model rather than simply accumulated is especially useful for production systems. Selective retrieval also seems like a practical way to improve reliability without unnecessarily increasing context and inference costs. It makes a strong case for thoughtful custom AI agent development and enterprise AI agent solutions, where memory, performance, and cost all need to be designed together. https://mobisoftinfotech.com/services/ai-agent-development-tech giant.

#23511. Industry News: Nvidia’s journey to forge the one CPU SKU to rule them all

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1001 w)
