📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This guide is a brief(ish) introduction to the Jujutsu (jj) version control system (VCS) for someone familiar with Git.

According to recent reports, jj provides primitives for version control that are simple to learn, but elegantly compose into powerful workflows. Features like automatic rebase and native undo soften the sharp edges of Git. Eventually, you’ll organically discover latest powerful workflows that would be too cumbersome to attempt with most other VCS tools.

In a recent development, if you work in a Git repository, you can try it today. Jujutsu and Git can be used side-by-side in the same repository, so you can try out jj on a git repo on your own, without fully ejecting from git.

Personally, I think jj considerably boosts my effectiveness, because it allows me to keep VCS bookkeeping out of my working memory. Automatic rebasing also makes stacked diff workflows quite easy, and reduces thrashing of my working memory. It’s also just a fun tool to use.

Official installation instructions are here, but here are a few common methods:.

In an existing git repository, run:.

From here on, jj and git repo state will be synchronized automatically.

To set your user details globally, run commands like these:.

You can edit jj’s TOML configuration for your user in an editor with:.

It has been revealed that in addition to the --user scope, jj config also has --repo and --workspace scopes. View the merged config with:.

Industry observers note that A commit, also called a revision, is essentially the same thing as a git commit. It represents a snapshot of repository state that descends from one or more parent repository snapshots. It is often visualized as a diff against a singular parent commit, or in the case of a merge commit, the diff against multiple parent commits once merged.

Recent findings suggest that when using a Git repo backend, the jj commit ID is the same as the git commit ID: a hash formatted as a hex string. In the output of jj log below, the hex hashes 2bea5e3d and 849165bc on the right are commit IDs.

According to recent reports, the IDs on the left hand side (royxmykx and kpqxywon) are change IDs, which are stable identifiers for logical changes as they physically evolve over time. We’ll discuss these more in the next section.

It has been revealed that commit IDs and change IDs can be referenced in shorthand with an unambiguous (unique) prefix. jj helpfully highlights the shortest unique prefix of most IDs to make it easy to type them manually. For example, instead of copying and pasting kpqxywon, we can type in a prefix, down to the shortest unique prefix k.

We can inspect the commit 2bea5e3d with jj show, using its short prefix 2.

Recent findings suggest that many folks configure a custom diff formatter, like Delta. See configuration docs if you’re interested.

Let’s take another look at our commit graph:.

Industry observers note that on commit 849165bc, you’ll see the symbol @ on the graph node. This represents a snapshot of our working copy, or the code we have actually checked out in our local directory. We can inspect this special commit pointer in a variety of ways:.

Sources indicate that jj show demonstrates commit details and a diff, which is empty here. $ jj show Commit ID: 849165bca19639dbd6ccb53e8c1340e78c36d59a Change ID: kpqxywonksrltlrkyqukqqsxpltznztk Author : Ethan Lowman (2026-11-15 12:17:12) Committer: Ethan Lowman (2026-11-15 12:17:12) (no description set).

According to recent reports, jj status indicates repo state with diff stats. $ jj status The working copy has no changes. Working copy (@) : kpqxywon 849165bc (empty) (no description set) Parent commit (@-): royxmykx 2bea5e3d main | Adjust config.

Recent findings suggest that jj diff works much like git diff. Its output is empty here, since there are no changes in the current working copy relative to the parent commit.

This output isn’t very interesting, since @ has no changes. Let’s make an example change to see what happens. If we edit main.py and rerun jj show, we see this:.

You’ll notice several things have changed. The working copy has been automatically committed, and @ is no longer marked (empty). The new commit ID for @ is 66b59f20, since we’ve added changes, but the change ID for 66b59f20 is still kpqxywon. jj has no staging area like in git, so we don’t have to manually add files. When we run a jj command to inspect or modify repo state after editing files, jj automatically snapshots the working copy as a new physical commit for the relevant logical change.

It has been revealed that let’s give this change a description (also called a commit message). We can either run jj desc, which opens an editor, or provide it directly with -m.

Notice again that the commit ID has changed, since the hash covers the commit message, but the change ID has remained stable.

Now, let’s say we’re ready to use this fresh feature, and we want to organize that change in a separate commit. We can create a new commit with jj new:.

Recent findings suggest that we’ve created an empty change nlrtlrxv on top of kpqxywon. jj status reflects that we are editing this upcoming revision which does not yet differ from its parent.

Recent findings suggest that jj commit is a shorthand for this common jj desc and jj fresh combo. Let’s make another change to use our new feature, and commit it.

To inspect the commit we just created (n), we can no longer use the bare jj show, which defaults to showing @. We have to pass the revision we want to inspect:.

It has been revealed that we can describe empty commits to record intent before starting work. Let’s create a newly introduced commit on top of k to remind ourselves that we need to document the feature.

It has been revealed that A separate jj desc would also work just fine instead of the -m flag on jj upcoming. Here’s the current commit graph:.

In a recent development, note how we’ve created branching commits without creating a named branch. This highlights a major difference between jj’s branchless model and git’s branch-centric model of organizing work streams. Instead of juggling your work-in-progress on branches, you work on a graph of commits. Once ready to share, you push branches to a Git forge from your commit graph (more on that later).

A revset, an idea borrowed from Mercurial, is an expression that selects a set of revisions from the commit graph. Most jj commands accept revsets in their arguments. When we ran jj new k, the argument k was actually a trivial revset that resolved to the single change with ID kpqxywon. The jj log command has an -r flag that we can use to preview a revset. Some demonstrative examples follow.

Commits between r and @, inclusive:.

Commits authored by ethan@example.com that also have ID k or q:.

I’ll defer to the official documentation for exhaustive detail. The Revsets language specification is easily my most referenced jj documentation page, so I would recommend skimming it to see what’s possible.

Let’s say in the course of documenting our feature in qwyusntz we realized we made a mistake in the implementation in parent change kpqxywon. We don’t need to manually commit or stash changes to switch tasks. We simply switch our working copy to kpqxywon with jj edit:.

Our working copy once again highlights the changes from kpqxywon.

jj hasn’t lost track of the changes above our working copy, including our most recent edits to q:.

It has been revealed that instead of switching commits with jj edit k, we could have run jj edit @-. The revset @- is evaluated before switching the working copy, so this moves to the parent commit. The built-in commands jj next [--edit] and jj prev [--edit] provide another way to move up and down a stack of commits.

Industry observers note that if we edit files in the working copy, the descendant commits will be automatically rebased upon the next jj invocation. For example, if we edit my_new_feature’s implementation in main.py and then run jj log, we’ll see that changes k, n, and q all get newly introduced commit IDs. jj also tells us that it performed a rebase.

Industry observers note that if the automatic rebase happened to cause merge conflicts, jj doesn’t require us to fix them immediately, like git rebase would. Instead, jj records that the commit is conflicted and lets you carry on with your current task. This is massively helpful to reduce mental context switching, as your stacked commits grow more complex.

To view the conflicts, we can edit the conflicted commit….

In a text editor, we can resolve these conflicts, and the next time we run any jj command, we’ll see that jj has marked the commit as unconflicted:.

Let’s say we made a mistake in that conflict resolution, and we want to undo it. In git, undoing an action, if it’s even possible, is often complicated. In jj, we can always run jj undo:.

Industry observers note that more generally, jj maintains a history of all actions in jj op log. We can inspect this log and jj op restore to a point in that history, or jj op revert an individual operation. If the jj undo itself was a mistake, we can jj redo.

The Hint in the output above is a bit of a spoiler for our next topic, the squash workflow.

Editing commits that have descendants can sometimes feel sketchy. If you’re iterating on a large diff that has left your working memory, it would be nice to separate your new changes from the existing diff. For example, we might like to inspect the diff that resolves a rebase conflict in isolation.

It has been revealed that let’s follow the instructions from the above output. We first create a fresh commit on top of the conflicted commit:.

Now we can resolve the conflicts in main.py in our editor, and rerun jj log:.

We can inspect the diff in @ if we like, and when we’re happy with the conflict resolution, we can squash it into the parent commit:.

The conflict is now resolved, and we can continue our work.

Industry observers note that one of the powerful qualities of jj is that it makes diffs malleable like clay. With automatic rebase and the confidence inspired by jj undo, we can move, combine, drop, and split diffs with ease.

Let’s try a few operations on our current commit graph. Here’s the starting point.

Let’s use jj rebase to coerce our branching commit graph into a linear history. Let’s say the documentation commit (q) should go between the implementation (k) and the usage (n). We could accomplish this by moving nlrtlrxv (and its empty descendant) on top of qwyusntz:.

Sources indicate that another way to accomplish the same effect would be to use jj rebase -r q --before n. Many jj commands have multiple ways to specify revsets. jj rebase --help documents these well.

Since arguments to jj rebase flags are all revsets, we can write a revset that selects a sequence of commits or commit subgraph, and move it elsewhere in the graph.

If we wanted to insert a commit below k, the most direct way is jj new --before k, but for demonstration purposes, we could alternatively create a new commit on top of r and rebase k:: on top:.

If you enjoy using TUIs, jj arrange provides a commit graph editor similar to git rebase -i for reordering commits.

If we decided documentation should be in the same commit as implementation, we can squash:.

jj will open an editor and give us a chance to write a combined commit message.

Sources indicate that to drop a commit from the graph, we can use jj abandon. Let’s drop the preparation commit:.

To abandon parts of a commit (hunks or changes to whole files), we can use the jj diffedit TUI (see docs).

The jj split TUI allows us to take a commit and split it into two consecutive commits by selecting which files or hunks should go in the first. Let’s use it to split up implementation and documentation again with jj split -r k:.

The jj-hunk project provides a means to automate commit splitting. If you are so inclined, agents are quite good at using this tool to split up commits into a sequence of smaller changes for easier review.

According to recent reports, jj does not have a native concept of a branch, but it does have a primitive called bookmarks that map to Git branches. When we need to manipulate Git branches, we do it by way of bookmarks.

You can go pretty far using Git without realizing this, but a Git branch is just a pointer to a commit. jj explicitly models bookmarks this way. jj bookmarks are essentially a named label attached to a commit that we can move around as we modify our commit graph, and push to/pull from a remote.

We’ll discuss a few basic workflows around Git branches below, but you can find a more complete guide in the jj docs on Working with GitHub.

Assuming we initialized jj in a git repository that has remotes, we should have some output for jj git remote list.

Since jj is branchless, the commits we’ve created locally don’t have a branch name. Luckily, jj doesn’t require us to pick one, and generates one for us. Generated branch names free you from thinking of a unique branch name so you can instead focus on writing a good commit message (usually the more durable descriptor of a change).

To create a generated bookmark for change ID nlrtlrxv and push up a corresponding Git branch, we can run a command like the following:.

Now jj log demonstrates our change with a correspondingly named bookmark push-nlrtlrxvuusk associated:.

We’re free to create a PR from this branch on GitHub now. You can customize the bookmark naming scheme with the git_push_bookmark template config documented here. It’s a common pattern to format branch names like /.

Recent findings suggest that since jj git push -c creates a branch name that corresponds to a change ID, it seems to encourage one evolving change per PR. I think it’s usually best to lean into these ergonomics, and have one change per PR.

To update a branch, the general process is to either squash commits into a change that is already bookmarked, or create new commits and move the bookmark forward.

If you choose to squash commits into an existing bookmark (recommended to keep one change per PR), the flow is as follows.

Sources indicate that first, create a fresh commit on top of our branch. $ jj new push-nlrtlrxvuusk Working copy (@) now at: stzvpxow f14a0cf7 (empty) (no description set) Parent commit (@-) : nlrtlrxv b1284f61 push-nlrtlrxvuusk | Use the feature Added 2 files, modified 0 files, removed 0 files.

Then make our edits. $ jj status Working copy changes: M README.md Working copy (@) : stzvpxow 6bdd43dc (no description set) Parent commit (@-): nlrtlrxv b1284f61 push-nlrtlrxvuusk | Use the feature.

It has been revealed that squash them into the bookmark branch. $ jj squash --from @ --into push-nlrtlrxvuusk Working copy (@) now at: xryuuprx 04d65a03 (empty) (no description set) Parent commit (@-) : nlrtlrxv aeb869ae push-nlrtlrxvuusk* | Use the feature.

In a recent development, we now see push-nlrtlrxvuusk has an asterisk next to it, indicating it has changes that haven’t been pushed to the remote. So let’s push them. $ jj git push -b push-nlrtlrxvuusk Changes to push to origin: bookmark: push-nlrtlrxvuusk [move sideways from b1284f61c417 to aeb869aef99b].

According to recent reports, the remote branch now reflects the fresh changes. The above output notes that we moved the branch sideways from one commit to another commit, which reflects that we did a force-push. jj git push runs the equivalent of a git push --force-with-lease, so if you’re ever unclear about what a push operation would do, you can use the jj git push --dry-run flag. jj protects you against most dangerous force pushes refusing to rewrite a configurable revset of immutable commits. The default immutable revset is sensible, but you can make it more or less conservative by configuring your own immutable heads.

In this flow, we add latest commits on top of our bookmark and then move the bookmark to point to our new commit.

In a recent development, let’s first prepare the new commit. $ jj new push-nlrtlrxvuusk Working copy (@) now at: pptrztmx 6e49ff1f (empty) (no description set) Parent commit (@-) : nlrtlrxv aeb869ae push-nlrtlrxvuusk | Use the feature.

The bookmark does not automatically move to our fresh commit. This is the biggest difference between bookmarks and Git branches. For now push-nlrtlrxvuusk still points at the commit below:.

It has been revealed that there are several ways to move the bookmark to the upcoming commit. The easiest is probably jj bookmark advance, which moves the closest bookmark to the given commit:.

Now we’re ready to push the moved bookmark.

Since jj is branchless, strictly speaking, we don’t “check out” a branch, but we can create a commit on top of a remote branch. First do the equivalent of a git fetch, importing remote bookmarks:.

And create a upcoming empty commit on top of the remote branch:.

Recent findings suggest that our working copy now contains all the commits on the remote branch. However, if we were to drop back to git, we see that from git’s perspective, we’re in a detached head state, not on any branch.

This is because jj is editing a commit above a bookmark, and does not have an equivalent to git’s “current branch” state.

Syncing with the trunk (e.g. main) is just a specific example of this flow. We would jj git fetch to update our main to the upstream main, and then rebase our commits on top. For example, the following would rebase my-branch on top of a latest main:.

Recent findings suggest that jj commit graph manipulation is easiest when you have a live commit graph on screen. There are different ways you can accomplish this.

jjui is a TUI for jj that allows you to edit the visual graph directly. I have not personally used this, but I know people who like it.

I recommend filtering down this log to a revset that represents your current work. Here’s a starting point:.

You might also consider trying my experimental project jj-stamp, which is a local code review GUI for the squash workflow. Even if you don’t use the squash review workflow, it makes a pretty good diff viewer with a live jj log on the side and a terminal for running jj operations.

According to recent reports, one of the biggest productivity gains from jj comes in its ability to support stacked PR workflows. This merits its own post, so I’ll keep it short.

According to recent reports, large changes are easier to understand when they’re broken up into a series of logical steps. Breaking up a large change into smaller sequential atoms of review makes the whole change easier to understand. Stacked PRs attempt to leverage this fact to optimize merge throughput, while simultaneously removing pipeline stalls in the review process.

Let’s say we’re building a new feature. We can decide we want to split up implementation into three stages:.

Sources indicate that jj’s ability to work on stacked changes with automatic rebase is a natural fit for implementing these three stages. Each of the three stages maps to a single commit, each with an associated bookmark/branch/PR:.

After you implement the first change, you can put up a PR for review and immediately start working on the next change. Your work stream becomes a long queue where you pop off the bottom as PRs are ready to merge and push to the top, with no pipeline stalls.

It has been revealed that it’s pretty easy to manually set up small PR stacks with jj and GitHub, but once you get hooked on the technique (making stacks 5–10 PRs deep), you’ll want a tool. jj-pancake is my entry into the ring of stacked PR tools. More on that soon.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Drew DeVault has announced that Redict, a fork of Redis that was created in response to Redis's 2024 license change, has been deprecated.
  • I had hoped to rally the Redis diaspora around a copyleft initiative, to protect ourselves from future rug-pulls, and made Redict to serve this purpose.
  • We recommend that Redict customers switch to valkey, which uses a permissive license but has better long-term prospects.

Drew DeVault has announced that Redict, a fork of Redis that was created in response to Redis's 2024 license change, has been deprecated. He recommends switching to Valkey, the permissively licensed Redis fork supported by the Linux Foundation. The two projects are mutually compatible, so switching should be as simple as changing which package is installed and renaming the configuration file.

I had hoped to rally the Redis diaspora around a copyleft initiative, to protect ourselves from future rug-pulls, and made Redict to serve this purpose. However, with the valkey project's success, and Redis's return to a copyleft license, Redict was not able to build a sustainable community.

We recommend that Redict customers switch to valkey, which uses a permissive license but has better long-term prospects. We advise against switching back to Redis; though it is once again open source, and copyleft, it uses a contributor license agreement which will facilitate another rug-pull when Redis has a bad financial quarter.

Breaking: Granite 4.2 LLMs: How They're Built

📅 25 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2721 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A technical walkthrough of how we built the Granite 4.2 reasoning model family.
  • TL;DR: Granite 4.2 is our first family of dense, decoder-only reasoning LLMs, released in three sizes: 3B, 8B, and 30B.
  • According to recent reports, granite 4.2 is the reasoning-focused release of the Granite language-model family.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A technical walkthrough of how we built the Granite 4.2 reasoning model family.

TL;DR: Granite 4.2 is our first family of dense, decoder-only reasoning LLMs, released in three sizes: 3B, 8B, and 30B. These models are post-trained from Granite-4.1 base models. Granite-4.1 base models were pre-trained from scratch on roughly 15T tokens with a five-phase strategy that extends the context window to 512K tokens, supervised fine-tuned on chain-of-thought, reasoning, and agentic-trajectory data, then post-trained with a multi-stage reinforcement learning pipeline. That pipeline includes agentic RL, where the 8B and 30B models learn to act with tools inside real sandboxed environments. Every model has a thinking / non-thinking switch, a low-effort thinking mode that spends a short reasoning budget on easy questions, and native tool calling. All Granite 4.2 models are released under the Apache 2.0 license.

According to recent reports, granite 4.2 is the reasoning-focused release of the Granite language-model family. Earlier Granite releases were strong instruction-following assistants; Granite 4.2 adds explicit reasoning. Every model can produce a chain of thought before its answer and can run in thinking or non-thinking mode depending on how much deliberation a task needs. A low-effort mode falls between the two, spending a short reasoning budget on easy questions.

The three sizes (3B, 8B, and 30B) share the same architectural design and follow the same training pipeline (base model, SFT, then multi-stage RL), each at its own scale. All three are strong reasoners and instruction followers. The clearest capability split highlights up in post-training. The 8B and 30B models additionally go through an agentic RL block that teaches them to operate as agents: calling tools, editing and running code, driving a terminal, and searching the web inside real environments. Every model supports native tool calling. Served through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint (for example, with vLLM), it emits tool calls in the OpenAI function-calling format and plugs into agentic harnesses without extra glue. Granite 4.2 is also supported in SGLang, see the SGLang cookbook for a ready-to-serve recipe.

The rest of this post walks through the build: architecture, pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, the multi-stage RL pipeline, and results.

Granite 4.2 models are built on a decoder-only dense transformer architecture with the following core components:.

In a recent development, granite 4.2 models are post-trained from Granite-4.1 base models. Granite-4.1 base models were trained from scratch on approximately 15 trillion tokens using a five-phase training strategy. Phases 1–2 focus on foundational pre-training, phases 3–4 perform mid-training with progressively higher-quality data annealing, and phase 5 introduces long-context training, extending the context window to 512K tokens. Each phase uses a distinct data mixture and learning-rate schedule, gradually shifting from broad web-scale data toward more curated, high-quality sources.

The pre-training recipe closely follows the previous generation; for a detailed treatment of the data blend, phase schedule, and long-context extension, see the Granite 4.1 blog.

Industry observers note that supervised fine-tuning (SFT) turns the base model into a reliable instruction-following, reasoning, and tool-using assistant. The SFT data mixture combines agentic (31.6%) and non-agentic (68.4%) data, totaling approximately 7.2 million samples, or roughly 100B tokens, of which about 65B are trainable.

In a recent development, the agentic corpus covers a broad range of domains, including software engineering (SWE, 69%), tool calling (12.1%), terminal use (8.0%), math (3.5%), search (0.8%), and action (0.2%). These samples and trajectories are generated using a diverse set of agent scaffolds and harnesses, including OpenHands, OpenCode, Terminus-2, SWE-agent, OpenResearcher, MiniSWE, OpenSeeker, EnvScaler, Gemini CLI, Hermes, Codex, and Goose. The agentic data combines samples from both open-source datasets and our own synthetically generated RL environments, spanning a variety of agent–harness combinations.

The non-agentic corpus consists of several major categories: instruction following (18.8%), coding (18.8%), math (14.6%), multilingual (7.0%), science (5.4%), reasoning (3.0%), and safety (0.8%).

We apply multiple stages of quality control before a sample enters the final SFT mixture. First, data from different sources is normalized and reformatted into a consistent OpenAI Chat format, making the conversation structure and tool interactions uniform across datasets and scaffolds.

We then use GPT-OSS-120B and Gemma 4 as LLM-based judges to assess sample quality. Low-scoring samples are removed, as are samples containing hallucinated or fabricated information, invalid tool interactions, or tool calls to functions that are not defined in the corresponding tool list. Several targeted, dataset-specific heuristic rules are also applied where appropriate to further improve quality and remove known sources of noise.

Sources indicate that finally, we perform both local and global deduplication. Deduplication is based on SHA-256 hashes computed over the combination of the tools and messages fields, removing duplicate samples both within individual data sources and across the overall SFT mixture.

The complete corpus is first globally shuffled to reduce ordering effects and ensure that samples from different domains are well mixed during training. The shuffled corpus is then partitioned into equally sized .parquet shards, which are tokenized using the model's tokenizer and chat template and prepared for large-scale distributed training.

Before launching the final large-scale runs, we tune hyperparameters on representative configurations, sweeping learning-rate schedules, initial learning rates, and warm-up ratios to find settings that train stably across model sizes. The final training configuration is summarized below:.

Recent findings suggest that for the 30B model, we additionally perform a second phase of SFT focused specifically on agentic coding. In this phase, agentic, SWE, and coding data are upsampled to increase their effective contribution to the training distribution, while approximately 16% of the mixture is retained as replay data from the original SFT corpus.

According to recent reports, the 30B model is then fine-tuned for roughly one additional epoch at a lower learning rate of 3.0e-6. This targeted second phase increases the model's exposure to agentic coding trajectories without discarding the capabilities acquired during the initial SFT phase.

Industry observers note that after SFT, we apply a multi-stage, multi-environment reinforcement learning pipeline. Rather than a single RL pass, we run a chain of focused stages spanning many environments: math, code, science, instruction following, tool use, and structured output, then software engineering, terminal use, and web search. Each stage is an independent RL run that targets one capability and warm-starts from the previous stage's checkpoint.

Figure 1. The staged RL curriculum. Foundational RL (verifiable rewards + skill boosters) runs for all sizes; the agentic RL block (SWE → Terminal → Search) runs for 8B and 30B only. Every model finishes with RLHF. Each stage is a separate GRPO run that warm-starts from the previous checkpoint.

It has been revealed that every stage trains with asynchronous GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization), so the generator and trainer halves of the loop never block on each other. A pool of generation workers keeps sampling responses and dropping the finished trajectories into a shared buffer; once the buffer holds a full step's worth, the trainer pulls that batch, takes an optimizer step, and streams the updated parameters back to the generator workers without pausing them. A refresh can land partway through a rollout, leaving a single trajectory stitched together from two adjacent policy versions. We allow this instead of paying to prevent it: the workers reuse their existing KV cache rather than rebuilding it after each refresh, and the one guardrail is a limit that keeps them from drifting more than a single update behind the trainer, which bounds how off-policy any sample can get. Whatever mismatch survives that limit is handled in the objective by truncated importance sampling, which clamps the train-versus-generation log-probability ratio to a fixed ceiling so a handful of stale tokens cannot dominate an update.

Industry observers note that advantages are group-relative with a leave-one-out baseline: each response is judged against the mean reward of the other samples drawn for the same prompt, which removes the need for a separate value network. To make this concrete, take RLVR, the first and longest-running stage: each step pairs 256 prompts with 16 sampled responses apiece for a 4,096-example batch, which the trainer consumes in a single optimizer step before the next rollout begins. Later stages keep this machinery unchanged and adjust only the per-stage shape, shown next.

The pipeline keeps a common backbone of hyperparameters across every stage, which makes the curriculum easier to run and compare. A handful of knobs are fixed everywhere:.

What changes from stage to stage is the shape of each run: how many prompts and generations per step, how long the context is, whether the agent loop runs, and how hard we pull back toward the reference policy. The table below gives the exact settings for the 30B chain, stage by stage:.

Parameters shown for the 30B model. Global batch size = prompts/step × generations/prompt (e.g. 256 × 16 = 4096 for RLVR). The 3B and 8B models use the same recipe and hyperparameters with fewer stages (see How the Three Sizes Differ); the stage list is what changes, not the knobs.

Industry observers note that the KL schedule follows the reward type: explore freely where the reward is objective and verifiable (RLVR and SWE 2 run at KL 0), and stay close to the reference where the objective is preference, safety, or a narrow skill graft (RLHF and the code booster use KL 0.05). The rollout-turns column counts the environment interactions GRPO itself sees per rollout. In every case the model is trained on complete, real-environment trajectories.

Each stage is a separate RL run with a single objective and its own reward signal. When it finishes, its policy is exported to Hugging Face format and becomes the base model for the next stage, so the pipeline is a sequence of warm-starts:.

Sources indicate that the 8B and 30B models follow the full ladder. The 3B model takes a shortened path: foundational RL and alignment, without the agentic block.

A stage is defined mostly by how it is rewarded. Across the pipeline there are three reward types, and a single stage can use more than one:.

Verifiable rewards are objective and hard to game, so the pipeline front-loads them. Judge- and preference-based rewards handle open-ended qualities that no checker can express. Agentic-outcome rewards are the sparsest: often a single bit at the end of a long tool-use trajectory.

RLVR is the foundational stage and the broadest data mix in the pipeline: a single blended dataset spanning many verifiable domains.

Sources indicate that each task type carries its own verifier, so the reward is grounded per example. RLVR runs for two rounds on 3B and 8B, and three on 30B. Each round is a fresh warm-started run on a re-weighted mix of public and internally curated RL data.

After RLVR, a few short booster stages sharpen specific capabilities that benefit from concentrated training focusing on the following domains:.

In a recent development, boosters are small, focused runs. A light KL penalty keeps the model close to its current behavior while nudging one skill.

In the agentic stages the model learns to act: call tools, observe results, and iterate inside a real environment, rewarded on whether the task was actually solved. These stages share the same shape: multi-turn tool use, real (not simulated) environments, sparse outcome rewards, and GRPO, warm-started from the coding-boosted checkpoint. They run in order: SWE → Terminal → Search.

In a recent development, figure 2. The three agentic-RL environments. Each pairs a real harness with a real environment and a sparse, outcome-based reward. The 3B model runs none of these.

The final stage of every model is RLHF for human preference and safety. It optimizes against a generative reward model (GenRM) for preference, plus a safety reward covering jailbreak resistance and appropriate refusals. This stage uses the highest KL penalty in the pipeline, aligning tone and safety without eroding the capabilities the earlier stages built. In addition to human preference and safety alignment, this stage also applies a reasoning-length penalty to discourage overly verbose reasoning behavior acquired during earlier stages.

Same method and infrastructure; the difference is how far up the ladder each model goes.

3B is a strong foundational-RL model; 8B and 30B add the agentic-RL block on top, learning to act with tools in real environments.

Reinforcement learning at this scale needs infrastructure that can drive a training loop and a fleet of live environments at the same time. This matters most in the agentic stages, where every training example is a multi-turn rollout that edits code, runs commands, or browses the web. Granite 4.2's RL runs on two open components: NeMo-RL on the training side and NeMo-Gym on the rollout side.

Industry observers note that figure 3. The RL system. NeMo-RL drives the GRPO loop (Megatron-Core training backend, vLLM generation, and Megatron-Bridge for HF⇄Megatron weight conversion). NeMo-Gym orchestrates rollouts and hosts the tools, sandboxes, and reward/verifier calls as pluggable Resources.

That uniformity is what makes the staged curriculum above practical: a booster's rule-based checker and a full SWE sandbox present the same interface to GRPO.

This split is also what makes the asynchronous training loop described above physically possible: generation and policy updates live on separate GPU pools, so the expensive generation fleet — including the live agentic environments — stays busy instead of idling through optimizer steps.

Granite 4.2 was evaluated across agentic coding, general agentic and tool use, reasoning, chat and instruction following, and long context. The full benchmark table is below, followed by charts that break out the headline results by model size.

Supported languages: English, German, Spanish, French, Japanese, Portuguese, Arabic, Czech, Italian, Korean, Dutch, and Chinese.

The charts below break these results out by capability area.

Figure 4. Reasoning (pass@1). Scores rise consistently with model size across math (AIME25, HMMT), science (GPQA), and code reasoning (LiveCodeBench, SciCode).

Figure 5. Agentic coding resolve rates. The agentic-RL block is trained only for 8B and 30B; the 30B model leads across SWE-Bench variants and Terminal-Bench.

Recent findings suggest that figure 6. General agentic and tool-use benchmarks, reported for all three sizes.

According to recent reports, we also released four quantized variants of the Granite 4.2 models for inference with vLLM. The models are converted to FP8, NVFP4, and MXFP4 using LLM Compressor, and to the GGUF format using the llama.cpp framework for reduced-memory deployment.

The FP8 version is quantized with dynamic per-channel weights and per-token activations. No calibration is used.

The NVFP4 and MXFP4 versions are quantized using GPTQ calibrated on 2K samples drawn from the SFT dataset. Max context length is 2K during calibration.

Conversion of the Granite 4.2 models to GGUF is done with the canonical llama.cpp tool as described in https://github.com/IBM/gguf#gguf-conversion--quantization.

Several GGUF formats are provided:.

We trained the Granite 4.2 language models on an NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 cluster hosted by CoreWeave, featuring:.

This infrastructure delivers the high-bandwidth, low-latency communication required for efficient large-scale distributed training.

Sources indicate that the training software stack is packaged into .sqsh container images, each giving a run a reproducible, portable environment with its SBSA-compatible CUDA targets, Linux aarch64 Python wheels, and GPU-specific binaries pinned. The large-scale SFT runs build on an NGC PyTorch base image (Ubuntu 22.04, CUDA 12.8, Python 3.12); the RL stack runs in its own NeMo-RL container.

In a recent development, granite models support tool calling with integrated reasoning: the model reasons about which tool to call and why before calling it. Tools are defined with the OpenAI function definition schema.

Granite models can serve as the backbone for agentic coding tools. Because they support reasoning and tool calling through the OpenAI-compatible API, they integrate with popular agentic harnesses without extra adapters. Start the vLLM server, then follow the harness-specific instructions below.

OpenCode is an AI coding agent that runs in your terminal.

Configure ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json:.

For full documentation, see opencode.ai/docs.

It has been revealed that pi is a minimal agent harness for AI-powered coding that runs in your terminal. It supports custom providers via a models.json configuration file.

Configure ~/.pi/agent/models.json:.

Then select the granite-4.2-30b model with /model or Ctrl+L in the interactive session.

For full documentation, see pi.dev/docs.

OpenHands is an AI software engineer that can blueprint, write code, and execute commands.

Install and launch OpenHands following the official installation guide.

Configure the LLM in the OpenHands settings with:.

Note: The openai/ prefix is required when connecting to OpenAI-compatible endpoints like vLLM. Refer to the OpenHands local LLM documentation for detailed setup instructions, troubleshooting, and alternative installation methods.

#23497. QCon San Francisco 2026: Use AI to Multiply Your Team as a Staff Engineer

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (873 w)

QCon San Francisco 2026: Use AI to Multiply Your Team as a Staff Engineer

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (873 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News QCon San Francisco 2026: Use AI to Multiply Your Team as a Staff Engineer.
  • Nov 19, 2026 4 min read.
  • At QCon San Francisco 2026, Jordan Cutler, Senior Staff Engineer and Web Platform Tech Lead at Pinterest, presented how the role of a staff engineer changes when every engineer has access to the same AI tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News QCon San Francisco 2026: Use AI to Multiply Your Team as a Staff Engineer.

Nov 19, 2026 4 min read.

At QCon San Francisco 2026, Jordan Cutler, Senior Staff Engineer and Web Platform Tech Lead at Pinterest, presented how the role of a staff engineer changes when every engineer has access to the same AI tools. The session argued that most "AI for engineers" content focuses on individual productivity, while the real question for staff engineers is where their leverage comes from now. According to Cutler, AI did not change what a staff engineer is for, but it changed where the leverage is.

The talk opened with a reflection on Cutler's previous conference talk, where he demonstrated how AI could turn a four-hour task into four minutes. At that point he was shipping roughly as much as his whole team, which he described as multiplying himself rather than his team. That framed the central question of the session: what does a 10x engineer look like when everyone has AI?

Industry observers note that to illustrate why this matters, Cutler shared internal Pinterest data on merged pull requests per engineer per week between Q1 2025 and Q3 2026. The top 10% of engineers went from 6.7 to 11.3 merged PRs per week, a 68% increase, while the bottom half went from 1.0 to 1.15, an increase of 14%. Everyone has AI, but not everyone uses it the same way, and the gap keeps growing. The presentation organized the response to that gap into three moves: multiply yourself, multiply your team, and multiply the system.

The first move, multiply yourself, is about going first. Cutler explained that he tries fresh tools before his team does, and that part of that work is hitting dead ends so others don't have to. He mentioned examples such as an agent harness that could not be steered mid-task and a remote agent runner that required too many follow-ups. Sharing those findings early means the team does not lose a week on the same experiments. Running many agents also revealed a new problem: he kept giving the same corrections in every session, such as avoiding em-dashes, adding a diagram to the PR description, and keeping pull requests small.

In a recent development, the second move, multiply your team, started from a limitation: the folder made him faster, but only he had it. With fresh people joining the team and a new area to ramp up on, Cutler found himself repeating the same comments in code review, such as asking why a value is null instead of fixing the cause, testing like a user would, and keeping PRs small. The talk emphasized that the value of encoding that judgment grows with every teammate who adopts it, compared to the flat curve of a single engineer working alone.

The third move, multiply the system, is about moving up a level. Cutler used the history of container shipping as an analogy: ports got better at loading cargo by hand, but the standard box changed the economics entirely, from $5.86 a ton to 16 cents a ton. At Pinterest, migrations were the cargo, one kind of change spread across hundreds of files and dozens of teams. Instead of running each migration by hand, the team built a system where a staff engineer points to a proposal and an example, an engineer puts it on a schedule, and an agent running in a sandbox splits the work into PRs team by team. A class component migration ran three to five times faster than by hand, in the background while teams worked on other things.

According to recent reports, the talk also covered what went wrong. One scheduled job looped and opened 16 PRs in two minutes, increasing CI wait times from under 30 seconds to 14 minutes. The lesson was not to wait for the perfect guardrail, but to ship a small one. Cutler encouraged attendees to find their own "any" problem: a first responder for any incident, a draft fix for any bug ticket, or an agent that triages any flaky test. Today, 40 engineers have scheduler jobs of their own.

Sources indicate that the results were significant. Using the same AI tools as other web teams, Cutler's team now ships about four times as much per engineer, without counting his own PRs.

The presentation concluded with practical steps: write down what you repeat, put it where people already work, and build for every case instead of one. Some parts of the job cannot be written down, like an honest conversation with a teammate who is struggling, and those remain the staff engineer's responsibility. As Cutler put it, a 10x engineer isn't ten times faster, they are the reason ten other people are. As AI agents become part of everyday development workflows, the role of senior engineers may increasingly shift from personal output toward encoding judgment into the tools, defaults, and systems that entire organizations use.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness.

Tech Report: Training and Finetuning Multi-Vector Embedding Models with Sentence Transformers

📅 26 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3733 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for a wide range of applications, such as retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, semantic textual similarity, and more.
  • Finetuning multi-vector models involves several components: the model itself, datasets, loss functions, training arguments, evaluators, and the trainer class.
  • Lastly, in the Evaluation section, I'll show you that my finetuned multi-vector-encoder/mLateOn-medical model, trained in 14.5 hours on a single RTX 3090 alongside this blogpost, easily outperforms every general-purpose retrieval model I could find on my medical retrieval evaluation: dense, sparse, lexical, and multi-vector alike.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for a wide range of applications, such as retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, semantic textual similarity, and more. Its v6.0 revision introduces a fourth model type: MultiVectorEncoder, for ColBERT-style late interaction retrieval, alongside a complete training approach for it. In this blogpost, I'll show you how to use it to finetune a multi-vector model that outperforms general-purpose retrievers on your data. This method can also train strong newly introduced multi-vector models from scratch. Everything below runs on pip install -U "sentence-transformers[train]".

Finetuning multi-vector models involves several components: the model itself, datasets, loss functions, training arguments, evaluators, and the trainer class. I'll have a look at each of these components, accompanied by practical examples of how they can be used for finetuning strong multi-vector models.

Lastly, in the Evaluation section, I'll show you that my finetuned multi-vector-encoder/mLateOn-medical model, trained in 14.5 hours on a single RTX 3090 alongside this blogpost, easily outperforms every general-purpose retrieval model I could find on my medical retrieval evaluation: dense, sparse, lexical, and multi-vector alike.

If you're interested in finetuning dense embedding models, sparse embedding models, or rerankers instead, then consider reading through my prior Training and Finetuning Embedding Models, Training and Finetuning Sparse Embedding Models, and Training and Finetuning Reranker Models blogposts.

It has been revealed that this blogpost is about training multi-vector models. If you want to learn how to use them, from loading and encoding to indexing in vector databases, see the companion Multi-Vector (Late Interaction) Embedding Models with Sentence Transformers blogpost.

A dense embedding model compresses a whole text into a single vector, and similarity is one dot product between two such summaries. A multi-vector model (also called a late-interaction or ColBERT-style model) skips that compression. It keeps one small vector per token and scores a query against a document with the MaxSim operator, where every query token finds its best-matching document token and the scores are summed. Token-level matching preserves exactly the fine-grained signals that a single vector has to average away, which usually means stronger retrieval, at the cost of a bigger index.

The companion Multi-Vector Embedding Models blogpost covers the architecture, encoding, scoring, and indexing in detail, so I'll keep this section short and get to the training.

It has been revealed that finetuning multi-vector models significantly improves their retrieval performance on your specific domain: the vocabulary, the query style, and the notion of relevance all differ between web search, legal discovery, code search, and scientific literature review. Because queries and documents are matched token by token, multi-vector models pick up fine-grained domain signals that single-vector models tend to average away, and they respond very well to even modest amounts of in-domain finetuning data.

It has been revealed that beyond that, most released retrieval models were configured for short passages. The classic ColBERT checkpoints truncate documents at 180 or 300 tokens, and many popular dense models at 256 or 512, because their MS MARCO-style training data rarely goes beyond that. If your documents are long, these models silently discard most of every document before scoring it. On my medical evaluation with passages averaging 941 tokens, I measured that this truncation costs up to 0.24 NDCG@10, considerably more than any difference between model architectures. When you train your own model, you configure the document length that your data needs.

According to recent reports, lightOn ran into this same dynamic with code retrieval, where general LateOn wasn't enough and they trained LateOn-Code. Your domain, whether that's medical, legal, financial, or your firm's internal documents, is not getting an official model. This blogpost indicates you how to build it yourself, in a matter of hours, on a single consumer GPU.

Training MultiVectorEncoder models involves the following components:.

Let's take a closer look at each component.

Multi-vector training gives you a real choice of starting point, and it matters more than you might expect.

If you want to further finetune an existing multi-vector model, you don't have to worry about the architecture at all:.

The checkpoint brings its own recipe along: its query and document marker tokens, its projection head, its scoring skiplist. For finetuning, you generally want to keep all of that and change only what your data demands. The first thing to check is the length configuration, since many released checkpoints cap documents at 180 to 512 tokens (see Why Finetune?), and my medical passages run to 1,400 tokens. The mLateOn family already serves the backbone's full 8192 token context, but if your starting checkpoint carries caps, lift them:.

With the per-task caps unset, truncation falls back to the tokenizer's model_max_length, which is why I configure that limit at load time above.

I made one more change, adding a punctuation skiplist that excludes punctuation tokens from document-side scoring and storage. In a 4-way ablation (none, punctuation, stopwords, both) it modestly won on quality, and it shrinks the document index by 9.6% on this data for free:.

You can also point MultiVectorEncoder at any base transformer, and a fresh, randomly initialized token-level projection is appended for you:.

Recent findings suggest that that's the classic ColBERT pipeline: a Transformer producing contextualized token embeddings, a token-level Dense projecting each of them down to 128 dimensions, a MultiVectorMask deciding which tokens count during scoring, and a token-level Normalize. The projection starts random, so training is required before this model is useful. Interestingly, this works with strong dense embedding backbones too. A fresh projection on Alibaba-NLP/gte-modernbert-base reached within 0.03 of the existing-checkpoint starting points in my experiments, from nothing but the projection and 25k training pairs.

The classic ColBERT tokenization tricks ([MASK] query expansion, [Q] / [D] prefix tokens, a document length cap, a punctuation skiplist) are all off by default and configurable. See Creating Custom Models for the full set. For what it's worth, I tested [MASK] query expansion in four configurations for my domain finetune and none of them made a measurable difference, so don't feel obliged to reach for the classic recipe.

I measured this directly while preparing this blogpost, taking six starting points and training each with the identical recipe on 25k medical question-passage pairs from MIRIAD, then evaluating on 1,000 held-out questions against a 50,000 passage corpus:.

Sources indicate that the result surprised me, and it replicated across two model families. *The -unsupervised checkpoints adapt to a fresh domain far better than their finished siblings, overtaking them despite starting lower. These checkpoints sit after large-scale contrastive pretraining but before supervised finetuning on general retrieval, so they carry all the late-interaction structure with none of the general-purpose tuning that domain training then has to undo. The finished checkpoints, by contrast, barely moved or even regressed, at every learning rate I tried.

In a recent development, so, if the model family you like publishes a pre-supervised checkpoint, start there. If not, a fresh projection on a strong retrieval-pretrained backbone is a close runner-up. Continuing from a fully finished checkpoint is the weakest option for domain adaptation, despite being the most natural-feeling one.

According to recent reports, the MultiVectorEncoderTrainer uses datasets.Dataset or datasets.DatasetDict instances for training and evaluation. You can load data from the Hugging Face Datasets Hub or use local data in whatever format you prefer (e.g. CSV, JSON, Parquet, Arrow, or SQL).

Note: Lots of public datasets that work out of the box with Sentence Transformers have been tagged with sentence-transformers on the Hugging Face Hub, so you can easily find them on https://huggingface.co/datasets?other=sentence-transformers. Consider browsing through these to find ready-to-go datasets that might be useful for your tasks, domains, or languages.

You can use the load_dataset function to load data from datasets on the Hub:.

This is the dataset I'll train on in this blogpost: 4.4 million medical questions from MIRIAD, each paired with the source passage that contains its answer (averaging 941 tokens). Simple (query, relevant passage) pairs like these are the easiest retrieval training data to collect for your own domain, and as you'll see, they're all you need.

You can also use load_dataset for loading local data in common file formats:.

And if your local data requires pre-processing, you can use datasets.Dataset.from_dict to initialize your dataset with a dictionary of lists:.

It is important that your dataset format matches your loss function (or that you choose a loss function that matches your dataset format). Verifying whether a dataset format works with a loss function involves two steps:.

There are two multi-vector specific conventions on top of this:.

Loss functions quantify how well a model performs for a given batch of data, allowing an optimizer to revision the model weights to produce more favourable (i.e., lower) loss values. The right loss function for your task depends on the data you have and what you're trying to achieve. You can find a full list of options in the Loss Overview.

For the common case of question-answer or question-passage pairs, the workhorse is in-batch negatives training with MultiVectorMultipleNegativesRankingLoss, where every other document in the batch acts as a negative for each query. Bigger batches mean more negatives and stronger training, so in practice you'll want its GradCache variant, CachedMultiVectorMultipleNegativesRankingLoss, which decouples the effective batch size from what fits on your GPU:.

Sources indicate that the mini_batch_size parameter bounds the memory by encoding documents in chunks of this size, while the effective contrastive batch size (128 in my run below, and in my ablations bigger batches bought nothing further) stays a free choice. GradCache guarantees identical results regardless of the chunk size, so lower it for smaller GPUs at only a wall-clock cost. When your document lengths vary a lot, consider its sibling mini_batch_num_tokens, which packs each chunk to a total token budget instead of a document count, so a chunk of unusually long documents can never spike your memory (my mini_batch_size=16 at roughly 940 tokens per document corresponds to mini_batch_num_tokens=15_000).

One multi-vector specific trap is that the contrastive losses default to scale=1.0, unlike the dense embedding equivalent which defaults to scale=20.0. That 20.0 exists because a cosine similarity is a single value in [-1, 1], too narrow a range for a sharp softmax. A MaxSim score instead sums one best-match similarity per query token, so it already spans roughly [0, query_length]: a 32-token query can score up to 32. So don't copy scale=20.0 over from a dense training script, since it would saturate the softmax and kill your gradients.

For distillation from a stronger teacher, which is how the strongest general-purpose late-interaction models are trained, see MultiVectorDistillKLDivLoss and the Knowledge Distillation tab in the Training Overview documentation.

In a recent development, you can customize the training process using the MultiVectorEncoderTrainingArguments class. This class lets you adjust parameters that can impact training speed and help you understand what's happening during training.

Recent findings suggest that for more information on the most useful training arguments, check out the Multi-Vector Encoder > Training Overview > Training Arguments. It's worth reading to get the most out of your training.

Here's an example, using the values from my actual training run:.

A few of these deserve a comment:.

To track your model's performance during training, you can pass an eval_dataset to the trainer for evaluation loss, but concrete retrieval metrics are much more informative. Sentence Transformers includes the following built-in evaluators for multi-vector models:.

In a recent development, for domain finetuning, the MultiVectorInformationRetrievalEvaluator built from your own held-out data is the one that matters. One tip on constructing it is that the corpus should be hard enough that models can be told apart. In my case the MIRIAD questions are generated from their own source passages, which makes retrieval unusually easy. Against just the 10k gold passages, nearly every model scored above 0.97 NDCG@10. If your evaluation saturates like that, add distractor passages (I use deduplicated passages from the training split) until the scores spread out:.

The MultiVectorEncoderTrainer is where all previous components come together. Here is the complete script that trained multi-vector-encoder/mLateOn-medical, the model from the introduction:.

Industry observers note that that's the whole recipe: a pre-supervised checkpoint, a million domain pairs, in-batch negatives, full document length, and a higher-than-usual learning rate. The run took 14.5 hours on my single RTX 3090 at a peak of 17.5 GB VRAM, and every one of those choices was the winner of a measured comparison rather than a guess.

Recent findings suggest that for readers on smaller budgets, my scaling experiments put 100k pairs (75 minutes of training) within 0.012 NDCG@10 of the full million-pair run. Most of the gain comes in the first hour.

The MultiVectorEncoder trainer supports various transformers.TrainerCallback subclasses, including:.

It has been revealed that enable these via the report_to training argument, e.g. report_to=["wandb", "codecarbon"], with the required dependencies installed. It defaults to "none", and report_to="all" activates every integration whose dependency is installed.

Refer to the Transformers Callbacks documentation for more information on these callbacks and how to create your own.

Typically, top-performing general-purpose models are trained on multiple datasets simultaneously. However, this approach can be challenging due to the varying formats of each dataset. Fortunately, the MultiVectorEncoderTrainer allows you to train on multiple datasets without requiring a uniform format. Additionally, it provides the flexibility to apply different loss functions to each dataset. Here are the steps to train with multiple datasets at once:.

Industry observers note that each training/evaluation batch will only contain samples from one of the datasets. The order in which batches are sampled from the multiple datasets is defined by the MultiDatasetBatchSamplers enum, which can be passed to the MultiVectorEncoderTrainingArguments via multi_dataset_batch_sampler. Valid options are:.

Recent findings suggest that to find out where the finetuned model stands, I evaluated it against over 50 retrieval model configurations across four architecture families on the MIRIAD evaluation set, built exactly as in the Evaluator section above, with 1,000 held-out medical questions searching 200,000 unique passages (the 10k gold passages hidden among 190k deduplicated distractors from the training split). This corpus is four times the size of the 50,000-passage one from Which starting point should you pick?, so scores are not comparable between the two tables.

The headline results, with the full table in the collapsible below:.

The finetuned model tops the table, beating the strongest zero-shot model of any architecture by +0.062 NDCG@10. In other words, the strongest zero-shot model returns the right passage as the very first hit for 75.8% of the queries, while the finetuned model does so for 84.9%, cutting the rank-1 error by more than a third.

It has been revealed that the architecture pattern is just as clear, with the top of the table exclusively late interaction. On long documents, one vector per token beats one vector per document, even at matched training and matched backbones. DenseOn and LateOn share training data and architecture except for the head, and the late-interaction sibling wins by +0.12, with the multilingual pair (mDenseOn and mLateOn) replicating this at +0.13. Scale doesn't rescue single vectors either. Qwen3-Embedding-4B, the strongest dense model with roughly 33x the active (non-embedding) parameters of mine, still stops 0.13 short, and the 8B version scores lower than the 4B.

BM25 also performs surprisingly well, beating every sparse model, every truncation-capped multi-vector model, and all but three dense models: the multi-billion Qwen3-Embedding-4B and 8B, and voyage-4-nano, which reads its full 32k token context to edge past by just 0.006. Don't expect that to transfer to your own data though. MIRIAD's questions are generated from the passages, so the lexical overlap between a query and its gold passage is far larger than in typical retrieval, and BM25's unlimited context length lets it use every one of those overlapping words while most neural checkpoints truncate. A BM25 baseline is cheap and always worth running, just don't count on this margin.

The full field at a glance, sorted by score and colored by architecture family.

Models marked @N are evaluated with their document length cap lifted to N tokens, since their native caps (180 to 512 tokens) would otherwise truncate the 941-token average passages. For every multi-vector model this lift was worth +0.08 to +0.24 NDCG@10 over the as-served row, and even the dense DenseOn gained +0.03 from the same treatment.

Recent findings suggest that note that this does not mean that multi-vector-encoder/mLateOn-medical is the strongest model on all domains. It's simply the strongest in my domain. This is totally fine, as I just need this model to work well on my data.

It has been revealed that don't underestimate the power of finetuning multi-vector models on your domain. Fourteen and a half hours on a single consumer GPU produced a model that no general-purpose retriever comes close to on this data, and the recipe is a single script with no teacher model and no mined negatives!

The fair objection to multi-vector retrieval is index size, and this domain is close to the worst case for it. Storing one vector per token, my model needs about 878 vectors per passage, so the 200,000-passage corpus takes roughly 45 GB at fp16, where a dense model needs well under 1 GB. Document length is what makes that gap so wide. The Natural Questions passages in the companion post average about 125 token vectors each, seven times fewer, so a corpus of short passages starts from a far smaller index than this one does. The HierarchicalTokenPooling module compresses exactly this by clustering each document's token embeddings and storing the cluster means, keeping roughly 1 / pool_factor of the vectors:.

I measured it post-hoc on the finished model, with no pooling-aware training, and on long documents it is remarkably cheap.

Recent findings suggest that the solid points are uncompressed embeddings, so that every family is counted the same way and scored with exact search. You would not deploy any of them like that, though. Dense indexes routinely use int8 or binary quantization with rescoring, sparse indexes compress their postings, and multi-vector indexes use PLAID-style residual compression. Don't read those points as the disk you need to buy, but as relative storage cost.

Token pooling is the solid line. Halving the vector count costs 0.0033 NDCG@10 and leaves rank-1 accuracy untouched, and keeping only a quarter of them, at 11.2 GB, still scores 0.8991. The curve keeps going (I measured out to a tenth of the vectors, still at 0.8765) but there is little reason to push pooling that far once quantization is on the table, which is what the dashed line below is about.

Sources indicate that the dashed line is what a real deployment might look like. I gave Omar Khattab early access to the model and the benchmark, and he measured these configurations with fast-plaid at 1-bit residual quantization, using compact 17-bit centroid ids and 18-bit document ids instead of its ordinary unpacked 64-bit integers, plus document-side pruning:.

That first row is 13x smaller than the raw embeddings, for 0.0155 NDCG@10. That is a far better trade than anywhere on the pooling curve. Quantization shrinks each vector while pooling and pruning cut how many you keep, so they compose, and quantization is the one to reach for first. Push further and the last row lands at 1.45 GB, smaller than the fp16 embeddings of Qwen3-Embedding-8B (1.64 GB), while scoring 0.0895 higher. The objection that multi-vector indexes are too massive does not survive a properly configured index.

The pruning here is naive, meant only to establish that token reduction works on top of quantization, so read the bottom two rows as a floor rather than the frontier. If you would rather not hand-tune quantization at all, the Indexing section of the companion post covers fast-plaid, Qdrant, Weaviate, and Vespa.

Multi-vector retrieval is only as expensive as its index. The raw embeddings for this corpus are 45 GB, and a properly configured index is at least 7x smaller at nearly the same accuracy. The index deserves as much of your attention as the checkpoint.

Thanks to Omar Khattab for measuring the quantized and pruned index configurations in Optimizing the index, and for the discussions around late-interaction index costs.

These pages have training examples with explanations as well as links to training scripts. You can use them to get familiar with the multi-vector training loop:.

For further learning, you may also want to explore the following resources on Sentence Transformers:.

And here is an advanced page that might interest you:.

And the companion blogpost, covering everything about using these models:.

Finetuning multi-vector models involves several components: the model itself, datasets, loss functions, training arguments, evaluators, and the trainer class. I'll have a look at each of playfy these components, accompanied by practical examples of how they can be used for finetuning strong multi-vector models.

This is a really interesting deep dive into multi-vector embedding models... 🔥 The introduction of MultiVectorEncoder in Sentence Transformers v6.0 looks especially useful for ColBERT-style late interaction retrieval, where keeping multiple representations can capture much finer-grained matching than a single dense embedding. The fact that the same framework supports RAG, semantic search, and reranking makes this a very practical direction for modern retrieval systems. 🚀.

Industry observers note that I also like how the post breaks the finetuning process down into the individual pieces... datasets, loss functions, training arguments, evaluators, and the trainer class. 🧠 Having practical examples around each component makes the approach much easier to understand and reproduce, especially for people who want to move beyond using a general-purpose retriever and actually optimize a model for their own domain.

Sources indicate that the medical retrieval results are probably the most impressive part... 💡 Training the mLateOn-medical multi-vector encoder for just 14.5 hours on a single RTX 3090 and getting better results than dense, sparse, lexical, and other multi-vector approaches demonstrates how valuable domain-specific finetuning can be. It’s a great reminder that the biggest gains in retrieval often come from matching the model and training data closely to the actual search task rather than simply choosing the newest general-purpose model. 👏📚.

Recent findings suggest that overall, this is a great practical resource for anyone experimenting with advanced retrieval pipelines... ⚡ The ability to train strong multi-vector models from scratch as well as finetune existing ones opens up plenty of possibilities for specialized search and RAG applications. I especially appreciate that the whole workflow can be set up with sentence-transformers[train]... it makes an otherwise fairly complex retrieval training process feel much more approachable. 👍🤖.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

November 21, 2026 in release.

Announcing the release of Alice v0.6.0!

This change introduces several new features needed to build a small collection of packages from the Opam repository which I’ve been manually porting to Alice’s package format in alice-ports.

In a recent development, alice packages may now refer to modules from the standard library which are excluded from the prelude, such as Unix and Str. A new builtins section in Alice.kdl can be used to list the built-in modules a package can access:.

Industry observers note that packages may include C source files in their src directory. All C files will be compiled and linked into the resulting executable when building a project. The ability to compile C code raises the question of how to pass custom linker arguments to the C compiler, and this is addressed with another latest feature: config scripts.

Industry observers note that A package may include a config script in a file named config.ml file in the package’s root directory (next to Alice.kdl). The config.ml file is compiled and executed as the first step of building a package, and any lines in its standard output beginning with alice: are interpreted by Alice as directives that can influence the build. At the moment the only supported directives are alice:print_endline which prints a message, and alice:add_c_linker_args which adds C linker arguments.

Config scripts can depend on other packages, and also access built-in modules from the standard library. This can be configured in Alice.kdl:.

It has been revealed that config scripts are expected to be run only once each time they are compiled because their output can be trivially cached in the build directory. For this reason it’s faster to compile config scripts with the bytecode compiler rather than the native compiler, and of course this means compiling all their dependencies with the bytecode compiler too.

This was a necessary feature for allowing config scripts to be built with the bytecode compiler, but it might also be something people find useful to integrate into their workflow, since the bytecode compiler backend is generally faster than the native backend (but of course the executables it produces are generally slower to run).

Commands that compile code (e.g. alice build, alice run) now take a --backend argument which can be passed native or bytecode. The default is native.

On macOS and Linux, the latest version of Alice can be installed with Homebrew:.

Alternatively, on macOS and Linux, Alice v0.6.0 can be installed by running the install script:.

On NixOS, Alice v0.6.0 can be installed via the flake github:alicecaml/alice#alice_0_6_0.default, e.g.:.

Read more about installing Alice here.

In a recent development, xint is reporting that it has discovered a collection of five critical vulnerabilities in the NGINX web server. The worst flaw, it says, would allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute commands on an affected nginx server with HTTP/2 enabled. The organization also reports a local-privilege escalation (LPE) kernel vulnerability, which was introduced in the 4.15 kernel, in the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) subsystem. If chained with the NGINX vulnerability, it would allow an attacker to gain root privileges on the host. A kernel patch for this is not yet available.

Industry observers note that xint recommends updating to NGINX 1.31.9, which was just released, and to block the SCTP module on hosts that do not need it until a kernel fix is available. See the mitigations section of their report for more information.

Note: you can avoid this step in the future by logging into your LWN account.
